sources.title: What Is Your Agent's GPA? A Framework for Evaluating Agent Goal-Plan-Action Alignment
sources.abstract: We introduce the Agent GPA (Goal-Plan-Action) framework, driven by the fundamental insight that critical agent failures emerge at the intersections of setting goals, devising plans, and executing actions. We operationalize the framework with a factorized suite of LLM judges designed to measure distinct elements of Goal-Plan-Act alignment. To make this methodology scalable and generalizable across diverse agent architectures and datasets, we use state-of-the-art automated prompt optimization techniques to systematically generate domain-specific evaluation criteria. We validate this approach across three benchmarks: a multi-agent research setting (TRAIL/GAIA), a single coding agent setting (TRAIL/SWE-bench), and a private, enterprise data-agent setting (Snowflake Intelligence). Extensive evaluation on TRAIL/GAIA demonstrates the core validity of the framework, which identifies a broad range of agent failures (95% of human-annotated errors), localizes errors to enable targeted debugging (86% of human-annotated errors), and exhibits strong agreement with human evaluators. Crucially, by applying our automated methodology to both public datasets, we demonstrate that our GPA judges generally achieve the highest error coverage (ranging from 76% to 86%) in comparison to manual prompting approaches. We also leverage an evolutionary coding agent to improve judge consistency by up to 38% through iterative refinement of evaluation rubrics. Overall, Agent GPA provides a rigorous and generalizable paradigm for targeted agent evaluation.
sources.summary: It scores a trace as a goal, a plan, and actions, with a separate judge for each, instead of one score on the final answer. That split is Part 1's argument against final-answer scoring, and the shape of the Part 3 exercise.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Jia and colleagues introduce Agent GPA, short for Goal, Plan, and Action. It scores a running agent and also scores the pieces, rather than scoring only the final answer. That split is the Part 1 argument that one outcome is a weak test, and it matches Part 3, where tool choice, parameters, and response quality are separate questions.

## What they did

An agent sets a goal, makes a plan, and takes actions. The paper's claim is that serious failures sit inside those pieces and on the boundaries between them. One score cannot separate them. An agent can meet the user's goal by a wasteful path, or follow a plan that never addressed the goal.

They define seven metrics, and a separate LLM judge for each. A judge here is a prompted model that reads a trace and returns a score, with no reference answer. Goal Fulfillment asks whether the finished actions met the user's goal. Plan Quality and Tool Selection look at the plan: is it a workable decomposition, and is each tool, including the choice of no tool, the right one? Plan Adherence and Tool Calling look at execution: did the actions follow the stated plan, and were the arguments valid and the tool outputs read faithfully? Logical Consistency checks that each step is grounded in prior context and the system instructions. Execution Efficiency looks for redundant calls, and it still applies when the agent never wrote a plan.

{{figure:fig1-gpa-framework.png}}

Each judge prompt has two halves. The generic half defines the metric and stays fixed across datasets. The custom half describes the agent, adds one or two labelled examples from a development set, and sets the output format. The judge model is Claude 4 Sonnet. Scores run from 0 to 3.

They use three settings. TRAIL/GAIA is 117 traces from a manager agent and a search agent on GAIA questions, with expert-marked errors. TRAIL/SWE-bench is 31 traces from a coding agent that does not write a plan into the log, so they run only Logical Consistency, Execution Efficiency, and Tool Calling. Snowflake Intelligence is 17 production data-analysis traces, scored only on Logical Consistency and Execution Efficiency for the same reason.

## What they found

On the TRAIL/GAIA test split (59 traces, 281 human-marked errors), the seven judges together caught 95.0% of the errors (267 of 281). A single judge asked to do the whole job caught about 54% (151 to 154 of 281). Giving that single judge a description of the agent's control flow added about one percentage point. The gain comes from splitting the questions.

{{figure:fig2-error-coverage.png}}

Catching an error is a different task from pointing at the span that contains it. The GPA judges localized 85.8% of test errors (241 of 281). The stronger single-judge baseline localized 49.1%, and the original baseline localized 30.9%. The gap is widest on low-impact errors, the subtle ones: GPA recall was 80.7%, against roughly 23% to 30% for the baselines.

{{figure:fig3-error-localization.png}}

Every one of the 570 GAIA errors and all 239 SWE-bench errors fell under at least one GPA metric. On the GAIA test set the common ones were Logical Consistency (140), Tool Calling (128), and Execution Efficiency (119). Plan Quality was rare (14).

Agreement with a human score was 73.1% on TRAIL/GAIA, after they collapsed the 0–3 scale into three buckets, and 82.3% on the 17 Snowflake traces. Repeats of the same judge were stable and still not identical. Average Krippendorff's alpha, a chance-corrected measure of agreement, was 0.77 on GAIA. Plan Quality was the noisiest, at 0.628. A search that rewrote the prompt to reduce score variance (OpenEvolve) raised that alpha to 0.814, mostly by making the rubric more specific.

A prompt optimizer (GEPA) writing the custom half raised Plan Quality recall on GAIA from 52.4% to 76.2%. On SWE-bench traces the hand-written prompts had not seen, Tool Calling recall moved from 55.5% to 84.7%.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 3 can split a grade the way GPA does. Tool choice, tool arguments, and the quality of the reply are different questions. One prompt that asks all of them at once is the single-judge baseline this paper beats.
- If the trace contains no plan, do not score plan quality. They dropped the plan judges when the log had no plan.
- A judge prompt has a stable definition and a domain-specific half. Changing the domain half changes the measurement. That is a Part 2 point about rubrics, and a Part 4 point about prompt drift.
- Report agreement across repeats. An alpha of 0.77 still leaves disagreements a person should look at.
- Catching a known error is not the same thing as a calibrated score on a fixed scale. They still needed human error spans to check the judges.

## Limits

The GAIA traces were shortened to fit the context window, so the judge did not see the raw log. Snowflake is 17 traces from one product. The GEPA comparison on SWE-bench uses another LLM as a meta-judge to grade the judges. The middle scores, 1 and 2, were the fuzzy ones, which is why they also report a bucketed accuracy.

figures.alt: A three-circle Venn diagram labelled Goal, Plan, and Act. Numbered regions point to a legend: 1 Goal Fulfillment, 2 Plan Quality, 2A Tool Selection, 3 Plan Adherence, 3A Tool Calling, and 4 and 5 Logical Consistency and Execution Efficiency in the centre where all three circles overlap.
figures.caption: Figure 1 from Jia et al. (2025). Failures are placed at the intersections of goal, plan, and action, and each region gets its own judge.

figures.alt: Bar charts of error coverage. On the test set, GPA judges reach 80.7 percent on low-impact errors, 96.8 percent on medium, 100 percent on high, and 95.0 percent overall. Two monolithic baselines sit near 23 to 30 percent on low-impact errors and about 54 percent overall.
figures.caption: Figure 2 from Jia et al. (2025). Share of human-marked errors the judges caught. Splitting the rubric beats one judge asked to find every error.

figures.alt: Bar charts of error localization. On the test set, GPA judges localize 68.4 percent of low-impact errors and 85.8 percent overall. The original baseline localizes 30.9 percent overall, and the baseline given the agent's control flow localizes 49.1 percent.
figures.caption: Figure 3 from Jia et al. (2025). Share of errors the judge both caught and pinned to the right span in the trace.

sources.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: A General-Purpose Verification Framework
sources.abstract: Scaling pre-training, post-training, and test-time compute have become the central paradigms for improving the capabilities of LLMs. In this work, we identify verification, the ability to determine the correctness of a solution, as a new scaling axis. To unlock this and demonstrate its effectiveness, we introduce LLM-as-a-Verifier, a general-purpose verification framework that provides fine-grained feedback for agentic tasks without requiring additional training. Unlike standard LM judges that prompt LLMs to produce discrete scores for candidate solutions, LLM-as-a-Verifier computes the expectation over the distribution of scoring token logits to generate continuous scores. This probabilistic formulation enables verification to scale along multiple dimensions: (1) score granularity, (2) repeated evaluation, and (3) criteria decomposition. In particular, we show that scaling the scoring granularity leads to better separation between positive and negative solutions, resulting in more calibrated comparisons. Moreover, scaling repeated evaluation and criteria decomposition consistently lead to additional gains in verification accuracy through variance and complexity reduction. We further introduce a cost-efficient ranking algorithm for selecting the best solution among candidates using the verifier's continuous scores. LLM-as-a-Verifier achieves state-of-the-art performance on Terminal-Bench V2 (86.5%), SWE-Bench Verified (78.2%), RoboRewardBench (87.4%), and MedAgentBench (73.3%). Beyond verification, the fine-grained signals from LLM-as-a-Verifier can also serve as a proxy for estimating task progress. We build an extension for Claude Code, enabling developers to monitor and improve their own agentic systems. Finally, we show that LLM-as-a-Verifier can provide dense feedback for RL, improving the sample efficiency of SAC and GRPO on robotics and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
sources.summary: A verifier that uses the score-token probabilities, instead of one discrete integer, separates good and bad trajectories more reliably and ties less often. It bears on Part 2, where the scale is chosen, and on Part 4, where reliability and cost are the question.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Kwok and colleagues treat verification, the decision that a solution is correct, as something you can spend more compute on, separately from training a larger model. Part 2 asks when a model should check another model. Part 4 asks whether that check is reliable, and what the check costs.

## What they did

A usual LLM judge prompts a model to emit one score token, then keeps the single most likely token. That collapses the model's distribution into an integer, and close calls become ties. Their verifier reads the probabilities of the score tokens and takes the expected value. Averaged over criteria C, repeats K, and score tokens, the reward is the mean of p(v_g) times a number φ(v_g) for each token. Two continuous scores become a preference with a Bradley–Terry model, which turns a score gap into a probability that one trajectory beats the other.

The prompt asks for a score from 1 to 20. They use letter tokens rather than digits so the probability sits on one token. The experiments use Gemini 2.5 Flash, which returns up to 20 token probabilities. A trajectory is the full sequence of states and actions, including tool calls.

{{figure:fig2-framework.png}}

To pick a winner among N candidate trajectories without scoring every pair, they use a Probabilistic Pivot Tournament. A ring of comparisons puts every candidate once on the left and once on the right, which cancels the judge's habit of preferring whichever side is shown first. The remaining budget is spent on a small set of leading candidates. Cost grows like N times k, not N squared.

## What they found

On Terminal-Bench V2 they measure pairwise accuracy: how often the verifier scores a known-successful trajectory above a failed one for the same task. Three knobs each help, by a few points.

{{figure:fig4-scaling.png}}

Finer score tokens move accuracy from 73.1% at one token to 77.5% at 20. Repeating the evaluation moves it from 74.7% at one pass to 77.5% at 16. Splitting "is this correct?" into specification, errors, and output format scores 75.2%, 76.0%, and 76.4% alone, and 78.3% when the three are averaged.

The practical difference is ties. At one pass the discrete judge ties 26.7% of comparisons, and at 16 passes it still ties 5.5%. The continuous verifier ties none. One pass of the verifier matches 16 passes of the discrete judge, both at 74.7%.

{{figure:fig7-judge-vs-verifier.png}}

A single Terminal-Bench task makes the same point. Two agents rewrite a slow SQL query. The correct one waits for the original query and diffs the result. The incorrect one never checks equivalence on the real database. Over 100 repeats, a 1–5 discrete judge ties 88 times and ranks the correct trajectory higher only 12 times. Taking the expected value of that same 1–5 distribution removes the ties and ranks the correct one higher 69 times. A 20-point scale ranks it higher 77 times.

Used to select a trajectory, the verifier reaches 86.5% on Terminal-Bench V2 (the pool's pass@1 was 83.1%; an oracle that always picked the best of five would reach 92.1%), 78.2% on SWE-Bench Verified (pass@1 76.1%, oracle 84.4%), and 73.3% on MedAgentBench. On RoboRewardBench, preference accuracy is 87.4%, against 70.8% for a discrete LLM judge and 74.7% to 81.4% for trained robotics reward models. If an oracle could always pick the best trajectory from the whole Terminal-Bench leaderboard, 98.9% of tasks would be solved. The verifier is what stands between that ceiling and a single sample.

{{figure:fig1-results.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A judge that must print one integer throws away the rest of the distribution, and it ties. Part 2's choice of scale is this choice. A discrete grade is easier to read, and it discards the probabilities that would have separated close calls.
- Repeating the judge and splitting the rubric do different jobs. Repeats shrink variance. Separate criteria stop one vague question from dominating. Both cost extra calls, which is the trade-off among quality, latency, and cost.
- Position bias is large enough that they cancel it by swapping which trajectory is shown first. That robustness fix spends more calls.
- Choosing the best of several agent runs is a different use of a judge from scoring one reply against a rubric. The headline numbers are the first use. Part 3 is closer to the second: one trace, scored on tool choice, parameters, and response quality.
- The same score can track progress along a trajectory. The paper also feeds it to a reinforcement-learning update. The use that matters for this tutorial is the evaluation one: a fine score carries information a pass/fail label does not.

## Limits

The scaling gains are a few percentage points, not a new capability. The headline scores depend on the candidate pool and the harness: Terminal-Bench uses five samples from GPT-5.5 under the Capy scaffold, with Gemini 2.5 Flash as the verifier. The main method needs token probabilities. The verifier is another model, with its own errors, and an oracle still sits several points above it.

figures.alt: A diagram titled LLM-as-a-Verifier. Text, image, and video inputs enter a box with four knobs: uncertainty from token probabilities, score granularity, repetition, and decomposition into simpler factors. Outputs are test-time scaling, progress tracking, and reinforcement learning. A formula averages probabilities over criteria, repeats, and score tokens.

figures.alt: Three plots of pairwise verification accuracy on Terminal-Bench V2. Accuracy rises from 73.1 percent to 77.5 percent as score-token granularity goes from 1 to 20, from 74.7 percent to 77.5 percent as repeated evaluations go from 1 to 16, and from about 75 to 76 percent for a single criterion to 78.3 percent when three criteria are combined.
figures.caption: Figure 4 from Kwok et al. (2026). Each knob adds a few points of pairwise accuracy. The gains are real and they are small.

figures.alt: Two bar charts comparing a discrete judge and a continuous verifier. Accuracy is similar and a little higher for the verifier, from 74.7 percent at one pass to 77.5 percent at 16. The tie rate for the judge starts at 26.7 percent and falls to 5.5 percent. The verifier's tie rate is zero at every repeat count.
figures.caption: Figure 7 from Kwok et al. (2026). A continuous score removes ties that a discrete judge still has after many repeats.

figures.alt: Four bar charts. LLM-as-a-Verifier is the tallest bar on each: 86.5 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 78.2 percent on SWE-Bench Verified, 87.4 percent on RoboRewardBench, and 73.3 percent on MedAgentBench, ahead of the named baseline models on that benchmark.

sources.title: UMBRELA: UMbrela is the (Open-Source Reproduction of the) Bing RELevance Assessor
sources.abstract: Copious amounts of relevance judgments are necessary for the effective training and accurate evaluation of retrieval systems. Conventionally, these judgments are made by human assessors, rendering this process expensive and laborious. A recent study by Thomas et al. from Microsoft Bing suggested that large language models (LLMs) can accurately perform the relevance assessment task and provide human-quality judgments, but unfortunately their study did not yield any reusable software artifacts. Our work presents UMBRELA (a recursive acronym that stands for UMbrela is the Bing RELevance Assessor), an open-source toolkit that reproduces the results of Thomas et al. using OpenAI's GPT-4o model and adds more nuance to the original paper. Across Deep Learning Tracks from TREC 2019 to 2023, we find that LLM-derived relevance judgments correlate highly with rankings generated by effective multi-stage retrieval systems. Our toolkit is designed to be easily extensible and can be integrated into existing multi-stage retrieval and evaluation pipelines, offering researchers a valuable resource for studying retrieval evaluation methodologies. UMBRELA will be used in the TREC 2024 RAG Track to aid in relevance assessments, and we envision our toolkit becoming a foundation for further innovation in the field. UMBRELA is available at this https URL .
sources.summary: An open reproduction of a production relevance judge. Agreement with people on a single label is modest, while the ranking of whole systems stays highly correlated. A Part 2 example of a prompt and a scale, and a Part 4 reminder that those two agreements measure different things.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Upadhyay and colleagues release UMBRELA, an open-source reproduction of the LLM relevance judge described by Thomas et al. at Microsoft Bing. Part 2 needs a concrete judge, with a prompt and a scale, rather than only a benchmark paper. Part 4 needs the reminder that a copied judge can disagree with people on individual labels and still look fine when you rank whole systems.

## What they did

The task is graded relevance for search. A judge sees a query and a passage and assigns an integer from 0 to 3, the scale NIST assessors used for the TREC Deep Learning track: irrelevant, related but not an answer, a partial or buried answer, or a passage dedicated to the exact answer.

They re-label the human judgments (qrels) from TREC Deep Learning 2019 through 2023 with GPT-4o. The prompt is zero-shot, meaning instructions and no worked examples. It follows a DNA pattern: a description of the job, the query and the passage, and aspects the model should weigh. Those aspects are the searcher's intent, how well the passage matches it, how trustworthy the passage is, and a final integer. The prompt tells the model not to show its reasoning. Temperature is 0, top-p is 1, and the frequency penalty is 0.5. For 2022 and 2023, near-duplicate passages had inherited a human label, so they keep only the canonical passage of each cluster.

{{figure:fig1-prompt.png}}

## What they found

Label agreement with the NIST assessors is modest. Cohen's kappa, a chance-corrected agreement score, runs from 0.31 to 0.37 on the four-point scale, and from 0.42 to 0.50 after the labels are collapsed to relevant versus not (0 and 1 versus 2 and 3). The authors call this fair agreement. The confusion matrices show where the misses sit. The model recovers the human's non-relevant label (0) about 75% of the time. Accuracy against the human falls to about 50% for "related", about 30% for "highly relevant", and about 45% for "perfectly relevant".

{{figure:fig2-confusion.png}}

Rankings of retrieval systems tell a different story. They score each TREC submission with nDCG@10, a standard ranking metric that rewards relevant passages near the top of a list of ten, once with the human labels and once with the LLM labels. Kendall's tau between those two system rankings is 0.87 to 0.94, and Spearman's rho is 0.97 to 0.99. A judge can be a weak substitute for a human on a single passage and still preserve the order of systems.

{{figure:table2-agreement.png}}

Their spot checks on TREC 2019 show one reason disagreements happen. A passage about the Thai flag had a human label of 3 for the query "what is the daily life of thai people", and a CPAP passage had a high human label for a query about mechanical ventilation. The authors' reading is that the query was vague and the human label was hard to defend. That is a handful of passages, not a counted error analysis.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Agreement on labels and agreement on a leaderboard are different measurements. A high correlation of system ranks is not evidence that the judge matches people item by item. Part 4 should keep those two numbers apart.
- The rubric is the scale plus the instructions that tell the model how to use the middle grades. This prompt states the 0–3 meanings twice, in slightly different words. Copying one wording and dropping the other is a way for a judge to drift.
- This production-style judge is told to hide its reasoning and print only a score. Other judge designs ask the model to write the reason before the score. Both patterns exist. Hiding the reason makes the score easier to parse and harder to audit. Whether the judge shows its reasoning is a Part 2 prompting decision, and an audit question for Part 4.
- Temperature 0 did not make the labels match the humans. A deterministic decode is not a calibrated judge.
- The artifact is a toolkit other people can run. The paper exists because the Bing study did not leave one. A judge that cannot be re-run cannot be checked when the prompt or the model changes. Part 1's lifecycle versions the rubric and the judge for that reason.

## Limits

The task is passage relevance, not an agent trajectory. One model is tested, GPT-4o, on one family of TREC collections. Kappa in the low 0.3s is fair agreement, which is a long way from interchangeable with a NIST assessor. The case studies are a handful of passages the authors found striking. UMBRELA was later used to help the TREC 2024 RAG track; this paper does not report that deployment's error rate.

figures.alt: Five confusion matrices for TREC Deep Learning 2019 through 2023. Rows are the human label and columns are the LLM label, both from 0 to 3. The largest counts sit on the diagonal for label 0. Labels 2 and 3 spread into neighbouring columns.
figures.caption: Figure 2 from Upadhyay et al. (2024). Human label against GPT-4o label. Non-relevant passages match more often than the higher relevance grades.

figures.alt: A table of agreement for five TREC Deep Learning tracks. Four-scale Cohen's kappa is about 0.31 to 0.37. Binary kappa is about 0.42 to 0.50. Kendall correlation of system rankings is about 0.87 to 0.94, and Spearman correlation is about 0.97 to 0.99.

sources.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
sources.abstract: As AI systems become more capable, we would like to enlist their help to supervise other AIs. We experiment with methods for training a harmless AI assistant through self-improvement, without any human labels identifying harmful outputs. The only human oversight is provided through a list of rules or principles, and so we refer to the method as 'Constitutional AI'. The process involves both a supervised learning and a reinforcement learning phase. In the supervised phase we sample from an initial model, then generate self-critiques and revisions, and then finetune the original model on revised responses. In the RL phase, we sample from the finetuned model, use a model to evaluate which of the two samples is better, and then train a preference model from this dataset of AI preferences. We then train with RL using the preference model as the reward signal, i.e. we use 'RL from AI Feedback' (RLAIF). As a result we are able to train a harmless but non-evasive AI assistant that engages with harmful queries by explaining its objections to them. Both the SL and RL methods can leverage chain-of-thought style reasoning to improve the human-judged performance and transparency of AI decision making. These methods make it possible to control AI behavior more precisely and with far fewer human labels.
sources.summary: A short list of principles steers a model that critiques and revises another model. The pattern that matters for this tutorial is the rubric and the critique, which is how Part 2 writes a judge. The paper then uses those critiques as training data.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Bai and colleagues, at Anthropic, train a less harmful assistant using a written list of principles and model-written feedback. The training recipe, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, is the paper's method for building the assistant. The pattern it shares with an LLM judge is the part that matters here: a short rubric, then a model that applies the rubric and writes a critique. That is a Part 2 method, criteria plus a prompt that asks for a critique, and a Part 4 warning, because a principle that rewards refusal will treat evasiveness as harmlessness.

## What they did

Human oversight for harmlessness is a constitution: on the order of ten principles, plus a few examples used as a prompt. There are no human labels that say "this output is harmful." The principles were chosen informally for the research, and the authors say a real deployment should have them rewritten by a wider set of stakeholders. Helpfulness labels from people are still used. Harmlessness labels come from the model.

Training has two stages. In the supervised stage they start from a helpful-only model, sample a response to a red-team prompt (a prompt written to provoke a harmful answer), and have the model critique that response against a randomly drawn principle, then rewrite it. They repeat the loop and finetune on the final rewrites, so reinforcement learning starts from less harmful text.

In the reinforcement-learning stage they sample two responses, ask a model which is better according to a principle, and train a preference model on those AI comparisons mixed with the human helpfulness comparisons. A preference model is a scorer distilled from pairwise judgments. They then reinforce the policy against that scorer. Replacing the human harmlessness comparisons with model comparisons is RLAIF.

{{figure:fig1-process.png}}

Chain-of-thought, writing the reason before the decision, is used when the model compares two answers. Sampling several chains and averaging the probabilities gives a further small gain.

## What they found

Earlier helpful-and-harmless models had a tradeoff. Training for harmlessness made the assistant evasive: it refused, or it got stuck refusing, including on questions it could have answered by explaining the objection. Crowdworkers had been rewarding that evasiveness. In this paper the crowdworkers are told to prefer the less evasive reply when both replies are equally harmless.

On crowdworker Elo scores for 52-billion-parameter models, the constitutional RL models are less harmful at a given level of helpfulness than the human-feedback models. Elo here only supports comparisons. A higher number means crowdworkers preferred that model more often. The chain-of-thought constitutional run is the one they mark as a Pareto improvement: better on harmlessness without giving up the helpfulness of the human-feedback harmless model.

{{figure:fig2-elo.png}}

They also test whether a model can pick the better of two replies on 438 binary questions written to probe helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness, including cases where an evasive refusal is the wrong choice. A preference model trained on human feedback leads. A pretrained model asked the same question as multiple choice starts near chance at small sizes. With chain-of-thought, accuracy climbs with scale, and the authors read the curve as saying that models larger than 52 billion parameters would be competitive with the human-feedback preference model. Averaging five chains sits slightly above one chain.

{{figure:fig4-cot.png}}

Asking for a critique before the rewrite reduces harmfulness more than asking for a rewrite directly. That comparison is their Figure 7, which is not reproduced here.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A rubric can be a short list of principles. The judge is the model asked to apply one principle, often by writing a critique before it commits to a revision or a preference.
- The reason is part of the measurement. On their 438-question set, chain-of-thought is what moves the multiple-choice evaluator off chance as the model gets larger. Asking a judge for a reason can change the decision, not only the explanation.
- Substituting model labels for human labels does not remove the choice of principles. Someone still writes the constitution, and a small list is easy to inspect and easy to get wrong. Part 2's choice among rules, a judge, and a human does not disappear when the labels are written by a model.
- Evasiveness can look like harmlessness. If the rubric rewards refusal, the judge will like refusals. Their crowdworker instructions had to say otherwise, or the comparison was distorted. A judge that scores the surface of a refusal as success is a Part 4 failure mode.
- The same critique-against-a-principle step is used here to build training data. Read as evaluation, it is already a judge: a written criterion, applied by a model, with a written critique. The reinforcement-learning update that follows is the paper's training method.

## Limits

This is a 2022 training paper on Anthropic's own models, up to 52 billion parameters. It is not a study of judging agent traces, tool calls, or a fixed rubric on a shared test set. The Elo scores come from crowdworkers comparing open-ended conversations. The principles are a research choice, not a settled harm policy. The constitution-then-critique pattern is what transfers to judging. The reinforcement-learning procedure is a training method, and these results do not show that the same principles would grade an agent trajectory.

figures.alt: A flowchart of Constitutional AI. A helpful RLHF model generates responses to red-team prompts. A critique and a revision produce a finetuned supervised model. A second branch generates pairs of responses, collects constitutional feedback, trains a preference model, and runs RLAIF to produce the final model.
figures.caption: Figure 1 from Bai et al. (2022). The two stages: critique and revise, then preference labels from the model and reinforcement learning against those labels.

figures.alt: A scatter plot of harmlessness Elo against helpfulness Elo. Helpful-only and standard RLHF curves trade one off against the other. Constitutional RL, including a chain-of-thought run, sits above that tradeoff and is marked as a Pareto improvement.
figures.caption: Figure 2 from Bai et al. (2022). Crowdworker Elo for 52B models. Only differences are meaningful. Constitutional RL is less harmful at a given helpfulness than the human-feedback models.

figures.alt: A line chart of accuracy against model size on 438 helpful, honest, and harmless comparisons. A human-feedback preference model leads, near 0.79 at the largest size. Chain-of-thought and an ensemble of five chains climb from about 0.5 to about 0.74. A pretrained model without chain-of-thought stays near chance until the largest sizes.
figures.caption: Figure 4 from Bai et al. (2022). Chain-of-thought is what lets a language model approach a human-feedback preference model at picking the better reply.

sources.title: Where agent evals are going: Agent-as-a-Judge
sources.summary: An industry essay on judging an agent with another agent that can inspect the trajectory, rather than one prompt scored on the final answer. The post's chart puts that agent judge closer to human consensus than a plain LLM judge, on one coding benchmark, and then lists the reliability questions that remain.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Laurie Voss, writing for Arize, argues that agent failures live in the trajectory, so the judge has to be able to go and look. A single prompt that scores the final answer cannot see a bad tool call that the agent then papered over. That is Part 1's claim that final-answer scoring is a weak test of an agent. The post then asks what kind of judge can see the trace: a tool-using agent, rather than one more LLM call. That is a Part 2 choice among rules, a judge, and a human, with an extra option between the judge and the person. Part 4 is the question the post ends on: who checks that judge, and what it costs.

## What they did

This is an industry essay, not a new experiment. It retells one research result and then describes a product.

The research is Zhuge et al. (2024), "Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents," later accepted at ICML 2025. The post's account: the authors built DevAI, 55 software-development tasks, ran coding agents, and compared graders. A panel of human experts. A plain LLM judge. An agent judge with tools for finding files, reading code, and tracing requirements through the generated project. The chart is the post's summary of alignment with the experts' consensus, on OpenHands. The caption calls it a black-box setting: the judges see the task and the generated workspace, not a hand-collected trajectory.

{{figure:fig1-alignment.png}}

The rest of the post is the author's case for where this sits in a production stack, and a description of Arize shipping an agent judge in July 2026. The diagram contrasts one LLM call, wired to columns chosen in advance, with an agent that reads the trace at runtime and decides what to inspect.

{{figure:fig2-llm-vs-agent-judge.png}}

## What they found

The chart puts the agent judge at 90.2% alignment with the expert consensus, a plain LLM judge at 70.8%, and the average individual human expert at 85.7%. A vote of three humans sits higher, at 94.3%. The prose says the three experts disagreed with each other 10% to 30% of the time and converged only after hours of debate, and that the agent judge matched the consensus more often than any one of them. The chart reports the average person and the majority vote, not each expert separately.

Cost, as the post reports it for that benchmark: about $31 of API calls, against nearly $1,300 of expert time, and about 2% of the time the humans took. A memory module that let the judge reuse past judgments made it less accurate, because an early mistake was reused later. The judge that worked gathered fresh evidence for every requirement.

The design claim is structural. A template judge maps columns such as input and output before anyone has seen the failure. If the failure is a stale argument at step 14, a judge pointed at the final answer never sees it. The post stacks the checks: deterministic code, then an LLM judge, then an agent judge for trajectory failures nobody wrote a specific check for, then a person. It calls this a Swiss-cheese model. Each layer has holes.

The reliability questions are listed, not measured here. Production traffic has no expert consensus, so spot-checks against people remain. A full agent per evaluation has a cost, so sampling is a decision. The same judge on the same trace can differ across runs. The post says later work is finding a bias toward longer trajectories, whether or not the extra steps helped.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 1: a final answer can look reasonable while the trajectory is the failure. The grader has to be able to read the steps, including tool calls.
- Part 2: a code check, a single LLM call with a fixed template, and a judge that can inspect the trace are different instruments. The post's rule is to use the cheapest one that can see the failure.
- Part 3 asks participants to analyse tool choice, parameters, and response quality. The first two live in the trace. A judge that only receives the final reply is the column-mapping design this post says cannot see them.
- Part 4: validate the judge against people where a consensus exists, and do not treat a benchmark alignment number as a production guarantee. The post is explicit that production traffic has no such consensus.
- The cost figures (about $31, about $1,300, about 2% of the time) and the memory-module failure are the post's report of one 55-task benchmark. An agent judge can also spread an early mistake if it reuses past verdicts. Neither point is a general price or a general failure rate.

## Limits

The alignment and cost numbers are this post's retelling of Zhuge et al. on DevAI, with OpenHands, not a result measured here. The chart's 90.2% is alignment with a consensus on generated workspaces, and the three-human vote is still higher. The product diagram describes Arize's own agent judge, including a claim that the verdict leads to a direct change in the codebase. The closing outlook, a flywheel in which judge feedback becomes a training signal, is the post's forecast. The piece that bears on this tutorial is the evaluation design: a judge that can look at the trajectory, checked against people.

sources.title: How to build LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators that hold up in production
sources.summary: A production guide to LLM judges: use code when the check is deterministic, write a rubric with anchored labels before choosing a model, and calibrate against people. It is Part 2 on how a judge is specified, and Part 4 on bias, drift, and cost.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Aaron Winston's guide, also from Arize, is a production recipe for an LLM judge: when to use code instead, how to write the criteria, which output scale to allow, and how to check the judge against people before trusting a dashboard. That is Part 2, on criteria, rubrics, scales, prompting, and the choice among rules, a judge, and a human. It is also Part 4, on consistency, drift, bias, and cost. The running example is a support agent whose final answer says a refund was processed, while the trace shows the refund tool was never called.

## What they did

The post is a design guide. It does not report a benchmark table. Where it describes the author's own testing, it does not print the numbers.

The first decision is whether a judge is needed at all.

{{figure:fig1-code-vs-judge.png}}

A check with no interpretation stays in code: valid JSON, a known identifier, a tool schema, latency. A check that depends on meaning goes to a judge: grounding, a reasonable tool sequence, a refusal that is evasive rather than unsafe. Ambiguous or high-stakes cases go to a person.

The rubric, in the post's terms, is the evaluator. The model only applies it. A strong one has five pieces: the target, meaning one quality, the evidence the judge may use, the allowed labels, decision rules for edge cases, and an example of each label. "Rate helpfulness from 1 to 5" is the weak prompt, because helpful is not defined.

{{figure:fig2-rubric.png}}

Output types are a spectrum. Boolean labels suit a gate. Categories suit a failure with a few distinct states. An ordered scale needs an anchor on every level. A continuous number needs a real continuum and a calibration set. The post says that numeric scores, in Arize's own testing, produced plateaus and changed shape when the scale changed, without becoming a better measurement.

{{figure:fig3-output-types.png}}

Calibration is a loop: label real traces, including disagreements among reviewers, run the judge, read the misses, tighten the rules, and repeat on a holdout. Agreement beyond chance is Cohen's kappa. A high overall agreement can still miss the failure that matters. The post's illustration is introduced with "suppose": 100 support sessions, the judge agreeing on 82, and 9 of the misses being a plausible final answer with no required tool call. That is a worked example of how to read disagreements, not a measured accuracy.

The bias diagram pairs each failure with a design response: swap sides for position, refuse to reward length, use another model family for self-preference, do not treat confidence as evidence, version the prompt and keep a canary set, and require quoted evidence so a fluent explanation is not mistaken for proof.

{{figure:fig4-biases.png}}

For agents, the post splits the grade into the final answer, tool selection, tool arguments, how the tool result was used, trajectory efficiency, and the session outcome. Some of those are code. The post names matching modes for a reference trajectory: strict, unordered, subset, and superset. The rest are judges, because a reasonable trajectory is not an exact string match.

## What they found

The post does not print a results table. A label without the trace cannot be audited, and an explanation can rationalize a wrong label, so the output separates the label, the explanation, and the evidence. Human disagreement, and a missing tool result, are signs to add a label such as insufficient evidence rather than force a pass or fail. Cost is part of the choice: a judge that gains a little agreement and doubles latency can be wrong for monitoring and right for a release gate. Measure agreement, latency, tokens, and cost, and re-run a canary set when the judge model changes.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 2's choice among rules, a judge, and a human is this decision tree. Schema, exact match, and latency stay in code. Meaning goes to a judge. Ambiguous or high-stakes cases go to a person.
- A rubric is one target, the evidence, the allowed labels, the edge-case rules, and an example of each label. An unanchored numeric score lets the model invent the scale.
- Part 3 analyses tool choice, parameters, and response quality. The post treats those as separate evaluations. Averaging them into one helpfulness score hides which one failed.
- Part 4: version the judge the way the lifecycle versions the agent. A canary set shows whether a new judge model moved the historical trend. Drift of the criterion is a failure mode of its own.
- Ask for a reason when it helps a person audit the label. Do not take the reason as evidence that the label is right. Quoted evidence is the check.
- Calibrate on real traces before a score is used as a gate. The post's 82-of-100 story is an illustration of that inspection, not a result to cite as accuracy.

## Limits

This is a vendor guide. The numeric-score warning is "our own testing," with no table. The 100-session story is a suppose. Product names in the post are the author's platform. The bias mitigations are advice, and telling the judge not to reward length is a prompt instruction, not a measured fix. The refund example is an illustration, not a dataset.

sources.title: SAGE: Scalable AI Governance & Evaluation
sources.venue: In Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2 (KDD '26), August 9–13, 2026, Jeju Island, Republic of Korea.
sources.abstract: Evaluating relevance in large-scale search systems is fundamentally constrained by the governance gap between nuanced, resource-constrained human oversight and the high-throughput requirements of production systems. While traditional approaches rely on engagement proxies or sparse manual review, these methods often fail to capture the full scope of high-impact relevance failures. We present SAGE (Scalable AI Governance & Evaluation), a framework that operationalizes high-quality human product judgment as a scalable evaluation signal. At the core of SAGE is a bidirectional calibration loop where natural-language Policy, curated Precedent, and an LLM Surrogate Judge co-evolve. SAGE systematically resolves semantic ambiguities and misalignments, transforming subjective relevance judgment into an executable, multi-dimensional rubric with near human-level agreement. To bridge the gap between frontier model reasoning and industrial-scale inference, we apply teacher-student distillation to transfer high-fidelity judgments into compact student surrogates at 92× lower cost. Deployed within LinkedIn Search ecosystems, SAGE guided model iteration through simulation-driven development, distilling policy-aligned models for online serving and enabling rapid offline evaluation. In production, it powered policy oversight that measured ramped model variants and detected regressions invisible to engagement metrics. Collectively, these drove a 0.25% lift in LinkedIn daily active users.
sources.summary: LinkedIn's SAGE turns a written relevance policy and a small set of expert precedents into a judge, then distills that judge so it can run on production traffic. Agreement with experts approaches, and does not pass, the agreement experts have with each other. A relevance failure showed up in the judge while an engagement metric stayed flat.

## Why it is here

Le and colleagues, at LinkedIn, describe SAGE, a way to turn a product expert's judgment into a judge that can run on live search traffic. The judge is not a generic prompt that asks whether a result is good. It is a written policy, a small set of precedent cases, and a model calibrated against those cases, then distilled until it is cheap enough to run every day. That is the industry lifecycle in Part 1: rubrics and code that are versioned, offline tests before a launch, and monitoring after it. It is also Part 2's rubric and its cost trade-off, and Part 4's question of whether a judge agrees with people and whether an engagement metric would have caught the same failure.

## What they did

The systems are LinkedIn Job Search and People Search. The standard they want is a product owner's judgment of whether a job or a profile matches a natural-language query. Clicks and dismissals only approximate that judgment, and they arrive late.

SAGE has three pieces. Policy is a natural-language rubric. Precedent is a few hundred examples labelled by product experts, not a crowd. The surrogate judge applies that policy to new pairs. The loop runs both ways: people rewrite the policy when they cannot apply it consistently, and the judge may challenge a human label when its reason shows missed evidence, or expose a hole when it invents a constraint.

{{figure:fig1-framework.png}}

Three design choices matter. Relevance is split into attributes such as title, seniority, and location, scored separately and then combined, so a failure can be named. The scale is absolute, 0 to 4, not a pairwise preference, because grades 3 and 4 keep a result and grades 0 and 1 suppress it. Recency and graph distance stay in ordinary code. The model is reserved for language.

The teacher is a frontier model, moved in the paper from GPT-4o to GPT-o3, with Figure 2 also marking a later switch toward GPT-5. It is too expensive for all traffic, so they distill it into an 8-billion-parameter student on 312,000 rebalanced teacher labels. A smaller online model then compresses that student into a one-token score for ranking.

{{figure:fig4-distillation.png}}

## What they found

Agreement is linear weighted Cohen's kappa on the 0–4 scale. On People Search, a baseline in the style of G-Eval, using GPT-o3 and the initial policy, scored 0.67 against experts (Table 1). Four calibration passes reached 0.77. The judge caught human labelling errors (0.71). People rewrote a name policy they could not apply consistently (0.73). The judge had invented a constraint the policy did not state (0.75). People standardized how non-human profiles are scored (0.77). Expert-versus-expert kappa is 0.83 on People Search and 0.78 on Job Search, which the paper treats as the ceiling. The teacher reaches 0.77 and 0.76. The student reaches 0.73 and 0.72. On People Search the student agrees with the teacher at 0.81.

{{figure:fig2-student-kappa.png}}

Relative cost, with the student set to 1, is 92 for the teacher and 154 for a lower-bound crowdwork judge (Table 2). That is what makes more than 10 million labels a day, and an online model at more than 10,000 queries a second, possible. Dataset size was not the whole gain. On People Search, full-parameter fine-tuning moved kappa from 0.56 to 0.67, and a better teacher plus the 312,000 examples moved it to 0.735 (Table 3). Figure 2 rounds that same point to 0.73.

In production, two job-alert experiments that enforced the policy cut the poor-match rate at rank 10 by 28.9% and then 50.9%. Together the paper reports a 0.25% lift in LinkedIn daily active users, +0.12% and +0.13% in the two iterations (Table 4, each with p < 0.05). Offline, the same judge caught a 16% drop in good recall before users saw the variant, and cut a candidate-selection cycle from two weeks to three days.

The monitoring plot is the reliability point. During an incident, the poor-match rate rose about 40% week over week. Dismiss-to-apply, the engagement proxy, did not move in step.

{{figure:fig5-pmr-incident.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 2: score separate attributes with anchored grades, then combine them. A single number cannot say whether title or location failed.
- Keep non-linguistic signals in code. The model judges the linguistic match. That is the rules-versus-judge split.
- Part 1 versions the rubric along with the system. A policy change moves the metric even when the retriever did not. Without a version, that looks like a model regression.
- Part 4: compare the judge with people, and compare people with each other. A kappa of 0.77 sits below the expert ceiling of 0.83.
- Publish the student and the teacher separately. They are not the same measurement.
- Figure 5 is one incident, not a law: the judge moved and the engagement proxy did not.

## Limits

This is search relevance at LinkedIn, not an agent trajectory and not a tool call. Precedent is a few hundred expert cases. The 0.25% figure for daily active users is two job-alert experiments. Table 3's 0.735 and Figure 2's 0.73 are the same People Search student. The online model's kappa of 0.767 is against the student, not against people. What transfers is the evaluation design: a versioned rubric, a human ceiling, and a monitor that saw a failure the engagement metric missed.

figures.alt: Three panels. Bidirectional calibration connects a policy, a teacher judge, and a precedent. Distillation sends the teacher to a student judge, marked 92 times cheaper and more than 10 million daily annotations. The student labels feed simulation-driven development and production oversight.
figures.caption: Figure 1 from Le et al. (2026). Policy, precedent, and judge are calibrated together, then distilled into a judge that can run at production scale.

figures.alt: Line chart of linear Cohen's kappa for a student judge. Job Search rises from 0.66 to 0.72. People Search rises from 0.54 to 0.73, with the largest jump when training switches from LoRA to full-parameter tuning.
figures.caption: Figure 2 from Le et al. (2026). Student–human agreement across training iterations. The People Search jump is the switch to full-parameter fine-tuning, then a stronger teacher.

figures.alt: A vertical cascade. A teacher judge at kappa 0.77 and 92 times the student's cost distills into a student judge at kappa 0.73 and more than 10 million labels a day, which distills into an online model that emits one token at more than 10,000 queries a second.
figures.caption: Figure 4 from Le et al. (2026). The serving cascade. The online model's agreement in the text is reported against the student, not against people.

sources.title: How to scale agentic evaluation: lessons from 200,000 SWE-bench runs
sources.summary: What changed when one team ran a coding agent on SWE-bench more than 200,000 times: isolation, repeated seeds, and a split between generating a patch and grading it. A Part 4 account of cost and reliability once each test case is a long trajectory.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Yaron Sternbach, at AI21, describes what broke when his team ran a coding agent on SWE-bench Verified more than 200,000 times. The post is about infrastructure, not a new rubric. It belongs with Part 1's evaluation lifecycle, where offline tests have to be repeatable, and with Part 4's questions of cost and reliability. A long agent trajectory turns both of those into engineering. Each case is a multi-minute session that writes to a filesystem, and a single run is not a measurement.

## What they did

SWE-bench Verified is a coding benchmark of about 500 repository tasks. AI21 Maestro, their test-time agent, explores a codebase and produces a patch. A separate step applies the patch and runs the tests. The post calls the repetition of one instance across random seeds "duplicity," and treats that repetition as the way to see variance.

The official SWE-bench harness assumes a local machine: a cached dataset, and a fresh Docker container for each evaluation. On Kubernetes that assumption failed twice.

In the first trial, every fresh pod re-downloaded the benchmark and hit rate limits. Running Docker inside a pod also needed privileged access.

In the second, they kept a fresh container per run. Two variants, repeated several times (the post's examples are 4, 8, and 16), meant on the order of 16,000 containers in one window, with resource contention and more rate limits.

The third trial split what can be shared from what is unique to a run.

{{figure:fig1-shared-vs-unique.png}}

About 500 pods, one per SWE-bench instance, hold the repository at the right commit, a server that can run commands, and installed dependencies. Many agent runs then share that pod. Because those runs would otherwise overwrite the same files, the team extended the tool protocol so each run's writes stay isolated.

{{figure:fig2-architecture.png}}

Generation and evaluation are separate steps. If the test runner dies, the patch is already stored and only the tests are repeated. The post says a campaign can be read when 80% of runs have finished, while the rest are retried.

## What they found

The comparison the post prints is per-run provisioning against the shared pods.

{{figure:fig3-before-after.png}}

Failure rate moves from 30% to 0. Repository downloads move from more than 8,000 redundant fetches to 500, once per instance. Pods are provisioned once per campaign rather than once per run. The same table lists global capacity as 10,000 parallel runs. An earlier paragraph says the architecture supports up to 8,000 parallel runs, and a later one says the current service target is 10,000, with a hope of ten times that by putting more executors on one pod. Those are three statements in one post, not one measured ceiling.

Wall-clock time, the post says, then depends on the agent variant rather than on setup. A light variant averages 3.5 minutes per example, a typical one about 10 minutes, and a thorough one can exceed 2 hours. With enough parallelism, a full pass takes as long as the slowest example, about 20 minutes for a typical variant.

A second table is the campaign tally: more than 200,000 runs, a peak of 35,000 in a day, about 100 billion tokens, 10,000 parallel runs, and about 500 pods.

{{figure:fig4-scale.png}}

The claim for why the scale matters is statistical. Small tests did not show the efficiency problems. Thousands of isolated runs did. The post does not report a pass rate, a judge agreement, or which variant was better at solving the issues.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 1's offline evaluation is not one run of each test. Variance across seeds is part of the measurement, and the post treats repeated runs as a requirement for confidence.
- Part 4's cost is dominated by trajectory length. A two-hour example and a three-minute example are not the same budget. A failed environment at the end of a long run wastes the tokens unless the generated patch is saved separately from the grading step.
- Isolation is an integrity constraint. An agent that writes files will contaminate the next case if they share a checkout. A shared environment is only valid if each run's writes are separated.
- A partial campaign is still evidence. Waiting for every retry before reading the finished majority hides a result the finished runs already have.
- None of these numbers is a quality score. A 0% infrastructure failure rate says the harness finished. It does not say the patches were correct.

## Limits

This is one team's account of one coding benchmark and one agent, AI21 Maestro. The tables are the post's own tallies, with no public log behind them. The 8,000 and 10,000 parallel-run figures are not reconciled in the text. There is no judge, no rubric, and no human baseline. Use it for what changes when agent evaluation is run at this volume. It is not a method for scoring a trajectory.

figures.caption: Diagram from Sternbach (2026). The third design shares the environment and isolates each run's writes.

figures.alt: A stack of SWE-bench pods. Each pod holds a repository and a Maestro code MCP server with several worker boxes. Below, stacked Maestro runs each carry an instance id.
figures.caption: Diagram from Sternbach (2026). About 500 pods, one per SWE-bench instance, serve many agent runs.

figures.alt: A table comparing per-run provisioning with a multi-tenant setup. Failure rate goes from 30 percent to 0. Repository downloads go from more than 8,000 to 500. Pods are provisioned once per campaign. Global capacity is listed as 10,000 parallel runs.
figures.caption: Table from Sternbach (2026). The post's before-and-after for sharing one environment per benchmark instance.

sources.title: Emerging Trends in AI Agent Evaluation
sources.summary: A survey of 33 shifts in agent evaluation — how to measure, what to measure, and who measures — and the wide frame for Part 1, where a final answer is a weak test of an agent.
sources.abstract: AI models are increasingly deployed as agents: rather than responding to a single prompt, they plan over many steps, call external tools, and act within software and real-world environments. This shift challenges the existing outcome-focused benchmarking paradigm for evaluating AI models. Evaluating these agent systems must now encompass an array of scaffolds, tools, and environments that present a far more complex challenge for evaluators today. First, this shift has necessitated many improvements to measurement methodology, scientific rigor, and evaluation infrastructure. Second, the deployment of agents in real settings has expanded the scope of evaluation from the lab to the field. Third, the accompanying changes within the broader evaluator ecosystem hold new implications for those interested in contributing to this work. We survey 33 shifts, practices, and questions driven by the AI agent paradigm across the above three dimensions—the “How,” “What,” and “Who” of AI agent evaluation. Our goal is to help consolidate the emerging discipline of agent evaluation, equipped with an evolving methodological toolkit (Part 1), an orienting research agenda (Part 2), and an updated portrait of the evaluation landscape (Part 3).

## Why it is here

Chen, Rabanser, Kapoor, Narayanan, and colleagues survey how evaluation changes once a model is used as an agent. It is the wide frame for Part 1: agents, tool use, and why a single final answer is a weak test. The survey sorts 33 trends into its own three parts, How, What, and Who. Those are the survey's parts, not this tutorial's four parts.

## What they did

They define an agent system as a large language model plus a scaffold (the harness that loops the model) and tools, planning and acting toward a goal without a person at every step. Evaluation, as they use the word, means any work that measures, characterises, or analyses a model or a system, before or after deployment.

The paper is a survey, not a new benchmark. They read public leaderboards, benchmarks, preprints, and essays, and followed citation chains. They describe the choice of 33 trends as opinionated, and the citations inside each trend as illustrative.

{{figure:fig1-trends.png}}

## What they found

The picture this tutorial keeps returning to is their Figure 2. A model evaluation sends a prompt, collects a response, and grades it against a reference answer. An agent evaluation watches a system of model, scaffold, and tools act in an environment. A person may step in at some points. The grader can look at the trajectory (every step), the final state, or both, and the grader itself can be a test, a rubric, or an LLM judge.

{{figure:fig2-model-vs-agent.png}}

Their Table 1 says why the older habits fail. The same outcome can be reached by different trajectories, including shortcuts, so an outcome score does not say which behaviour was measured. Accuracy leaves out cost, latency, and reliability. Runs vary more, because a small difference early in a long trajectory can compound. When the score moves, the cause might be the model, the scaffold, the tools, or the environment, and the same scaffold need not interact with every model in the same way.

Two later sections are the bridge into Parts 2 and 4. In the survey's section 1h, long traces and open-ended outputs make LLM judges and monitors useful, and they also create a risk of trusting the judge too much. The practice they recommend is to check an autograder against human-labelled holdouts, and to review a sample of the cases the judge passed. In section 1i, Figure 11 is a fictional log. The outcome is marked as a success. The log shows the agent opened the benchmark's answers and reported those numbers. They call that search-time contamination. The outcome line cannot show it.

{{figure:fig11-log-excerpt.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- An agent, in this survey, is a model, a scaffold, and tools, and the record of the run is a trajectory. Part 1 treats a score on the final answer as a weak test of that record.
- A grader is one of three instruments: a test, a rubric, or an LLM judge. Part 3 builds a rubric and an LLM judge, and looks at tool choice, parameters, and response quality. A check that a tool call matches a schema is a different instrument from that judge.
- A leaderboard accuracy number is one measurement. The missing questions are cost, variance across runs, and what the log shows.
- When a score changes, name which component changed. Their section on causal attribution is the warning against crediting the model for a gain that came with a new scaffold. Part 1's lifecycle versions prompts, tests, datasets, rubrics, and code, because those pieces move separately.
- Judges appear in the survey because traces are too long to read by hand. The same section says to sample the judge's passes and failures, rather than treat the judge as self-checking. Holding out human labels, and reviewing a sample of the cases the judge passed, is a Part 4 practice.

## Limits

This is a map of the literature, not a measurement of a judge. A trend being listed is not evidence that the practice works. Figure 11 is a constructed example, and the paper labels it as fictional. The best-practice bullets are the authors' recommendations. The survey does not report how often these failures occur.

sources.title: Mitigating the Bias of Large Language Model Evaluation
sources.venue: In Proceedings of the 23rd Chinese National Conference on Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Main Conference), pages 1310–1319.
sources.abstract: Recently, there has been a trend of evaluating the Large Language Model (LLM) quality in the flavor of LLM-as-a-Judge, namely leveraging another LLM to evaluate the current output quality. However, existing judges are proven to be biased, namely they would favor answers which present better superficial quality (such as verbosity, fluency) while ignoring the instruction following ability. In this work, we propose systematic research about the bias of LLM-as-a-Judge. Specifically, for closed-source judge models, we apply calibration to mitigate the significance of superficial quality, both on probability level and prompt level. For open-source judge models, we propose to mitigate the bias by contrastive training, with curated negative samples that deviate from instruction but present better superficial quality. We apply our methods on the bias evaluation benchmark, and experiment results show our methods mitigate the bias by a large margin while maintaining a satisfactory evaluation accuracy.
sources.note: The organiser reading list spells the first author Zhuo. The anthology record for this URL names Zhou.
sources.summary: LLM judges prefer fluent, verbose answers over answers that follow the instruction. Calibration and contrastive training reduce that gap on adversarial pairs, and they can also lower accuracy on ordinary pairs if the correction is pushed too far.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Zhou, Huang, Long, and colleagues study a specific judge failure. The judge prefers an answer that is fluent, long, and well written, and ignores whether the answer followed the instruction. That is a Part 4 failure mode, and it is a Part 2 problem of criteria. If the rubric does not say what is being scored, surface quality fills the gap. Part 3 asks participants to judge response quality for a tool-using agent. This paper is the warning that quality will be read as style unless the criterion says otherwise.

## What they did

The test bed is LLMBar, from Zeng et al. (2023). It has a Natural set, preference pairs drawn from ordinary benchmarks, and four adversarial sets: Neighbor, Manual, GPTOut, and GPTInst. The adversarial pairs are built so that the answer which looks better is the one that does not follow the instruction. The judge's job is pairwise: which answer is better.

They use two fixes, depending on whether the judge can be retrained.

For a closed model, they subtract a separate score of superficial quality. Probability calibration uses a model that was not instruction-tuned. Text-davinci-003 is the judge. Davinci-002, its predecessor without instruction tuning, estimates fluency alone. The calibrated score is the judge's score minus α times that fluency score, after both are scaled onto the same range. Prompt calibration is the fallback when token probabilities are unavailable: three prompts score style and ignore the question, and that score is subtracted the same way.

{{figure:fig1-superficial-prompts.png}}

For an open judge they can retrain, they build negative examples and continue training. From JudgeLM's data they take 20,000 of 100,000 pairs. For each instruction they find a nearby but different instruction, using Instructor embeddings, and attach an answer that followed the other instruction. The new pair is fluent and off-instruction. Vicuna-7B is then trained on the original pairs and these adversarial pairs together. No new human labels are collected.

{{figure:fig3-contrastive.png}}

## What they found

Table 1 is accuracy on LLMBar, in percent. Higher means the judge picked the instruction-following answer more often.

{{figure:table1-llmbar.png}}

Probability calibration is the large movement. For text-davinci-003 scored from token log probabilities, average accuracy goes from 48.88 to 67.02. The Natural set barely moves, from 70.00 to 71.50. Neighbor goes from 43.33 to 72.83, and GPTInst from 38.67 to 68.38. A second probability variant, using the log probabilities of the generated judgment, moves the average from 42.99 to 66.87, while Natural dips from 76.00 to 72.50. Davinci-002 on its own, with no instruction tuning, averages 40.85. That is why the paper uses it as a fluency meter rather than as a judge.

Prompt calibration on GPT-4 is smaller. Uncalibrated, GPT-4 averages 65.15, with 88.00 on Natural and 37.31 on Neighbor. The third of the three prompts reaches an average of 69.69. Natural falls to 82.00. GPTOut, the set where the tempting answer was written by GPT-4, rises from 79.79 to 86.17. The paper reads that cell as a reduction in self-enhancement, the judge favoring its own style. It is one cell.

Contrastive training on Vicuna-7B lifts the average from 39.74 to 57.20 when the negative example is the swapped answer. Neighbor goes from 25.00 to 65.67 and GPTInst from 23.91 to 72.83. GPTOut goes the other way, from 48.94 to 39.36. The authors say those GPT-4-written temptations have a pattern their automatic negatives do not imitate. Natural slips from 71.50 to 69.00.

Figure 4 is the compromise. As α grows, adversarial accuracy rises and Natural holds, until α passes about 0.8, after which both fall. Fluency is also something people like. Removing all of it is not the goal.

{{figure:fig4-alpha.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 2: the criterion has to name the decision. A judge asked for quality will use fluency, length, and tone, because those are what a pretrained score already likes.
- Part 3's response-quality question needs a definition that can disagree with style. An answer can read well and still miss the instruction, the tool result, or the user's request.
- Part 4: one accuracy on ordinary data hides this bias. GPT-4's 88% on the Natural set sits next to 37% on Neighbor. Without the adversarial cut, the bias is invisible.
- Subtracting a fluency score is a calibration with a knob. Past a point it starts discarding signal people want. In Figure 4 both curves turn down after α of about 0.8.
- The probability method needs an instruction-free model and access to probabilities. Prompt subtraction, which is what remains without them, moved GPT-4's average by a few points. Contrastive training helped where the negatives resembled the test and hurt on GPTOut. A mitigation is only as wide as the pairs it was built from.

## Limits

The task is pairwise grading of instruction-following answers, not an agent trace and not a tool call. LLMBar's adversarial sets are constructed to provoke the bias. Two closed models and one 7-billion-parameter judge are tested. The paper says fluency should not be removed entirely, because human preference includes it. A higher adversarial score together with a lower Natural score is a trade, not a pure win. The pattern that transfers is the test: build examples where style and correctness point in opposite directions, and read those separately from the ordinary set.

sources.title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge
sources.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has been widely utilized as an evaluation method in various benchmarks and served as supervised rewards in model training. However, despite their excellence in many domains, potential issues are under-explored, undermining their reliability and the scope of their utility. Therefore, we identify 12 key potential biases and propose a new automated bias quantification framework-CALM-which systematically quantifies and analyzes each type of bias in LLM-as-a-Judge by using automated and principle-guided modification. Our experiments cover multiple popular language models, and the results indicate that while advanced models have achieved commendable overall performance, significant biases persist in certain specific tasks. Empirical results suggest that there remains room for improvement in the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge. Moreover, we also discuss the explicit and implicit influence of these biases and give some suggestions for the reliable application of LLM-as-a-Judge. Our work highlights the need for stakeholders to address these issues and remind users to exercise caution in LLM-as-a-Judge applications.
sources.summary: Ye and colleagues name 12 biases in LLM-as-a-judge and introduce CALM, which injects one bias at a time into an answer and measures whether the verdict moves. It shows that even advanced judges remain vulnerable on specific biases, which is central to Part 4.
sources.note: The reading checklist dates this 2025. The primary list and the arXiv record are 2024.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Ye, Wang, Huang, and colleagues ask how easily an LLM judge's verdict can be moved by something that should not matter: answer length, a fake citation, the stated popularity of an answer, or the identity attached to it. That is a Part 4 — Reliability, Limitations, and Future Directions — question, and it also disciplines Part 2 — LLM-as-a-Judge Methods: a judge whose score shifts under irrelevant changes is not measuring the criterion it was given. The paper supplies both a taxonomy of such failure modes and a way to measure each one without new human labelling.

## What they did

The authors name 12 biases (Table 1 of the paper): position, verbosity, compassion-fade (treating a named model differently from an anonymised one), bandwagon (following a stated majority), distraction (attending to irrelevant detail), fallacy-oversight (missing a logical error when the final answer looks right), authority (crediting a claim because it carries a citation), sentiment, diversity (reacting to a stated group identity), chain-of-thought (the verdict changing when step-by-step reasoning is requested), self-enhancement (favouring one's own generations), and refinement-aware (scoring an answer higher when told it is a refined version).

Their framework, CALM (Comprehensive Assessment of Language Model Judge Biases), injects one bias at a time. A model (GPT-4o, as printed) rewrites an answer under a stated principle — for example, expanding a poor answer to make it longer, or inserting a fabricated citation — while keeping its underlying quality fixed. The judge then re-judges the modified pair. The main metric is robustness rate: the share of samples where the judgment after modification matches the judgment that the unmodified, quality-ordered pair should receive; consistency rate compares against a randomised baseline judgment instead. Six judges were tested: ChatGPT, GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5, GLM-4, and Qwen2-72B-Instruct. Data came in three families: fact-related sets (including GSM8K, MATH, and ScienceQA), alignment sets built from Direct Preference Optimization pairs (439 samples in the table shown for that family), and a refinement-aware set of 500 samples.

{{figure:fig2-calm-framework.png}}

## What they found

No judge was uniformly robust, and the strongest overall judge was not strongest on every bias. Figure 1 plots robustness per bias for all six judges; the authors report Claude-3.5 as generally the most resilient, while noting cases such as GPT-4-Turbo proving inconsistent on emotional (sentiment) content where ChatGPT was steadier. Position bias worsened sharply as the number of answers grew from two to three or four, with most models' robustness falling below 0.5 (Figure 6a). Making an answer longer without improving it generally reduced robustness, though some models showed the opposite pull toward longer answers (Figure 6b). Chain-of-thought prompting improved evaluation accuracy for most models in their comparison (Figure 7d). Sentiment and diversity effects were model-specific: the paper reports GPT-4o showing pronounced sensitivity to female and refugee status in the diversity tests, while Claude-3.5 stayed close to the random baseline there. Their practical recommendations include randomising answer order, avoiding the same model as generator and judge, and choosing a judge by its measured bias profile rather than its general reputation.

{{figure:fig1-robustness-radar.png}}

{{figure:fig6-combined-plot.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Bias in a judge is measurable one factor at a time. Change only length, only order, or only a citation, and see whether the verdict moves; that is a test design Part 3 participants can imitate on a small scale when they analyse response quality.
- A single headline score for a judge hides its profile. Two judges with similar overall robustness failed on different biases here, so Part 4's question is which failure modes a given use can tolerate.
- Adding candidate answers is not a neutral change. Position robustness collapsing below 0.5 with three or four options warns against quietly widening a pairwise judge into a ranking judge.
- Several mitigations are procedural and cheap to state — randomise order, separate generator and judge, hide identities — but the paper shows they address specific biases, not bias in general.
- Chain-of-thought helped accuracy in these tests. The paper does not show it removes position, authority, or diversity effects, so it should not be carried in as a general debiasing step.

## Limits

CALM's biased answers are themselves model-generated, so a measured effect is partly an effect of how GPT-4o performs the modification; the authors validate the approach but the modification quality bounds what the test can detect. The judges and datasets are those available to the authors in 2024 and are text-only, single- or few-answer judgments — nothing here directly measures judges of multi-step agent trajectories or tool calls. Robustness rate measures stability against the injected change, not correctness against human preference on the original task, so a judge could be stably wrong and score well on robustness while disagreeing with humans.

figures.caption: Figure 2 from Ye et al. (2024). The CALM framework: one bias is injected into an answer at a time and the judge's verdict is re-measured.

figures.caption: Figure 1 from Ye et al. (2024). Robustness rates of six judges across the 12 biases; higher is more resistant, and the crossing lines show no judge is best on every bias.
