sources.title: Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents
sources.abstract: LLM-based agents represent a paradigm shift in AI, enabling autonomous systems to plan, reason, and use tools while interacting with dynamic environments. This paper provides the first comprehensive survey of evaluation methods for these increasingly capable agents. We analyze the field of agent evaluation across five perspectives: (1) Core LLM capabilities needed for agentic workflows, like planning, and tool use; (2) Application-specific benchmarks such as web and SWE agents; (3) Evaluation of generalist agents; (4) Analysis of agent benchmarks' core dimensions; and (5) Evaluation frameworks and tools for agent developers. Our analysis reveals current trends, including a shift toward more realistic, challenging evaluations with continuously updated benchmarks. We also identify critical gaps that future research must address, particularly in assessing cost-efficiency, safety, and robustness, and in developing fine-grained, scalable evaluation methods.
sources.summary: Yehudai and colleagues survey how LLM-based agents are evaluated, from tool use and memory to web, coding, science, and conversation benchmarks. The comparative table covers eight benchmarks, and only one of them is marked as testing safety.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Yehudai, Eden, Li, and colleagues survey evaluation of LLM-based agents, a backbone model plus a harness that lets it plan and call tools. They do not release a benchmark or a grader. The survey is a Part 1 frame: what gets measured once the system acts, and why one end score is a thin description of that action. Its own section numbers, §2 through §6, are the paper's, not this tutorial's four parts.

## What they did

The survey's §2 covers planning, tool use, self-reflection, and memory. Its §3 covers web, software, science, and conversation benchmarks. Its §4 covers generalist agents. Its §5 is the comparison scheme: how the data were built, whether the environment is static or dynamic, what interface the agent uses, what the metric is, and whether safety is part of the benchmark. Its §6 lists developer tools. §7 is trends and gaps.

Early tool-use scores are rule-based: a pass rate, or a match on the abstract syntax of the call. Later scores execute something. Unit tests for a software patch, a match against a gold database state, a match against a gold click sequence, or an exact short answer. They also describe LLM-as-a-judge and agent-as-a-judge methods, including reference-based trajectory match and reference-free judges that score a trace without a gold path. Their own judgment, stated as a judgment, is that reference-based checks are precise and miss other valid paths, and reference-free checks are more flexible and less reliable.

Robustness, in their definition, is pass^k: the fraction of tasks on which the agent succeeds in every one of k independent runs. They print no pass^k value.

{{figure:fig1-taxonomy.png}}

## What they found

Figure 1 is the map of the survey's sections with the papers they treat as the core citations. Table 1 applies the five dimensions to eight benchmarks. Seven of the eight build data with a mix of human and synthetic or harvested sources. GAIA is the only row marked human-curated. Mind2Web is the only static environment. The others are dynamic, so a wrong action can change what the agent sees next. Interfaces are code, tools with a schema, or a GUI. The metric column is the tutorial's point in one place: unit tests, end-to-end completion, action match, a mix, state match, or answer match. Only TAU-Bench is marked Safety = Yes. The other seven are No. The prose uses the name τ-bench for that row.

The survey reports a few sizes rather than a leaderboard of its own. SWE-bench Verified is a human-filtered subset of 500. SWE-bench Pro, in the survey's §3.2, is 1,865 tasks across 41 repositories, with performance described as below 25% Pass@1. The recommendation appendix in the same version says the state of the art on SWE-bench-pro hovers around 46%. The survey does not say whether those are the same split or the same metric. Both are citations, not runs the authors did.

A second table checks eight developer frameworks. Trajectory evaluation is claimed by three of them. The authors say these tools are still weak at root-cause analysis across many traces, at the cost of the evaluation itself, and at built-in safety checks.

{{figure:table1-benchmarks.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 1 can use the five columns. Data, environment, interface, metric, and safety are a way to read any agent benchmark before trusting its headline number. In this table, safety is a yes on one row.
- Static and dynamic environments do not support the same claim. On a static trace a wrong action does not change the next state, so cascading errors are invisible. The survey states that as a reason dynamic sandboxes exist.
- The metric column is why a final answer is a weak test. Unit tests, state match, and action match are different measurements, and a benchmark that reports one of them has not reported the others.
- Reference-based judges and reference-free judges fail differently. The survey's claim, which it does not measure, is precision and reproducibility on one side and coverage of valid paths on the other. Part 2 has to pick.
- pass^k, success on all k runs, is the robustness definition they adopt. They do not print a value, so the definition is the thing to carry, not a result.
- Cost, safety, and fine-grained trajectory metrics are listed as missing. That is the authors' gap list in §7, and it matches Part 4's open problems. It is a forecast, not a measurement.

## Limits

The limitations section says the survey is a snapshot, the coverage is selective, and each benchmark is not described in full. There is no count of papers screened or excluded. Appendix A describes the search and never prints N. The 25% and 46% figures for SWE-bench Pro should not be collapsed into one number. The WebArena figure of 74.3% and the SWE-bench Verified figure of about 80% live in the recommendation appendix as leaderboard citations, with the WebArena number dated 19 April 2026. They are not results of an evaluation these authors ran.

sources.title: Evaluation and Benchmarking of LLM Agents: A Survey
sources.venue: In Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2 (KDD '25), August 3–7, 2025, Toronto, ON, Canada.
sources.abstract: The rise of LLM-based agents has opened new frontiers in AI applications, yet evaluating these agents remains a complex and underdeveloped area. This survey provides an in-depth overview of the emerging field of LLM agent evaluation, introducing a two-dimensional taxonomy that organizes existing work along (1) evaluation objectives -- what to evaluate, such as agent behavior, capabilities, reliability, and safety -- and (2) evaluation process -- how to evaluate, including interaction modes, datasets and benchmarks, metric computation methods, and tooling. In addition to taxonomy, we highlight enterprise-specific challenges, such as role-based access to data, the need for reliability guarantees, dynamic and long-horizon interactions, and compliance, which are often overlooked in current research. We also identify future research directions, including holistic, more realistic, and scalable evaluation. This work aims to bring clarity to the fragmented landscape of agent evaluation and provide a framework for systematic assessment, enabling researchers and practitioners to evaluate LLM agents for real-world deployment.
sources.summary: Mohammadi, Li, Lo, and Yip survey how LLM agents are evaluated and draw a two-axis map: what to measure, and how the measurement is run. The paper is a taxonomy, not an experiment, and the figure's leaf names do not all match the section headings.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Mohammadi, Li, Lo, and Yip survey evaluation of LLM agents, systems that use a language model to reason, plan, and act. The paper is a map, not a new benchmark and not a leaderboard. It is useful for Part 1, which has to say why scoring one final answer is a weak test of an agent, and for Part 2, which has to choose among rules, a model judge, an agent judge, and a human. The four future-work items at the end line up with Part 4's open problems: coverage, realism, scale, and cost.

## What they did

They propose a two-dimensional taxonomy. The first dimension is the objective, what is being evaluated. The section headings are agent behavior, agent capabilities, reliability, and safety. Behavior is the outcome a user would notice: task completion, output quality, latency, and cost. Capabilities are the process: tool use, planning, memory, and multi-agent collaboration. In this survey, tool use means one call, including whether a call was needed, which tool, which parameter names, and which parameter values. Planning is the sequence. Reliability splits into consistency, repeating the same task, and robustness, surviving a changed input or environment. They define pass@k as success at least once in k attempts, and pass^k, from the τ benchmark, as success on all k attempts. They argue that pass^k matches mission-critical use better. They do not measure either one.

The second dimension is the process, how the evaluation is run. Section 4 has five branches: interaction mode, data, how the metric is computed, tooling, and context. Interaction mode is offline, a fixed dataset, against online, a live or simulated environment. Metric computation is the distinction this tutorial keeps using. Code-based checks are rules, tests, and assertions. LLM-as-a-judge scores from an instruction. Agent-as-a-judge, which they treat as a recent extension, uses further agents to refine the assessment. Human review is what they call the gold standard for subjective and safety-critical judgments, and they call it expensive. Context is the environment: a mock API, a sandbox, a web simulator, or the live system.

{{figure:fig1-taxonomy.png}}

## What they found

There is no experiment, so there is no success rate of theirs to quote. The contribution is the map, and the map is not perfectly stable inside the paper. Figure 1 labels the middle behavior branch "Interaction Quality." Section 3 and Table 1 call it output quality. Figure 1's reliability leaves are robustness, hallucinations, and error handling. The section and the table use consistency and robustness, and they do not give hallucinations their own heading. Figure 1's metric leaves are code-based, human-as-a-judge, and LLM-as-a-judge. The section adds agent-as-a-judge and calls the human case human-in-the-loop. The abstract's process list also drops evaluation context, which Figure 1 and Section 4.5 both include.

Table 1 is the objective side only. It pairs each category with metric names and with papers that use them. It is a set of examples, not a count of the literature. The reference list runs to 127, and the authors never say how many papers were included or what the inclusion rule was.

{{figure:table1-objectives.png}}

The enterprise section is an argument, not a measurement. They say current evaluations often miss role-based access, a guarantee of repeated success, long interactions, and policy constraints such as GDPR or HIPAA. They do not fill those gaps with numbers. The last section names four directions: evaluate the dimensions together, use more realistic settings, automate with simulators and judges, and bound time and cost.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 1 can use the behavior-versus-capability split. Task completion is the outcome. Tool choice, parameter names, and parameter values are a different question, and this survey puts them under capabilities.
- pass@k and pass^k are definitions worth keeping. One success in k tries is not the same measurement as success on all k tries. The survey defines them and does not report a value.
- Part 2's menu is already in their process axis: code, an LLM judge, an agent judge, and a human. They state the usual trade, consistency against coverage, and they do not compare the four on one task.
- Offline and online are the industry lifecycle in miniature. A fixed dataset and a live monitor are different evaluations, and they say the dataset is the cheaper and less faithful of the two, without a table that shows the gap.
- Latency and cost sit under behavior, next to success. A leaderboard that reports only success has dropped two of their behavior metrics.

## Limits

No new metric, no head-to-head, and no count of what was left out. Short-horizon benchmarks are argued to miss drift and cumulative effects. That is not shown here. The phrase "current agents struggle with consistency" cites τ-bench and reprints no pass^k. Safety is described as something that should have a numeric rate, and no rate is given. Read Figure 1 next to Table 1. The leaves are not the same list.

Process branches into interaction mode, data, metrics, tooling, and context. Reliability's leaves on this figure are Robustness, Hallucinations, and Error Handling. The metrics leaves are Code Based, Human-as-a-Judge, and LLM-as-a-Judge.

Rows cover task completion, output quality, latency and cost, tool use, planning, memory, multi-agent collaboration, consistency, robustness, fairness, harm, and compliance. The consistency metric cell names pass^k and τ-Bench.

sources.title: Evaluating LLM-based Agents for Multi-Turn Conversations: A Survey
sources.abstract: This survey examines evaluation methods for large language model (LLM)-based agents in multi-turn conversational settings. Using a PRISMA-inspired framework, we systematically reviewed nearly 250 scholarly sources, capturing the state of the art from various venues of publication, and establishing a solid foundation for our analysis. Our study offers a structured approach by developing two interrelated taxonomy systems: one that defines \emph{what to evaluate} and another that explains \emph{how to evaluate}. The first taxonomy identifies key components of LLM-based agents for multi-turn conversations and their evaluation dimensions, including task completion, response quality, user experience, memory and context retention, as well as planning and tool integration. These components ensure that the performance of conversational agents is assessed in a holistic and meaningful manner. The second taxonomy system focuses on the evaluation methodologies. It categorizes approaches into annotation-based evaluations, automated metrics, hybrid strategies that combine human assessments with quantitative measures, and self-judging methods utilizing LLMs. This framework not only captures traditional metrics derived from language understanding, such as BLEU and ROUGE scores, but also incorporates advanced techniques that reflect the dynamic, interactive nature of multi-turn dialogues.
sources.summary: Survey of evaluating agents in multi-turn conversation. Relevant because the hands-on cases are short dialogues, and because a single-turn score misses later turns.

sources.title: A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge
sources.abstract: Accurate and consistent evaluation is crucial for decision-making across numerous fields, yet it remains a challenging task due to inherent subjectivity, variability, and scale. Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, leading to the emergence of "LLM-as-a-Judge," where LLMs are employed as evaluators for complex tasks. With their ability to process diverse data types and provide scalable, cost-effective, and consistent assessments, LLMs present a compelling alternative to traditional expert-driven evaluations. However, ensuring the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge systems remains a significant challenge that requires careful design and standardization. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of LLM-as-a-Judge, addressing the core question: How can reliable LLM-as-a-Judge systems be built? We explore strategies to enhance reliability, including improving consistency, mitigating biases, and adapting to diverse assessment scenarios. Additionally, we propose methodologies for evaluating the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge systems, supported by a novel benchmark designed for this purpose. To advance the development and real-world deployment of LLM-as-a-Judge systems, we also discussed practical applications, challenges, and future directions. This survey serves as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners in this rapidly evolving field.
sources.summary: Gu and colleagues survey LLM-as-a-judge from pipeline design to meta-evaluation, and add a small experiment comparing judges on human-labelled pairs and a bias benchmark. It maps the Part 2 design choices and the Part 4 question of how a judge itself should be evaluated.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Gu, Jiang, Shi, and colleagues survey the LLM-as-a-judge literature end to end: how a judge is built, how it can be improved, how its own quality is measured, and where it is used. A survey is a map, not an experiment, although this one also runs a small comparison of its own. For Part 2 — LLM-as-a-Judge Methods — it organises the choices a team actually faces (criteria, prompt format, model choice, and how the raw output becomes a score), and for Part 4 — Reliability, Limitations, and Future Directions — it collects the bias, robustness, and meta-evaluation problems that decide whether a judge's numbers can be trusted. Meta-evaluation means evaluating the evaluator: checking a judge against human judgments rather than trusting its scores directly.

## What they did

The survey's organising frame (Figure 1) asks what LLM-as-a-judge is, how to use it, how to improve it, how to evaluate it, where it is applied, and what remains hard. The pipeline they describe (Figure 2) has three stages. First, in-context learning: presenting the task inside the prompt, in one of four output formats — a numeric score (their example is 1 to 10), a yes/no answer, a pairwise choice between two responses, or a multiple-choice selection. Second, model selection: a general LLM used as-is, or a model fine-tuned (further trained) on evaluation data to act as a dedicated judge. Third, post-processing: turning model output into a usable value by extracting a token or sentence, or by using token probabilities (logits, the model's scores for possible next tokens). Improvement strategies are grouped as prompt design, capability enhancement such as fine-tuning and feedback-driven refinement, and output optimisation such as combining several judges or repeated samples.

Their own empirical section meta-evaluates judges on LLMEval² (2,553 samples with human preference labels) and EvalBiasBench (80 samples covering six biases: length, concreteness, empty reference, content continuation, nested instruction, and familiar knowledge), using percentage agreement with humans, accuracy on the bias sets, and position consistency (whether the verdict survives swapping the two answers). Target judges included GPT-4-turbo and GPT-3.5-turbo plus open models Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, LLaMA3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, and Mixtral-8×7B, with temperature set to 0.

{{figure:fig2-pipelines.png}}

## What they found

Table 1 lines up twelve meta-evaluation benchmarks by year, size, format, and which dimensions they cover — agreement, position bias, length bias, and number of bias types. The coverage is uneven: most check agreement, few check bias, and CALM is the only row marked as covering 12 bias types, at 4,356 samples. In the authors' own runs, GPT-4-turbo outperformed the other tested judges across the meta-evaluation dimensions and showed fewer biases, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct surpassed GPT-3.5-turbo on most dimensions except position and nested-instruction bias. For strategies layered on GPT-3.5-turbo (Table 4 of the paper), adding an explanation step lowered human agreement from 54.72% to 52.47%, while combining multiple LLM judges raised it to 57.66% and 58.19% in their two configurations — gains of a few points, not a transformation, and the authors note that alignment differences between models were generally not large, leaving clear room for improvement. Their summary advice is to run a small meta-evaluation before choosing a judge, because even a strong model can be badly affected by a specific bias such as empty-reference bias.

{{figure:table1-meta-evaluation.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Judge design is a pipeline, not a prompt alone: output format, model choice, and post-processing each change the resulting scores, which is the menu Part 2 presents when a team chooses rules, a judge, or a human.
- Meta-evaluation comes before trust. The survey's own experiment is small, but its procedure — agreement on human-labelled pairs, a bias set, and a swap test for position consistency — is the shape of a pre-flight check for any judge, including the one built in Part 3.
- Combining judges helped a little and explanations hurt a little in these runs (58.19% versus 52.47% agreement for the GPT-3.5 configurations). Strategy choices are empirical questions with costs attached, not defaults to assume.
- Table 1 shows the field's blind spot in one view: agreement is routinely measured, bias much less often. A judge reported only on agreement has not been reported on the failure modes Part 4 cares about.
- Fine-tuned specialist judges and general models are presented as alternatives with different costs; the survey does not crown either, so the choice stays open for a team's quality, latency, reliability, and cost constraints.

## Limits

As a survey, most claims summarise other papers rather than new measurements, and the literature it covers moves quickly — the version read here is a later revision than the 2024 first version recorded in this bibliography, with added material on reasoning models, so some model names and results postdate 2024. The authors' own experiment is deliberately simple: one bias benchmark of 80 samples, with some bias cells as small as 24 samples, so those percentages are coarse. Nothing in the survey directly evaluates judges of agent trajectories or tool-use traces; its applications sections discuss such uses, but the meta-evaluation evidence is from text-response judging.

sources.title: From Generation to Judgment: Opportunities and Challenges of LLM-as-a-judge
sources.abstract: Assessment and evaluation have long been critical challenges in artificial intelligence (AI) and natural language processing (NLP). Traditional methods, usually matching-based or small model-based, often fall short in open-ended and dynamic scenarios. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) inspire the "LLM-as-a-judge" paradigm, where LLMs are leveraged to perform scoring, ranking, or selection for various machine learning evaluation scenarios. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of LLM-based judgment and assessment, offering an in-depth overview to review this evolving field. We first provide the definition from both input and output perspectives. Then we introduce a systematic taxonomy to explore LLM-as-a-judge along three dimensions: what to judge, how to judge, and how to benchmark. Finally, we also highlight key challenges and promising future directions for this emerging area. More resources on LLM-as-a-judge are on the website: this https URL and this https URL .
sources.summary: Li and colleagues survey LLM-as-a-judge as a taxonomy of what to judge, how to judge, and how to benchmark the judge, covering six attributes and both tuning and prompting methods. It is background for Part 2 on a judge as a measurement instrument with its own errors.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Li, Jiang, Huang, and colleagues survey the shift named in their title: LLMs first used to generate text are now used to judge text — to score it, rank it, or select among alternatives. The survey's value for this tutorial is its taxonomy, a structured classification that separates three questions a judge designer must answer independently: what is being judged, how the judging is done, and how the judge itself is benchmarked. That separation is directly usable in Part 2 — LLM-as-a-Judge Methods — and its closing challenges (bias, scaling judgment, human–LLM co-judging) belong to Part 4 — Reliability, Limitations, and Future Directions.

## What they did

This is a literature survey; it runs no new experiment. It first defines LLM-as-a-judge by input and output (Figure 1): the input is point-wise (one candidate at a time), pair-wise (two candidates), or list-wise (several ranked at once), and the output is a score, a ranking, or a selection. It then classifies the field along three dimensions (Figure 5). Attributes — what to judge — are six: helpfulness, safety and security, reliability, relevance, logic, and overall quality (Figure 2), each defined in the survey's Table 1 (for example, reliability covers factual correctness and freedom from hallucination, meaning confident but false content). Methodology — how to judge — splits into tuning (training a model to judge, from manually labelled data or synthetic feedback generated by models, using supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning) and prompting (using a model as-is, with techniques including swapping answer order, rule augmentation with explicit criteria, multi-agent collaboration between several judging models, demonstrations, multi-turn interaction, and comparison acceleration). Applications are grouped as evaluation, alignment (using judgments as training signal), retrieval, and reasoning. Finally, benchmarks for judging the judges are sorted into four families: general performance, bias quantification, challenging tasks, and domain-specific performance, catalogued in the survey's Table 4.

{{figure:fig1-io-formats.png}}

{{figure:fig5-taxonomy.png}}

## What they found

Because this is a synthesis, its findings are organised claims about the literature rather than measurements. Three carry weight for the tutorial. First, the choice of what to judge is separable from the machinery: the same prompting or tuning method can be pointed at helpfulness or at logic, and a judge good on one attribute is not thereby good on another — the benchmark families in their Table 4 exist precisely because general performance, bias, hard-task, and domain performance diverge. Second, the bias picture is consistent across the work they review: judges tend to prefer longer, authoritative-looking, and well-formatted responses regardless of content, alongside judge-specific effects such as egocentric bias (favouring answers resembling one's own output). Third, their challenge list is specific about what is unsolved: mitigating bias beyond surface fixes, scaling judgment at inference time (spending more computation per judgment, through longer reasoning or repeated sampling) without efficiency and over-thinking costs, dynamic judging strategies for complex tasks, and human–LLM co-judgement, where human and model judges divide the work rather than one replacing the other. The survey also records that traditional overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE (which count shared words against a reference) perform poorly in open-ended settings, which is the gap LLM judges are meant to fill.

{{figure:fig2-attributes.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Name the attribute before the method. Helpfulness, reliability, relevance, and logic are different criteria; Part 2's work on criteria, rubrics, and scales starts from picking which of these a score is supposed to mean.
- Input format is a commitment. Point-wise scoring, pairwise choice, and list-wise ranking give different outputs and different failure modes (a pairwise judge can be order-sensitive; a point-wise judge needs a calibrated scale), and Part 3's judge design makes exactly this choice.
- Tuning and prompting are the two routes to a better judge, with opposite cost profiles: training data and training runs on one side, longer prompts and more calls on the other. The survey supports presenting both, not a winner.
- Benchmark the judge on the dimension you fear. Their four benchmark families imply that a general-performance result says little about bias or domain performance, which is a Part 4 caution in compact form.
- Human–LLM co-judgement is named as an open direction, not a solved pattern. The survey does not provide a tested division of labour, so the tutorial should not present one as established.

## Limits

The survey reports no new data, so every quantitative impression comes from papers it cites, under those papers' judges, datasets, and dates; it should not be quoted for an effect size. Coverage is broad rather than systematic in the reproducible sense — no screening counts are given — and the version read here is a later revision than the 2024 first version recorded in this bibliography, so parts of the taxonomy cite work from after 2024. Its applications in alignment, retrieval, and reasoning go well beyond evaluation, so only part of the map bears on judging agent behaviour, and agent trajectories as something to be judged are not its focus.

sources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
sources.venue: In International Conference on Learning Representations. arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.03629.
sources.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across tasks in language understanding and interactive decision making, their abilities for reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought prompting) and acting (e.g. action plan generation) have primarily been studied as separate topics. In this paper, we explore the use of LLMs to generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner, allowing for greater synergy between the two: reasoning traces help the model induce, track, and update action plans as well as handle exceptions, while actions allow it to interface with external sources, such as knowledge bases or environments, to gather additional information. We apply our approach, named ReAct, to a diverse set of language and decision making tasks and demonstrate its effectiveness over state-of-the-art baselines, as well as improved human interpretability and trustworthiness over methods without reasoning or acting components. Concretely, on question answering (HotpotQA) and fact verification (Fever), ReAct overcomes issues of hallucination and error propagation prevalent in chain-of-thought reasoning by interacting with a simple Wikipedia API, and generates human-like task-solving trajectories that are more interpretable than baselines without reasoning traces. On two interactive decision making benchmarks (ALFWorld and WebShop), ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learning methods by an absolute success rate of 34% and 10% respectively, while being prompted with only one or two in-context examples. Project site with code: this https URL
sources.summary: ReAct prompts a model to alternate a written thought with a tool action, and reads back each observation. Its traces are the kind of agent output Part 1 says a final-answer check cannot see, and its own human error analysis already scores steps rather than answers.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Yao and colleagues introduced ReAct, short for reasoning and acting. A language model writes a thought, takes an action such as a search, reads the result, and repeats. That loop is the working definition of a tool-using agent behind most of the tutorial. The paper scores success with exact match, accuracy, and environment rewards, not a judge. It still matters for Part 1, because its own human error analysis shows that a right answer can come from a wrong trace, and a wrong answer from a reasonable one.

## What they did

The model is a frozen PaLM-540B, prompted with a few hand-written example trajectories. A trajectory is the sequence of thoughts, actions, and observations for one task. A thought changes nothing in the environment.

There are four tasks:

- **HotpotQA**, multi-hop question answering. Multi-hop means the answer needs facts from more than one Wikipedia page. The tools are `search`, `lookup`, and `finish` against a deliberately simple Wikipedia interface. The metric is exact match (EM), where the answer string must equal the gold label.
- **FEVER**, claim verification with three labels, using the same tools. The metric is accuracy.
- **ALFWorld**, a text game in a simulated house. Success is decided by the environment on 134 unseen games.
- **WebShop**, a shopping site with 1.18 million products. Score is the share of requested attributes the bought item has. Success rate (SR) is the share of episodes where every requirement is met.

The baselines are prompts cut down from the same trajectories. Standard has no thoughts or actions. Chain-of-thought (CoT) keeps the reasoning and drops the tools. CoT-SC samples 21 reasoning chains and takes a majority vote. Act keeps the tools and drops the thoughts. Two hybrids fall back from one method to the other when it gives no answer or is unsure.

{{figure:fig1-trajectories.png}}

## What they found

On its own, ReAct is not the best question answerer. In Table 1, HotpotQA EM is 27.4 for ReAct, 29.4 for CoT, and 28.7 for Standard. FEVER reverses that order: 60.9 for ReAct against 56.3 for CoT. The best numbers come from the hybrids: 35.1 on HotpotQA and 64.6 on FEVER. Supervised systems reach 67.5 and 89.5.

{{figure:table1-hotpotqa-fever.png}}

Table 2 is the closest thing in the paper to trajectory evaluation. People labelled 200 HotpotQA runs, 50 correct and 50 incorrect for each of ReAct and CoT, by why they succeeded or failed. Among CoT's correct answers, 14% rested on hallucinated reasoning or facts, against 6% for ReAct. Hallucination was 56% of CoT's failures and 0% of ReAct's. ReAct failed in other ways: 47% reasoning errors, including repeated loops of the same step, and 23% unhelpful search results. Label ambiguity, a right answer that did not match the label string, was 29% and 28%. The paper does not say who labelled the runs or how well they agreed.

{{figure:table2-error-modes.png}}

On the decision tasks the gap is larger. In Table 3, ALFWorld success is 71% for the best of six ReAct prompts, 57% averaged over the six, and 45% for the best Act prompt. In Table 4, WebShop success rate is 40.0 for ReAct against 30.1 for Act and 59.6 for human experts. The abstract's 34-point ALFWorld gain is ReAct's best prompt (71) minus an imitation-learning agent's best of eight (37). That agent also used beam search, while ReAct used greedy decoding.

{{figure:table3-4-alfworld-webshop.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- An agent's output is a trajectory, not only an answer. In Table 2, 6–14% of answers that exact match accepts rest on a hallucinated trace. That is Part 1's case against final-answer scoring, in the paper's own numbers.
- Different methods fail in different ways. CoT invents facts, and ReAct loops or gets stuck on bad search results. A rubric for a tool-using agent, as in Part 3, needs criteria for both tool choice and reasoning, because one score cannot tell those failures apart.
- Best-of-k and average are different claims. Best-of-six ALFWorld is 71% and the average is 57%. Part 4's point about consistency applies to the agent before any judge is involved.
- Exact match fails in both directions. About three in ten failures were right answers that did not match the label. A judge can recover some of these, and that is one reason Part 2 compares rules with judges.
- The failure categories are a ready-made first draft of trajectory criteria. They come from 200 labelled runs with no reported agreement, so treat them as a starting point to validate.

## Limits

This paper evaluates the agent, not an evaluator. There is no LLM judge, and the human labels have no annotator description or agreement figure. Table 1 does not print its evaluation set size, and no table reports variance or significance. The Wikipedia tool is deliberately weak, so the paper cannot separate the value of reasoning from the cost of poor retrieval. Baselines from earlier papers were copied, not re-run. The ReAct failure column in Table 2 has odd percentages and sums to 99%, which 50 runs with one label each cannot produce, and the paper does not explain it. There is no cost, latency, or step-count comparison.

On top, a HotpotQA question about the Apple Remote answered four ways: Standard answers iPod, chain-of-thought reasons its way to a wrong list of devices, Act-only searches and finishes with yes, and ReAct alternates thoughts with searches and answers keyboard function keys, marked correct. Below, an ALFWorld task to put a pepper shaker in a drawer: Act-only repeats a failed action, and ReAct thinks about where to look and succeeds.

sources.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
sources.abstract: Language models (LMs) exhibit remarkable abilities to solve new tasks from just a few examples or textual instructions, especially at scale. They also, paradoxically, struggle with basic functionality, such as arithmetic or factual lookup, where much simpler and smaller models excel. In this paper, we show that LMs can teach themselves to use external tools via simple APIs and achieve the best of both worlds. We introduce Toolformer, a model trained to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to best incorporate the results into future token prediction. This is done in a self-supervised way, requiring nothing more than a handful of demonstrations for each API. We incorporate a range of tools, including a calculator, a Q\&A system, two different search engines, a translation system, and a calendar. Toolformer achieves substantially improved zero-shot performance across a variety of downstream tasks, often competitive with much larger models, without sacrificing its core language modeling abilities.
sources.summary: Toolformer fine-tunes a 6.7B model to insert its own API calls, keeping only calls that make the following text easier to predict. It separates tool use from answer quality in one table, and its results depend on a decoding rule that forces calls, which is why tool choice needs its own check.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Schick and colleagues at Meta AI teach a language model to decide when to call a tool, which tool to call, and with what input. The tools are a question-answering model, a calculator, Wikipedia search, a translator, and a calendar. It is not an agent benchmark, and there is no judge. It is here for Part 1 and Part 3, because the paper reports how often the model called a tool separately from whether the answer was right. Those are the two things a tool-using agent's evaluation has to keep apart: did it pick the right tool with the right parameters, and was the answer good.

## What they did

An API call is written into the text as a short marked span: the tool name, its text input, an arrow, and the result. Figure 1 shows four examples.

{{figure:fig1-api-calls.png}}

Training data is made in three steps (Figure 2):

1. **Sample.** For each tool, a few-shot prompt asks GPT-J, a 6.7-billion-parameter model, to propose calls at positions in ordinary web text from CCNet.
2. **Execute.** Each proposed call is run, and the result is kept as text.
3. **Filter.** A call is kept only if inserting it with its result lowers the model's loss on the next few tokens. Loss is the negative log-probability of the actual text. The call has to beat both no call and a call with no result, by a threshold.

GPT-J is then fine-tuned on the text with the kept calls inserted. No person labels which calls are good. The only human input is a handful of examples per tool, plus the per-tool data filters and thresholds the authors set.

{{figure:fig2-pipeline.png}}

At test time, decoding starts a call whenever the call token is among the 10 most likely next tokens, at most once per input. Some tools are switched off for some tasks: search for the fact-completion probes and the QA tool for question answering. Correctness is lenient. On the fact probes the right word must appear in the first five predicted words. On question answering it must appear in the first 20.

## What they found

Tools help most where the base model is weakest. In Table 4, math word-problem accuracy is 40.4, 29.4, and 44.0 on ASDiv, SVAMP, and MAWPS. GPT-3 (175B) scores 14.0, 10.0, and 19.8. Toolformer called the calculator on 97.9% of math examples. On question answering the picture reverses. GPT-3 is higher on all three datasets, for example 65.9 against 48.8 on TriviaQA (Table 5).

{{figure:table4-math.png}}

The ablation separates tool use from fine-tuning. "Toolformer (disabled)" is the same model with calls blocked. On math it scores 14.8, 6.3, and 15.0, so most of the gain comes from the calls.

Table 9 is the evaluation lesson. With ordinary greedy decoding (k = 1), the model calls a tool on 40.3% of T-REx fact probes and 8.5% of WebQS questions. At k = 10 those rise to 98.1% and 100.0%, and WebQS accuracy rises from 19.3 to 26.3. At k = 1 the model is somewhat calibrated: on the examples where it chose not to call, it beats the no-tool model (44.3 against 34.9 on T-REx). That calibration disappears as k grows.

{{figure:table9-decoding.png}}

Tool use also has a size threshold. In Figure 4, models below about 775 million parameters score about the same with and without tools. Wikipedia search is the exception, which the paper calls comparatively easy to use.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Report tool use and answer quality separately. Table 9 splits accuracy by whether a call was made. A Part 3 judge for a tool-using agent can do the same, scoring tool choice and parameters as their own criteria.
- A high call rate is not good tool choice. Most of these call rates come from a decoding rule that pushes the model to call. Whether a call was needed is a separate question, and the paper does not test it.
- "Was a tool called" is not "were the arguments right". The paper never checks whether the calculator input or the search query was correct. That gap is exactly the parameter check Part 3 names.
- Lenient string matching shapes the result. First-five-words and first-20-words rules reward longer outputs. Part 2's comparison of rules with judges starts with what the rule actually accepts.
- Name the comparison. "Beats GPT-3" holds for math and not for question answering, in the same paper.

## Limits

Each input gets at most one call, and calls are never chained, so this is not multi-step agent behaviour. The model cannot refine a search or browse results, and it does not weigh the cost of a call. There is no judge and no human rating of outputs. Evaluation set sizes, variance, and significance are not printed. Perplexity with tools switched on is not measured. Language-modelling ability is reported only for the model with calls disabled. The calendar barely contributes to the temporal-fact result (0.2% of examples). No other tool-use method is run as a baseline.

sources.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
sources.abstract: Existing benchmarks do not test language agents on their interaction with human users or ability to follow domain-specific rules, both of which are vital for deploying them in real world applications. We propose $\tau$-bench, a benchmark emulating dynamic conversations between a user (simulated by language models) and a language agent provided with domain-specific API tools and policy guidelines. We employ an efficient and faithful evaluation process that compares the database state at the end of a conversation with the annotated goal state. We also propose a new metric (pass^k) to evaluate the reliability of agent behavior over multiple trials. Our experiments show that even state-of-the-art function calling agents (like gpt-4o) succeed on <50% of the tasks, and are quite inconsistent (pass^8 <25% in retail). Our findings point to the need for methods that can improve the ability of agents to act consistently and follow rules reliably.
sources.summary: Yao and colleagues propose τ-bench, where a tool-using agent must converse with a simulated user, follow a written domain policy, and leave the database in the goal state. Its pass^k metric shows that agents succeeding once often fail on repeat trials, grounding Part 1 and Part 4 in a concrete reliability measure.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Yao, Shinn, Razavi, and Narasimhan build a benchmark for a situation most agent tests avoid: the agent must talk to a user while it works. In τ-bench (tau-bench, after the Greek letter in the name), a language-model agent (software that uses a language model to decide actions) has database tools and a written domain policy, and must gather missing information from a simulated user, follow the policy, and change the database correctly. That combination is the core difficulty in Part 1 — AI Agents and Evaluation Challenges: why final-answer scoring is insufficient when success depends on the conversation, the tool calls, and the rules in between. Its reliability metric also belongs to Part 4 — Reliability, Limitations, and Future Directions.

## What they did

The benchmark has two domains. τ-retail simulates an online shop (500 users, 50 products, 1,000 orders, 15 API tools) and τ-airline simulates flight reservations (500 users, 300 flights, 2,000 reservations, 13 API tools), with 115 retail and 50 airline tasks (Table 1 of the paper). An API (application programming interface) tool here is a named database operation, such as cancelling a reservation, that the agent invokes with arguments. The user is simulated by a language model given a hidden instruction, so the agent does not receive every fact up front and must ask. Scoring is automatic and state-based: at the end, the database state is compared with the annotated goal state, so a task passes only if the right records changed. The authors add pass^k: the share of tasks the agent passes on all k independent trials (i.i.d., independent and identically distributed repeats). pass^1 is therefore ordinary single-trial success, and falling pass^k exposes inconsistency that one run hides. Agents were mostly function-calling agents (the model emits structured tool calls directly), with ReAct (interleaving reasoning text and actions) and Act (actions without the reasoning text) compared on retail; models included gpt-4o, gpt-4-turbo, gpt-3.5-turbo, Claude 3 variants, Gemini 1.5 variants, Mistral, and Llama-3-70B, with model names as printed.

{{figure:fig1-setup.png}}

## What they found

Even the strongest agent solved well under half the tasks overall. In Table 2, gpt-4o with function calling scored pass^1 of 61.2% on retail and 35.2% on airline (weighted average 48.2%); gpt-4-turbo reached 57.7% and 32.4%, and gpt-3.5-turbo only 20.0% and 10.8%. Function calling beat ReAct and Act on retail for the models compared in Figure 3 of the paper. Consistency collapsed with repetition: Figure 4 shows gpt-4o's pass^k falling to roughly 25% by k = 8 on retail, so an agent that passes a task once passes it every time only about a quarter of the time. Removing the domain policy from the prompt (an ablation, removing one component to measure its contribution) cut gpt-4o on airline from 33.2% to 10.8% in Table 3, showing the harder domain actually depends on reading the rules. Manually examining 36 genuine failures of gpt-4o on retail, the authors group them into wrong tool arguments from complex database reasoning, wrong decisions, and partially completed compound requests.

{{figure:table2-pass1.png}}

{{figure:fig4-passk.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 1 can use this as the worked example of a dynamic test: the user withholds information, the state changes with each tool call, and a wrong early action changes what is possible later — none of that is visible in a final-answer check.
- State-based scoring is a middle path between grading the text reply and grading the whole trajectory (the step-by-step record of actions). The database either ends in the goal state or it does not, regardless of how polished the closing message sounds.
- pass^k turns reliability into a number. A single successful run overstates a stochastic (randomness-influenced) agent; Part 4's consistency question is exactly the gap between pass^1 and pass^8 here.
- Policy following can be isolated. The airline ablation shows a model can look competent in a commonsense domain while barely using the written rules, which matters when a rubric assumes the agent read its instructions.
- Simulated users make such tests repeatable and cheap enough to run, but the result is conditional on the simulator's behaviour — a point to state, not a defect the paper hides.

## Limits

The user simulator is itself a language model, so conversation realism and instruction-anchoring failures in the simulator can create or mask agent failures; the authors had to fix some tasks after finding simulator-side ambiguity. There are only two domains and 165 tasks, both customer-service shaped, so the pass rates do not transfer to coding, web, or research agents. The paper reports its own cost analysis for one pairing (about $0.38 per retail task with a gpt-4 agent and gpt-4 user), but cost is not compared across all models. Nothing here evaluates an LLM judge; scoring is database comparison, so this source cannot support claims about judge quality.

Right: an example airline trajectory where the user asks to change a flight, the agent reads the reservation, explains the basic-economy rule, and cancels after the user agrees.

sources.title: τ^2-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
sources.abstract: Existing benchmarks for conversational AI agents simulate single-control environments, where only the AI agent can use tools to interact with the world, while the user remains a passive information provider. This differs from real-world scenarios like technical support, where users need to actively participate in modifying the state of the (shared) world. In order to address this gap, we introduce $\tau^2$-bench, with four key contributions: 1) A novel Telecom dual-control domain modeled as a Dec-POMDP, where both agent and user make use of tools to act in a shared, dynamic environment that tests both agent coordination and communication, 2) A compositional task generator that programmatically creates diverse, verifiable tasks from atomic components, ensuring domain coverage and controlled complexity, 3) A reliable user simulator tightly coupled with the environment, whose behavior is constrained by tools and observable states, improving simulation fidelity, 4) Fine-grained analysis of agent performance through multiple ablations including separating errors arising from reasoning vs communication/coordination. In particular, our experiments show significant performance drops when agents shift from no-user to dual-control, highlighting the challenges of guiding users. Overall, $\tau^2$-bench provides a controlled testbed for agents that must both reason effectively and guide user actions.
sources.summary: τ²-bench scores conversational agents in a telecom setting where the user and the agent both call tools on a shared world. Success is a set of assertions on the final state, not an LLM judge, and pass^1 on telecom is far below retail for the same models.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Barres, Dong, Ray, Si, and Narasimhan extend τ-bench from a conversation where only the agent acts to one where the user acts too. The new domain is telecom support: the user's phone is a set of tools, and the agent's account system is another set, and both write the same world. Part 1 needs this distinction. A final database that looks right is not the same fact as a trajectory you would trust, and one run is not yet a measurement. The score they report is pass^k, the fraction of k independent runs that succeed.

## What they did

Retail (115 tasks) and airline (50 tasks) stay single-control, as in the earlier benchmark. Telecom adds user tools: 15 that write and 15 that read, against the agent's 6 write and 7 read tools. Tasks are built from atomic subtasks, service, mobile data, and MMS, composed so that the assertions pass only after the full solution. The generator yields 2,285 tasks. The reported results use a balanced subsample of 114.

Success in telecom is assertion functions on the final world state. The paper does not name an LLM as the scorer. The user, though, is an LLM, gpt-4.1 for every run, following a persona that is empty, easy, or hard. Agents are gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, o4-mini, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet, at temperature 0, four runs per task. Two ablations, on gpt-4.1 and o4-mini only, pull the collaboration apart. In no-user mode the agent receives a ticket and controls every tool, including the ones the user would have called. In oracle-plan mode the agent is given the solution's tool sequence and still has to carry it out with the user.

{{figure:fig2-trajectory.png}}

## What they found

Figure 3 prints pass^k. For gpt-4.1, pass^1 is 0.74 on retail, 0.56 on airline, and 0.34 on telecom. At k = 4 those fall to 0.53, 0.40, and 0.19. The other three models show the same shape: telecom is the low bar, and the bar drops as k grows. Claude 3.7 Sonnet's telecom pass^1 is 0.49, close to its airline pass^1 of 0.50, and its telecom pass^4 is 0.25.

Figure 4 is the ablation, pass^1 on telecom. Under the original policy, gpt-4.1 goes from 0.52 with no user, to 0.34 in the default dual-control setting, to 0.73 with an oracle plan. o4-mini goes from 0.67, to 0.42, to 0.96. The paper calls the no-user to default change an 18-point drop and a 25-point drop. A more specific workflow policy raises default and no-user, and it lowers the oracle-plan scores, 0.73 to 0.57 for gpt-4.1 and 0.96 to 0.88 for o4-mini. Giving the agent the ground-truth sequence and a more detailed policy at the same time made the agent worse.

{{figure:fig3-passk.png}}

{{figure:fig4-modes.png}}

A manual look at the user simulator finds errors on 16% of 50 telecom conversations, 6% of them critical, against 40% of retail conversations and 47% of airline ones (Table 2). The telecom errors they list are all a premature transfer to a human.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- The score is a rule on the final state. Part 1's point stands even so: the same assertions fail much more often when the user has to act, so the trajectory, not only the end state, is doing the work.
- pass^k makes the reliability visible. gpt-4.1's telecom success falls from 0.34 at one run to 0.19 when all four runs must succeed. A single demo is a weaker measurement than the paper's own metric.
- Splitting reasoning from collaboration is a useful ablation for Part 3. No-user mode is the agent with every tool. Default mode is the agent that must ask the user to use theirs. The gap is large for both models tested.
- An oracle plan does not remove the need for the conversation, and a more detailed policy can hurt the agent that already has the plan. More instructions are not automatically a better evaluation.
- The user simulator is itself a model, and it makes mistakes. A failed task is not automatically an agent failure. They measured that, at 6% critical on the telecom sample they read.

## Limits

Retail and airline never receive user tools. The authors say they have not tried. Results are the 114-task subsample, not the 2,285 generated tasks. The workflow policy is pass^1 only, and only for two models. Figure 5, success against the number of actions, does not print a value per bin. The prose says default-mode pass^1 is close to zero beyond seven actions. No LLM judge grades these tasks, so the paper does not say how a judge would have scored the same traces.

On the right the agent reads line details, sees roaming disabled, and enables roaming with agent tools. The caption says the user's phone state changes because the agent wrote the shared world.

sources.title: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation of Large Language Models
sources.venue: In Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, volume 267 of Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, pages 48371–48392.
sources.abstract: Function calling, also called tool use, refers to an LLM’s ability to invoke external functions, APIs, or user-defined tools in response to user queries—an essential capability for agentic LLM applications. Despite its prominence, there did not exist a standard benchmark to evaluate function calling abilities, due to two reasons – the challenging nature of evaluating when a function call is valid, and the challenge of acquiring diverse, real-world functions. We present the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL), a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate function calling capabilities in a wide range of real-world settings. The BFCL benchmark evaluates serial and parallel function calls, across various programming languages using a novel Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) evaluation method that can easily scale to thousands of functions. We construct the benchmark using a combination of expert curated, and user-contributed functions and associated prompts. Finally, BFCL benchmark evaluates the ability of models to abstain and reason in stateful multi-step agentic setting. Evaluating a wide range of models, we observe that while state-of-the-art LLMs excel at singleturn calls, memory, dynamic decision-making, and long-horizon reasoning remain open challenges. Since its preview, BFCL has become the defacto standard for evaluating function-calls, and can be accessed at gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/leaderboard.html.
sources.summary: A standard benchmark for whether a model emits a valid tool call, including multi-step calls. Part 1 and Part 3 both need this distinction: checking the call can be deterministic, while judging the advice often cannot.

sources.title: ToolSandbox: A Stateful, Conversational, Interactive Evaluation Benchmark for LLM Tool Use Capabilities
sources.abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) advancements sparked a growing research interest in tool assisted LLMs solving real-world challenges, which calls for comprehensive evaluation of tool-use capabilities. While previous works focused on either evaluating over stateless web services (RESTful API), based on a single turn user prompt, or an off-policy dialog trajectory, ToolSandbox includes stateful tool execution, implicit state dependencies between tools, a built-in user simulator supporting on-policy conversational evaluation and a dynamic evaluation strategy for intermediate and final milestones over an arbitrary trajectory. We show that open source and proprietary models have a significant performance gap, and complex tasks like State Dependency, Canonicalization and Insufficient Information defined in ToolSandbox are challenging even the most capable SOTA LLMs, providing brand-new insights into tool-use LLM capabilities. ToolSandbox evaluation framework is released at this https URL
sources.summary: A stateful, conversational benchmark for tool use. Relevant where the tutorial contrasts a single tool call with an interaction that depends on earlier state.
sources.note: arXiv id 2408.04682 is a 2024 submission. The reading checklist dates the paper 2025.

sources.title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
sources.abstract: Recent advances in Language Model (LM) agents and tool use, exemplified by applications like ChatGPT Plugins, enable a rich set of capabilities but also amplify potential risks - such as leaking private data or causing financial losses. Identifying these risks is labor-intensive, necessitating implementing the tools, setting up the environment for each test scenario manually, and finding risky cases. As tools and agents become more complex, the high cost of testing these agents will make it increasingly difficult to find high-stakes, long-tailed risks. To address these challenges, we introduce ToolEmu: a framework that uses an LM to emulate tool execution and enables the testing of LM agents against a diverse range of tools and scenarios, without manual instantiation. Alongside the emulator, we develop an LM-based automatic safety evaluator that examines agent failures and quantifies associated risks. We test both the tool emulator and evaluator through human evaluation and find that 68.8% of failures identified with ToolEmu would be valid real-world agent failures. Using our curated initial benchmark consisting of 36 high-stakes tools and 144 test cases, we provide a quantitative risk analysis of current LM agents and identify numerous failures with potentially severe outcomes. Notably, even the safest LM agent exhibits such failures 23.9% of the time according to our evaluator, underscoring the need to develop safer LM agents for real-world deployment.
sources.summary: Ruan and colleagues introduce ToolEmu, which uses a language model to emulate tools in a sandbox and a model-based evaluator to flag risky agent behaviour. Human validation found most identified failures credible, while even the safest agent tested still failed in about a quarter of high-stakes cases.
sources.note: The arXiv submission is 2023 (2309.15817). The reading checklist dates it 2024.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Ruan, Dong, Wang, and colleagues tackle a problem that appears as soon as agents can act: how do you find dangerous failures before deployment without building every real tool and letting the agent loose on it? Their answer, ToolEmu, uses a language model to emulate (imitate the behaviour of) tool execution inside a sandbox (an isolated test environment), and another model-based evaluator to flag risky trajectories (the sequence of actions an agent took). For Part 1 — AI Agents and Evaluation Challenges — this is the risk side of the evaluation lifecycle, including production-like testing before release. For Part 4 — Reliability, Limitations, and Future Directions — it is also a caution: the test harness is itself a model, so its failures can hide or invent the agent's failures.

## What they did

ToolEmu has three parts. First, an emulator: given a tool specification (a description of what a tool does, without a working implementation), a language model plays the tool, validating inputs and inventing plausible outputs and state changes. A second, adversarial emulator (deliberately steered toward edge cases, in a red-teaming style — actively trying to provoke failures) searches for situations that expose the agent. Second, automatic evaluators for safety and helpfulness, which are qualitative labels converted to scores on a 0–3 scale (Table 1 of the paper), with safety judging whether the trajectory created risk and helpfulness whether it served the user. Third, a curated benchmark of 36 high-stakes toolkits (finance, email, home devices, and similar) and 144 test cases, written so the correct behaviour is often to clarify, refuse, or take a safer action rather than simply execute. Crucially, both emulator and evaluators were validated against human annotators before the authors trusted them to score agents. The base agents tested were GPT-4, ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), Claude-2, and Vicuna-1.5 models using ReAct-style prompting (reasoning interleaved with actions), at temperature 0.

{{figure:fig1-framework.png}}

## What they found

The validation is the headline for evaluators. Human checking found that 68.8% of the failures ToolEmu identified would be valid real-world agent failures, and the paper reports its emulator producing simulations free of critical issues over 80% of the time (Table 4), with the adversarial emulator finding more true failures than the standard one at a small precision cost (Table 3; precision is the share of flagged cases that are genuine). The safety evaluator's agreement with human annotations was comparable to agreement between human annotators on the binarised labels.

On the benchmark itself, no agent was safe. In Table 5, the GPT-4 agent had the best basic safety score (2.007 of 3) yet still had identified failures in 39.4% of test cases. Adding safety requirements to its prompt improved that to a 23.9% failure incidence with a higher helpfulness score (1.824), while Claude-2, ChatGPT, and the Vicuna models sat between roughly 44% and 62% failure incidence under the basic prompt. A do-nothing NoAct agent scores perfectly on safety and near zero on helpfulness, which is why the authors always report the two together (the safety–helpfulness frontier in Figure 6).

{{figure:table5-agents.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Emulation trades fidelity for coverage. A model-emulated sandbox can test 36 toolkits without implementing them, which is why Part 1's lifecycle needs a stage like this before production monitoring; the price is that the simulator's realism bounds every conclusion.
- An automatic evaluator earns trust by validation, not by construction. Comparing the evaluator with human annotators — and reporting where they disagree — is the step that separates this from simply asking a model whether things went well.
- Safety without helpfulness is gameable. The NoAct result is the cleanest demonstration that a single safety score rewards inaction; any rubric needs the second axis.
- Prompted safety instructions helped the strongest agent here (39.4% down to 23.9% failure incidence). That is evidence about this benchmark and prompt, not a general guarantee that safety prompting works.
- Even the best result is a failure rate, not a pass. A benchmark whose safest agent fails about a quarter of high-stakes cases supports Part 4 claims about open problems, not claims that current agents are deployment-ready.

## Limits

Everything is filtered through GPT-4-class models as emulator and evaluator, so correlated model blind spots can hide the same failure in both the test and the grading; the authors' human validation covers samples, not every trajectory. The benchmark is small (144 cases) and deliberately high-stakes, so its failure rates are not estimates of everyday agent failure rates. Tool specifications were generated rather than taken from real implementations, and the authors note the results at temperature 0 were still not fully deterministic. The work predates function-calling agents as the default, using ReAct-style agents throughout.

figures.caption: Figure 1 from Ruan et al. (2024). Overview of ToolEmu: an LM-emulated sandbox executes tool actions and an LM evaluator assesses the resulting trajectory for risk.

figures.alt: Safety and helpfulness table on a 0 to 3 scale. GPT-4 with a basic prompt has safety 2.007 and 39.4% failure incidence; with the safety prompt it reaches 2.359 safety, 23.9% failures, and 1.824 helpfulness. A no-action agent has perfect safety and 0.063 helpfulness.

sources.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
sources.abstract: The potential of Large Language Model (LLM) as agents has been widely acknowledged recently. Thus, there is an urgent need to quantitatively \textit{evaluate LLMs as agents} on challenging tasks in interactive environments. We present AgentBench, a multi-dimensional benchmark that consists of 8 distinct environments to assess LLM-as-Agent's reasoning and decision-making abilities. Our extensive test over \num API-based and open-sourced (OSS) LLMs shows that, while top commercial LLMs present a strong ability of acting as agents in complex environments, there is a significant disparity in performance between them and many OSS competitors that are no larger than 70B. We identify the typical reasons of failures in environments and LLMs, showing that poor long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction following abilities are the main obstacles for developing usable LLM agents. Improving instruction following and training on high quality multi-round alignment data could improve agent performance. And different from existing assumptions, training on code present ambivalent impacts on different agent tasks. Datasets, environments, and an integrated evaluation package for AgentBench are released at this https URL .
sources.summary: A benchmark of eight interactive environments (shell, SQL, knowledge graph, games, household, web) on which 29 LLMs act as agents. It reports outcome scores and a breakdown of how runs end, and one environment uses an LLM as host and grader.
sources.note: arXiv id 2308.03688 is a 2023 submission. The reading checklist dates the paper 2024.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

AgentBench is one of the first broad benchmarks that treats an LLM as an agent: it acts in an environment over many turns, and the environment answers back. It is a reference point for Part 1's definition of agent evaluation and its argument that a final-answer score is not the whole story. The paper shows both sides. Its headline is an outcome score, but its most useful table classifies how each run ended. One environment also uses gpt-3.5-turbo to answer the agent's questions and grade its progress. That makes it an early agent benchmark with an LLM judge inside it, which matters for Parts 2 and 4.

## What they did

There are eight environments, grouped by what grounds them (Figure 1):

- **Code.** Operating system: real bash in an Ubuntu Docker container, scored by success rate. Database: SQL over real tables, success rate. Knowledge graph: answering questions through Freebase query tools, answer F1.
- **Game.** Digital card game: a simplified turn-based battle against a scripted opponent. Lateral thinking puzzles: the agent asks yes/no questions to uncover a hidden story, scored by "game progress". House-holding: ALFWorld, a text simulation of household tasks, success rate.
- **Web.** Web shopping (WebShop), scored by reward. Web browsing (Mind2Web), scored by step success rate.

{{figure:fig1-overview.png}}

Every model gets the same prompt format: a "Thought" and an "Action" each turn, in the style of ReAct, at temperature 0 with no retries. The test set has 1,014 problems, about 11,000 model calls per model. Twenty-nine models were tested: API-only commercial models and open-weight models up to 70B parameters. Raw scores differ greatly between environments, so each environment's score is divided by the average of all tested models on it. These are averaged into an overall score, "OA", and the weights are frozen for later comparisons.

Each run's ending is classified as Complete, Context Limit Exceeded, **Invalid Format** (the reply broke the output format), **Invalid Action** (well formed but not an allowed action), or **Task Limit Exceeded** (ran out of turns or kept repeating itself).

In the lateral thinking puzzles, the "host" is gpt-3.5-turbo. It answers the agent's questions and checks which key points of the hidden story the agent has reached. The key points were themselves summarised by gpt-3.5-turbo.

## What they found

gpt-4 scored highest, with OA 4.01, and was best on 6 of 8 environments, reaching 78% success on house-holding (Table 3). API models averaged 2.32 and open models 0.51. The best open model, codellama-34b, scored 0.96. Several open models scored zero on whole environments.

{{figure:table3-results.png}}

Averaged across models, the commonest non-completion was running out of turns. Task Limit Exceeded covers 82.5% of lateral-puzzle runs and 67.9% of knowledge-graph runs (Table 4). Other environments failed differently. Invalid Format was 53.3% on the database and 38.5% on the card game. Invalid Action was 64.1% on house-holding. The authors read the turn-limit failures as weak long-horizon reasoning, and the format failures as poor instruction following.

{{figure:table4-outcomes.png}}

They also report that code fine-tuning helped some environments and hurt others. Alignment on GPT-generated conversations let vicuna-13b roughly match codellama-34b, and llama-2-13b and llama-2-70b scored about the same. These are comparisons between a few model pairs, not controlled ablations.

Human validation of the puzzle host found the automatic grader more lenient than people on two secondary metrics, especially for open models. The authors say the main game-progress metric matched human evaluation, but give no numbers for the comparison.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A normalised, averaged outcome score ranks models but does not say what went wrong. The ending categories do, and they are cheap to log.
- Environments fail in different ways. One "agent reliability" number would hide that format errors dominate one task and running out of turns dominates another.
- Format and action validity can be checked by rules. Only some agent failures need a judge.
- An LLM grader inside a benchmark is a measuring instrument. This one was checked against people and found lenient on some metrics, more so for weaker agents. Part 4's reliability concerns apply to it.
- The overall score depends on the models used to set its weights. Compare OA only within that frame.

## Limits

The scores are for 2023–2024 models with one fixed prompt style, greedy decoding, and history truncated to about 3,500 tokens. The overall score's weights come from this model set. Success is judged on outcomes and step matches; intermediate reasoning and tool parameters are not graded. The puzzle host's validation is described only in words. The model-family comparisons are observational.
