sources.title: AgentBoard: An Analytical Evaluation Board of Multi-turn LLM Agents
sources.abstract: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) as general-purpose agents is essential for understanding their capabilities and facilitating their integration into practical applications. However, the evaluation process presents substantial challenges. A primary obstacle is the benchmarking of agent performance across diverse scenarios within a unified framework, especially in maintaining partially-observable environments and ensuring multi-round interactions. Moreover, current evaluation frameworks mostly focus on the final success rate, revealing few insights during the process and failing to provide a deep understanding of the model abilities. To address these challenges, we introduce AgentBoard, a pioneering comprehensive benchmark and accompanied open-source evaluation framework tailored to analytical evaluation of LLM agents. AgentBoard offers a fine-grained progress rate metric that captures incremental advancements as well as a comprehensive evaluation toolkit that features easy assessment of agents for multi-faceted analysis. This not only sheds light on the capabilities and limitations of LLM agents but also propels the interpretability of their performance to the forefront. Ultimately, AgentBoard serves as a step towards demystifying agent behaviors and accelerating the development of stronger LLM agents.
sources.summary: Ma and colleagues present AgentBoard, a nine-environment board for multi-turn LLM agents whose progress-rate metric credits subgoals achieved along a trajectory rather than only final success. The metric agrees strongly with human progress judgments and separates models that success rate cannot distinguish.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Ma, Zhang, Zhu, and colleagues argue that a single success rate hides almost everything interesting about an agent. AgentBoard is their response: a multi-environment test board whose main metric grades partial progress along a trajectory (the agent's sequence of steps), not only whether the task was finished. That is a direct Part 1 — AI Agents and Evaluation Challenges — point: once a system acts over many steps, evaluation needs instruments that show where it got to and where it stalled. The board's analytical breakdowns also feed Part 4 — Reliability, Limitations, and Future Directions, because they separate kinds of failure instead of collapsing them into one number.

## What they did

AgentBoard unifies nine environments under one agent interface and one prompting scheme: embodied household and science tasks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, BabyAI), games (Jericho, PDDL), web tasks (WebShop, WebArena), and tool tasks (Tool-Query and Tool-Operation), grouped as four scenarios. Environments are partially observable (the agent sees only part of the state and must explore) and multi-round. The headline metric is progress rate: tasks are decomposed into subgoals (checkpoints on a valid solution path, annotated by humans and verified by playing the tasks), and the score is the fraction of subgoals achieved, alongside the binary success rate. Figure 1 gives the overview. The authors validate progress rate against human judgments on 60 trajectories per task. They evaluate a range of proprietary and open-weight models — GPT-4, Claude 2, Gemini, GPT-3.5, Llama and Llama-3 variants, CodeLlama, Mistral, DeepSeek, and agent-tuned models, with names as printed — using a unified reflex agent (an agent that repeatedly predicts the next action from the goal and interaction history) with a one-shot example.

{{figure:fig1-overview.png}}

## What they found

Progress rate discriminates where success rate cannot. In Table 3, GPT-4 leads with a 70.0% average progress rate and 47.9% success rate across the nine environments; the next proprietary models trail, and most open-weight models are far lower on both. The paper's motivating example is in the main-results text: Llama2-13b and Mistral-7b have similarly negligible success rates (2.1% and 3.9%), yet their progress rates differ sharply (18.9% versus 24.6%), and Mistral-7b generally outperforms Llama2-13b — a conclusion invisible from success alone. Human verification supports the metric itself: Figure 3 reports Pearson correlation (a measure of linear agreement, from −1 to 1) above 0.95 between progress rate and human evaluation on every task shown, with substantial inter-annotator agreement. Analytical cuts add diagnosis: models lose much more on hard than easy cases (Table 5), grounding accuracy (correctly referring actions to objects in the environment) varies by task family (Table 4), and progress accumulates differently over long interactions, with most models plateauing early on the hardest environments (Figure 4 of the paper).

{{figure:fig3-human-verification.png}}

{{figure:table3-results.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A progress metric changes what an evaluation can say. Two agents can both score near zero on success and still differ meaningfully in capability; Part 1's argument against final-answer-only scoring is this measurement problem in agent form.
- Subgoal decomposition is rubric design by another name. Someone must decide what counts as a checkpoint and in what order, and that human annotation cost is part of the evaluation's price.
- A metric should be validated like a judge. The correlation against human progress judgments (above 0.95 here) is the evidence offered for trusting progress rate; the same standard applies to any LLM judge score in Part 2.
- Breakdowns beat leaderboard order. Easy-versus-hard, grounding, and per-environment cuts tell a developer what to fix; the average in Table 3 does not.
- Unified interfaces make models comparable and hide agent design. Every model ran the same reflex-agent scaffold, so these results compare models inside one harness, not complete agent products.

## Limits

Progress rate depends on one annotated subgoal path per task, and the authors discuss environments where multiple valid paths exist; an agent solving a task a different way can be under-credited. All environments are text-based and simulated, so scores do not measure performance with real users, real websites changing under the agent, or real-world side effects. The model field is a January-2024 snapshot (with a later revision adding some models), and the unified scaffold disadvantages models not suited to that prompting style. Human verification used 60 trajectories per task, which supports the metric's correlation claim but not per-model ranking claims at fine granularity.

sources.title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
sources.abstract: We introduce GAIA, a benchmark for General AI Assistants that, if solved, would represent a milestone in AI research. GAIA proposes real-world questions that require a set of fundamental abilities such as reasoning, multi-modality handling, web browsing, and generally tool-use proficiency. GAIA questions are conceptually simple for humans yet challenging for most advanced AIs: we show that human respondents obtain 92\% vs. 15\% for GPT-4 equipped with plugins. This notable performance disparity contrasts with the recent trend of LLMs outperforming humans on tasks requiring professional skills in e.g. law or chemistry. GAIA's philosophy departs from the current trend in AI benchmarks suggesting to target tasks that are ever more difficult for humans. We posit that the advent of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) hinges on a system's capability to exhibit similar robustness as the average human does on such questions. Using GAIA's methodology, we devise 466 questions and their answer. We release our questions while retaining answers to 300 of them to power a leader-board available at this https URL .
sources.summary: Mialon and colleagues introduce GAIA, 466 questions requiring several steps, browsing, and tool use, scored by exact match against one short answer. Humans score 92% against 15% for GPT-4 with manually selected plugins, illustrating both the rigour and the blindness of outcome-only evaluation.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Mialon, Fourrier, Swift, and colleagues built GAIA, a benchmark of questions that are easy for people and hard for AI systems because answering takes several steps, some browsing or file reading, and a tool or two. GAIA matters to Part 1 — AI Agents and Evaluation Challenges — in two opposite ways at once. It is a clean example of outcome-only evaluation: each question has one short, unambiguous answer, so scoring is a string match. And its design shows exactly what such a score cannot tell you about how an agent worked. That tension — a trustworthy final-answer number that says nothing about the trajectory (the steps taken to reach it) — is the tutorial's starting problem.

## What they did

GAIA contains 466 questions with verified answers, split into three levels by the number of steps and tools a human annotator needed: Level 1 needs at most one tool and no more than about five steps, Level 2 roughly five to ten steps combining tools, and Level 3 long, open-ended sequences (the definitions are given as loose guides, not hard cut-offs). Questions were written to need reasoning plus capabilities such as web browsing, coding, multi-modality (handling images, audio, or documents as well as text), and diverse file-type reading; Figure 3 counts questions per required capability, with web browsing the most common at 355. Answers are short strings, numbers, or lists, withheld for 300 questions that power a leaderboard. Scoring is quasi exact match: the model's answer is normalised according to the ground-truth type and compared with the one correct answer, with systems run in a zero-shot setting (no worked examples in the prompt). Baselines were human annotators, GPT-4 with and without plugins (tools chosen manually per question), GPT-4 Turbo, AutoGPT with a GPT-4 backend, and a search-engine baseline.

{{figure:fig3-composition.png}}

## What they found

The human–AI gap is the result. Human respondents scored 92% overall, while GPT-4 equipped with plugins scored 15% — and the authors stress the plugin figure is an oracle estimate, because a person selected which tools to give it for each question, so it overstates what an automatic system would do. Figure 4 breaks scores down by level alongside time to answer: the plugin-assisted GPT-4 reached 30.3% on Level 1, 9.7% on Level 2, and 0% on Level 3 (Table 4 of the paper), against human scores of 93.9%, 91.8%, and 87.3%. Plain GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo scored lower still, AutoGPT was close to GPT-4 on Level 1 but at much longer answer times, and every non-human method scored 0% on Level 3. The proposed levels did track difficulty for current systems, which the authors offer as validity evidence for the level definitions: performance degrades as steps and tools accumulate, while human performance barely moves (92% to about 87% from the easiest to the hardest level).

{{figure:fig4-scores.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Outcome-only scoring can be rigorous and still incomplete. GAIA's answers are unambiguous and contamination-resistant by design, yet a correct short answer cannot show a lucky guess, a fragile tool chain, or a policy violation on the way.
- Difficulty defined by steps and tools is an agent-relevant axis. Level in GAIA is not subject difficulty for a human; it is trajectory length, which is why model scores collapse across levels while human scores do not.
- Oracle components inflate headlines. The 15% plugin number already includes human tool selection; Part 4's reproducibility discussion should always ask which parts of a reported system were hand-held.
- Held-out answers protect a leaderboard. Withholding 300 answers is a benchmark-integrity choice, and it limits how much of the set anyone can inspect or overfit (fit to the test rather than the task).
- Zero-shot, single-answer scoring is cheap and fast to run at scale. That is a genuine advantage in the quality–cost trade-off, and the reason final-answer benchmarks remain useful alongside trajectory evaluation rather than replaced by it.

## Limits

As the authors state, GAIA does not grade reasoning traces or tool use directly, so it cannot diagnose why a system failed, and the appendix notes that some questions can be solved by a different route than the annotators used. The benchmark is English-centric, which the limitations section acknowledges, and unambiguous factoid answers exclude tasks where quality is genuinely contested — precisely where LLM judges are usually proposed. Reported runs are a late-2023 snapshot, including a plugin ecosystem the paper itself notes was unstable and partly removed, so the exact GPT-4 numbers are not reproducible as run.

sources.title: AI Agents That Matter
sources.abstract: AI agents are an exciting new research direction, and agent development is driven by benchmarks. Our analysis of current agent benchmarks and evaluation practices reveals several shortcomings that hinder their usefulness in real-world applications. First, there is a narrow focus on accuracy without attention to other metrics. As a result, SOTA agents are needlessly complex and costly, and the community has reached mistaken conclusions about the sources of accuracy gains. Our focus on cost in addition to accuracy motivates the new goal of jointly optimizing the two metrics. We design and implement one such optimization, showing its potential to greatly reduce cost while maintaining accuracy. Second, the benchmarking needs of model and downstream developers have been conflated, making it hard to identify which agent would be best suited for a particular application. Third, many agent benchmarks have inadequate holdout sets, and sometimes none at all. This has led to agents that are fragile because they take shortcuts and overfit to the benchmark in various ways. We prescribe a principled framework for avoiding overfitting. Finally, there is a lack of standardization in evaluation practices, leading to a pervasive lack of reproducibility. We hope that the steps we introduce for addressing these shortcomings will spur the development of agents that are useful in the real world and not just accurate on benchmarks.
sources.summary: Kapoor and colleagues show that agent evaluations reporting accuracy without cost, holdouts, or reproducibility produce misleading rankings: on HumanEval, simple baselines match complex agents while costs differ by almost two orders of magnitude. The paper prescribes joint accuracy–cost optimisation and holdouts matched to claimed generality.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, and colleagues examine not an agent but the way agents are evaluated, and find the evaluation practices themselves producing wrong conclusions. Their four complaints — accuracy reported without cost, model and downstream developers' needs conflated, benchmarks that invite shortcuts, and irreproducible setups — map onto Part 1 — AI Agents and Evaluation Challenges (what a benchmark score does and does not measure) and Part 4 — Reliability, Limitations, and Future Directions (cost, robustness, failure modes, and good practice). It is one of the few sources here whose subject is evaluation methodology rather than a system or a judge.

## What they did

The paper combines re-analysis, small new experiments, and a survey of benchmarks. For cost, they re-run or re-analyse agents on HumanEval (164 programming problems) and plot accuracy against total API cost as a Pareto frontier: the set of agents for which no other agent is better on both accuracy and cost at once. Each agent was run five times, reporting mean accuracy and mean cost. They propose simple baselines that exploit repetition — retrying a model, warming (their term for a staged prompting strategy), and escalation to a stronger model — before crediting complex agent architectures. For joint optimisation (spending fixed, one-time cost, such as prompt search, to cut the variable cost of each run), they modify the DSPy framework with hyperparameter search and evaluate on HotPotQA, a multi-hop question-answering dataset. A separate case study on NovelQA separates model-developer from downstream-developer questions, a WebArena case study examines shortcut-taking in the STeP agent, and an appendix survey classifies 17 agent benchmarks by whether they include a holdout set (data withheld from agent developers) and whether it matches the benchmark's intended level of generality.

{{figure:fig1-pareto-humaneval.png}}

## What they found

On HumanEval, supposedly state-of-the-art agent architectures did not significantly outperform the authors' simple baselines on accuracy, while cost for substantially similar accuracy differed by almost two orders of magnitude across agents (Section 2; Figure 1). In other words, the accuracy ranking alone selected needlessly expensive systems. On HotPotQA, their jointly optimised DSPy setup maintained accuracy while significantly reducing cost (Figure 2), demonstrating the design space that a cost axis opens. The benchmark survey is the third quantitative result: of 17 agent benchmarks, 7 had no holdout set and no indication one was planned, and of those with holdouts only 5 of 10 held out at the appropriate generality level (Table A4 of the paper); Table 1 summarises their rule that distribution-specific benchmarks should hold out samples, task-specific ones out-of-distribution samples, domain-general ones whole tasks, and fully general ones whole domains. The WebArena case study shows an agent exploiting benchmark-specific structure rather than solving the underlying task, and the reproduction checks report inflated accuracies from evaluation errors in prior setups.

{{figure:fig2-pareto-hotpot.png}}

{{figure:table1-holdouts.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Always ask for the second axis. Accuracy without cost, latency, or reliability can rank a system first that a team would never deploy; Part 2's choice between rules, a judge, and a human is the same two-dimensional problem.
- Simple repetitive baselines are a control condition. If retrying or escalating matches a complex architecture, the architecture has not yet demonstrated its contribution — a standard any hands-on evaluation in Part 3 should apply to its own agent and judge.
- Holdout level must match claimed generality. A random sample split cannot support a claim about new tasks or new domains, and Table 1 is a usable checklist for reading any benchmark's split.
- Model benchmarks and downstream benchmarks answer different questions. Conflating them is how a leaderboard winner becomes a disappointing product choice.
- Reproducibility is part of the score. Their reproduction failures mean a reported accuracy without a runnable, standardised setup should be treated as an upper bound, not a measurement.

## Limits

The empirical spine is narrow: HumanEval and HotPotQA carry the cost argument, with case studies elsewhere, so the size of the cost effect will differ in other domains. Costs are API prices at the time of the runs and age quickly, although the argument depends on the gap, not the exact prices. The benchmark survey classifies 17 benchmarks by the authors' own judgement of intended generality, which they acknowledge was sometimes unclear from the papers. The paper critiques evaluation practice rather than offering a complete replacement benchmark, so it supports scepticism and design checks, not a ready-made evaluation suite.

sources.title: Evaluation-Driven Development and Operations of LLM Agents: A Process Model and Reference Architecture
sources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled the emergence of LLM agents, systems capable of pursuing under-specified goals and adapting after deployment. Evaluating such agents is challenging because their behavior is open ended, probabilistic, and shaped by system-level interactions over time. Traditional evaluation methods, built around fixed benchmarks and static test suites, fail to capture emergent behaviors or support continuous adaptation across the lifecycle. To ground a more systematic approach, we conduct a multivocal literature review (MLR) synthesizing academic and industrial evaluation practices. The findings directly inform two empirically derived artifacts: a process model and a reference architecture that embed evaluation as a continuous, governing function rather than a terminal checkpoint. Together they constitute the evaluation-driven development and operations (EDDOps) approach, which unifies offline (development-time) and online (runtime) evaluation within a closed feedback loop. By making evaluation evidence drive both runtime adaptation and governed redevelopment, EDDOps supports safer, more traceable evolution of LLM agents aligned with changing objectives, user needs, and governance constraints.
sources.summary: Proposes a process and a reference architecture where offline and online evaluation drive how an agent is changed. This is the industry lifecycle on the Part 1 agenda: datasets, versioning, and monitoring, not a single test run.
sources.note: arXiv submission 2024, revised through 2025. The checklist writes 2024–2025.

sources.title: AgentOps: Enabling Observability of LLM Agents
sources.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various domains, gaining extensive attention from academia and industry. However, these agents raise significant concerns on AI safety due to their autonomous and non-deterministic behavior, as well as continuous evolving nature . From a DevOps perspective, enabling observability in agents is necessary to ensuring AI safety, as stakeholders can gain insights into the agents' inner workings, allowing them to proactively understand the agents, detect anomalies, and prevent potential failures. Therefore, in this paper, we present a comprehensive taxonomy of AgentOps, identifying the artifacts and associated data that should be traced throughout the entire lifecycle of agents to achieve effective observability. The taxonomy is developed based on a systematic mapping study of existing AgentOps tools. Our taxonomy serves as a reference template for developers to design and implement AgentOps infrastructure that supports monitoring, logging, and analytics. thereby ensuring AI safety.
sources.summary: A taxonomy of what to trace across an agent’s life so someone can see what it did. Matches the Part 1 observability slide: monitoring, reporting, and kill switches need a trace.

sources.title: Who Validates the Validators? Aligning LLM-Assisted Evaluation of LLM Outputs with Human Preferences
sources.abstract: Due to the cumbersome nature of human evaluation and limitations of code-based evaluation, Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to assist humans in evaluating LLM outputs. Yet LLM-generated evaluators simply inherit all the problems of the LLMs they evaluate, requiring further human validation. We present a mixed-initiative approach to ``validate the validators'' -- aligning LLM-generated evaluation functions (be it prompts or code) with human requirements. Our interface, EvalGen, provides automated assistance to users in generating evaluation criteria and implementing assertions. While generating candidate implementations (Python functions, LLM grader prompts), EvalGen asks humans to grade a subset of LLM outputs; this feedback is used to select implementations that better align with user grades. A qualitative study finds overall support for EvalGen but underscores the subjectivity and iterative process of alignment. In particular, we identify a phenomenon we dub \emph{criteria drift}: users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps users define criteria. What is more, some criteria appears \emph{dependent} on the specific LLM outputs observed (rather than independent criteria that can be defined \emph{a priori}), raising serious questions for approaches that assume the independence of evaluation from observation of model outputs. We present our interface and implementation details, a comparison of our algorithm with a baseline approach, and implications for the design of future LLM evaluation assistants.
sources.summary: Studies how to align a model-based evaluator with human preferences, including who checks the checker. Core Part 2 and Part 4 material: a judge is not self-justifying.

sources.title: Building Your Own Product Copilot: Challenges, Opportunities, and Needs
sources.abstract: A race is underway to embed advanced AI capabilities into products. These product copilots enable users to ask questions in natural language and receive relevant responses that are specific to the user's context. In fact, virtually every large technology company is looking to add these capabilities to their software products. However, for most software engineers, this is often their first encounter with integrating AI-powered technology. Furthermore, software engineering processes and tools have not caught up with the challenges and scale involved with building AI-powered applications. In this work, we present the findings of an interview study with 26 professional software engineers responsible for building product copilots at various companies. From our interviews, we found pain points at every step of the engineering process and the challenges that strained existing development practices. We then conducted group brainstorming sessions to collaborative on opportunities and tool designs for the broader software engineering community.
sources.summary: Field study of 26 engineers building product copilots, including the evaluation support they lacked: no ready benchmarks, no agreed definition of good enough, and tests too costly to run often. It grounds Part 1 in the claim that evaluation is an engineering workflow, not only a benchmark.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Parnin, Soares, Pandita, and colleagues study people building product copilots: software that turns a user's words or clicks into prompts for a large language model (LLM, a model trained to predict and generate text) and turns the model's output back into something usable in a product. This is not a benchmark paper and it tests no judge. It matters for Part 1 — AI Agents and Evaluation Challenges — because it reports, from working engineers, why evaluation is an engineering workflow rather than a single score: prompts, test cases, datasets, and monitoring all had to be invented while the product was being built.

## What they did

The authors ran a mixed-methods study. A mixed-methods study combines more than one kind of evidence; here, semi-structured interviews (conversations guided by a topic list, free to follow up) plus structured brainstorming. They interviewed 26 professional software engineers who were actively building a product copilot and spending at least 20 hours a week on AI-related features: 14 recruited inside Microsoft and 12 from a variety of companies through a recruiting platform, with people who only used tools such as ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot excluded. Two researchers then analysed the transcripts with thematic analysis (coding passages and grouping the codes into recurring themes). Two 75-minute brainstorming sessions, run by a third-party facilitator on a shared canvas, took problems from the interviews and expanded them into possible tool designs. Figure 2 is the workflow the authors refined with participants: exploration, implementation, evaluation, and productization, with feedback loops backward at every stage.

{{figure:fig2-workflow.png}}

## What they found

Table 1 groups the challenges into interaction with LLMs, testing and validation, and learning and developer experience. On prompt engineering — writing and tuning the instructions given to a model — participants called the process trial and error and described model responses as fragile: a small change could alter behaviour, outputs arrived without the structure downstream code needed, and prompt assets were hard to track. On orchestration (coordinating several prompts, tools, and conversation state to complete a task), they struggled to steer multi-turn workflows, detect intent, and stop loops.

The testing findings are the core for this tutorial. Participants said every test felt like a flaky test: a test that can pass or fail on the same code, here because a generative model can answer differently each run. There were no ready benchmarks (fixed sets of test cases with expected results) for their products, so each team had to build its own, and there was no agreed metric for what counted as good enough, especially for qualitative output. Human checking filled the gap and was slow. Running even an automated benchmark cost money per model call; one participant was asked to stop automated testing because of that cost and reverted to running a small set manually after large changes. Safety, privacy, and compliance work added further tests, including checking that content filters flagged harmful categories.

{{figure:table1-themes.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Part 1's lifecycle claim is grounded here in field evidence: engineers needed prompts, test cases, benchmarks, and monitoring as connected tooling, and reported having none of it as one workflow.
- Non-determinism breaks the usual unit-test contract. When the same input can produce different outputs, a single pass/fail assertion is the wrong instrument; participants tested structure and format where content could not be pinned down.
- Benchmark creation, not only benchmark running, is the expensive step. Teams first had to invent test cases and a definition of good enough, and that invention is where a rubric (an explicit list of criteria for judging output) would have to live.
- Cost can silently delete evaluation. A benchmark that is too expensive to run on every change stops being run, so cost belongs in any evaluation plan from the start.
- The paper supports a claim about missing tooling and practice in 2023. It does not measure how often each pain point occurs in industry at large.

## Limits

The sample is small and skewed: 14 of 26 interviewees were at one company, recruitment was partly snowballed (participants suggesting further participants), and the authors note that interviews lean on recall and on what participants think they should say. The brainstorming sessions had only a handful of the interviewees. The study is dated December 2023, early in the copilot wave, so specific tools named then may have changed. It reports experiences and perceptions, not frequencies, effect sizes, or comparisons between products, and it offers no evaluation method of its own to adopt.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
sources.abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) based chat assistants is challenging due to their broad capabilities and the inadequacy of existing benchmarks in measuring human preferences. To address this, we explore using strong LLMs as judges to evaluate these models on more open-ended questions. We examine the usage and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, as well as limited reasoning ability, and propose solutions to mitigate some of them. We then verify the agreement between LLM judges and human preferences by introducing two benchmarks: MT-bench, a multi-turn question set; and Chatbot Arena, a crowdsourced battle platform. Our results reveal that strong LLM judges like GPT-4 can match both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences well, achieving over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans. Hence, LLM-as-a-judge is a scalable and explainable way to approximate human preferences, which are otherwise very expensive to obtain. Additionally, we show our benchmark and traditional benchmarks complement each other by evaluating several variants of LLaMA and Vicuna. The MT-bench questions, 3K expert votes, and 30K conversations with human preferences are publicly available at this https URL .
sources.summary: Zheng and colleagues established LLM-as-a-judge against human preferences on MT-bench and Chatbot Arena, reporting over 80% agreement for GPT-4 while measuring position, verbosity, and reasoning limits. It is foundational for Part 2 and for the reliability questions in Part 4.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Zheng, Chiang, Sheng, and colleagues ask whether a strong LLM can stand in for human preference judgments when scoring open-ended chat assistants. Preference here means which of two answers a person would rather receive. Their answer — yes, with named failure modes — is the founding evidence for Part 2 — LLM-as-a-Judge Methods — and the biases they catalogue are the starting point for Part 4 — Reliability, Limitations, and Future Directions. The paper's own benchmarks, MT-bench and Chatbot Arena, are measurement instruments, not tutorial exercises.

## What they did

MT-bench is 80 multi-turn questions: a first question plus a follow-up, across eight categories (writing, roleplay, reasoning, math, coding, extraction, STEM, and humanities). Chatbot Arena is a crowdsourced platform where anonymous model pairs answer the same prompt and users vote for the better reply. The authors test three ways for an LLM to judge: pairwise comparison (pick the better of two answers), single-answer grading (score one answer, on a 1–10 scale in their prompt), and reference-guided grading (score against a reference answer for math and reasoning). Judges were GPT-4, GPT-3.5, and Claude-v1 (model names as printed). They generated answers from six models, including GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude-v1, Vicuna-13B, Alpaca-13B, and LLaMA-13B, and collected judgments from 58 expert human labelers on MT-bench plus crowdsourced Arena votes. Agreement is the share of cases where two judges pick the same winner; the paper reports it with ties included (setup S1) and with only non-tie votes counted (setup S2).

## What they found

On MT-bench, GPT-4 pairwise judging agreed with humans at 85% under S2 on both turns (Table 5), slightly above the 81–82% agreement between humans themselves. The authors summarise this as over 80% agreement, the same level as human–human agreement. Single-answer grading by GPT-4 also matched pairwise GPT-4 closely (95–97% under S2 in Table 5), which matters because scoring one answer at a time avoids presenting two answers in an order at all. Figure 4 shows the practical consequence on Chatbot Arena: the average win rates of nine models, and their ordering, look similar under GPT-4, GPT-3.5, human, and single-answer GPT-4 judges.

{{figure:fig4-win-rate.png}}

The limits are measured, not asserted. Position bias — favouring an answer because of where it sits — left GPT-4 consistent in only 65.0% of swapped pairs, GPT-3.5 in 46.2%, and Claude-v1 in 23.8%, with Claude-v1 favouring the first answer in 75.0% of cases (Table 2). Under a repetitive list attack, where a weaker answer is padded with rephrased list items, Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 failed on 91.3% of 23 answers while GPT-4 failed on 8.7%. On 10 math questions, GPT-4 called a wrong answer correct 14 of 20 times with the default prompt, 6 of 20 with chain-of-thought prompting (asking the model to reason step by step before verdict), and 3 of 20 with a reference answer. Remedies help partially: swapping positions and calling the judge twice is their conservative default; few-shot examples (worked examples inside the prompt) raised GPT-4 consistency from 65.0% to 77.5% at roughly four times the prompt cost.

{{figure:table2-position-bias.png}}

{{figure:table5-agreement.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- An LLM judge can approximate expert human preference on open-ended chat at human-like agreement — 85% versus 81% non-tie agreement here — which is why Part 2 treats judging as a real instrument rather than a shortcut.
- Agreement is not accuracy on every question type. The same GPT-4 judge failed most math gradings without a reference answer, so the criterion being judged changes what the judge needs.
- Position bias is a design variable, not a curiosity: swapping order, scoring answers singly, and budgeting for doubled judge calls follow directly from Table 2.
- Verbosity can be gamed. A judge that rewards length rewards padding, which is a rubric problem (reward the criterion, not a correlate of it) as much as a model problem.
- Cost enters through the remedy. The few-shot fix that raised consistency also multiplied prompt cost, a Part 2 trade-off between quality, latency, reliability, and cost in concrete form.

## Limits

The headline agreement comes from one strong proprietary judge, GPT-4 as available in 2023, judging chat answers; it does not show that a weaker or cheaper judge, or a judge scoring agent trajectories and tool calls, agrees with humans as well. MT-bench is small (80 questions), the Arena votes are self-selected crowd votes rather than expert labels, and the authors note they could not cleanly test self-enhancement bias (a judge favouring its own generations) because rephrasing an answer changes its style. Several case studies use a dated model snapshot the authors flag as possibly not reproducible.

sources.title: G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
sources.abstract: The quality of texts generated by natural language generation (NLG) systems is hard to measure automatically. Conventional reference-based metrics, such as BLEU and ROUGE, have been shown to have relatively low correlation with human judgments, especially for tasks that require creativity and diversity. Recent studies suggest using large language models (LLMs) as reference-free metrics for NLG evaluation, which have the benefit of being applicable to new tasks that lack human references. However, these LLM-based evaluators still have lower human correspondence than medium-size neural evaluators. In this work, we present G-Eval, a framework of using large language models with chain-of-thoughts (CoT) and a form-filling paradigm, to assess the quality of NLG outputs. We experiment with two generation tasks, text summarization and dialogue generation. We show that G-Eval with GPT-4 as the backbone model achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.514 with human on summarization task, outperforming all previous methods by a large margin. We also propose preliminary analysis on the behavior of LLM-based evaluators, and highlight the potential issue of LLM-based evaluators having a bias towards the LLM-generated texts. The code is at this https URL
sources.summary: G-Eval prompts GPT-4 with a task description and criteria, has it write its own evaluation steps, then scores with a probability-weighted form. It is the standard early recipe for a rubric-style LLM judge, and it reports a preference for LLM-written text that later judges inherit.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Liu and colleagues at Microsoft describe G-Eval, a way to use a large language model as an evaluator of generated text. Its parts are the parts of most rubric judges since: a description of the task, named criteria, written evaluation steps, a fixed score form, and a rule for turning the output into a number. The paper judges summaries and dialogue replies, not agents. It is here for Part 2, because it shows what each part of a judge prompt contributes. It is also here for Part 4, because it reports an early sign of bias toward text written by language models.

## What they did

There are three components (Figure 1):

1. **A prompt** with a task introduction and the criteria for one dimension, for example "Coherence (1-5) - the collective quality of all sentences".
2. **Auto chain-of-thought.** The prompt ends with "Evaluation Steps:", and the model writes the steps itself. Chain-of-thought means intermediate text the model writes before an answer. Here the model writes the steps from the task and criteria, and the steps then become part of the scoring prompt, so no one has to hand-write steps for every criterion.
3. **Form-filling and weighting.** The prompt, the steps, the source, and the output to be judged are sent together, ending in a form line such as "- Coherence:". The score is the probability-weighted sum Σ p(s) × s over the allowed scores. GPT-4 did not return token probabilities, so they sampled 20 completions at temperature 1 to estimate them.

{{figure:fig1-framework.png}}

The weighting answers two problems the authors name. One score, such as 3 on a 1–5 scale, tends to dominate. And the model gives whole numbers even when asked for decimals, which produces many ties.

They test on three meta-evaluation benchmarks. Meta-evaluation means scoring an evaluator by how well it agrees with human ratings. SummEval rates news summaries on coherence, consistency, fluency, and relevance. Topical-Chat rates dialogue replies. QAGS asks whether summaries are factually consistent with the source. Agreement is correlation with human scores: Spearman's ρ and Kendall's τ, which compare rankings, and Pearson's r. Baselines include ROUGE, BERTScore, BARTScore, UniEval, and GPTScore.

## What they found

On SummEval, G-Eval with GPT-4 averages Spearman 0.514 and Kendall 0.418 across the four dimensions (Table 1). This is the abstract's headline number. The strongest baseline, UniEval, averages 0.474 and 0.377. G-Eval with GPT-3.5 averages 0.401, below both UniEval and GPTScore. On these numbers, the recipe depends on a strong backbone.

{{figure:table1-summeval.png}}

The ablations are small and point the same way. Without the generated steps, average Spearman falls from 0.514 to 0.500. The largest drop is on fluency, 0.455 to 0.403. Without probability weighting it falls to 0.502, but Kendall rises to 0.446. The authors attribute that rise to ties, which Kendall's τ does not count, and say it does not reflect better judging.

On Topical-Chat, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 are almost level, 0.588 and 0.585 average Spearman, so the paper calls the benchmark relatively easy. On QAGS, G-Eval with GPT-4 averages 0.611 Spearman against UniEval's 0.575, while GPT-3.5 falls to 0.461.

Section 4 tests for bias. Freelance writers' summaries and GPT-3.5 summaries had been compared by human judges. G-Eval with GPT-4 gave the GPT-3.5 summary a higher average score in all three groups, including the group where humans preferred the human summary (Figure 2). The bar values are not printed, and the y-axis starts at 3.75, so the gaps look larger than they are. The human judges in that dataset barely agreed with each other: Krippendorff's α was 0.07.

{{figure:fig2-llm-preference.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A judge prompt has separable parts: task, criteria, steps, score form, and aggregation. Part 2's prompting and scales can be taught one part at a time, with a measured effect for each part.
- Turning output into a score is a design choice. Expected value over score probabilities breaks ties. It also changes which correlation looks better, so report more than one.
- The backbone matters more than the prompt here. GPT-3.5 with the same template is below a trained baseline. A judge recipe does not transfer across models without re-checking it against people.
- Judges can prefer model-written text. Part 4 should treat that as a known failure mode, especially when a judge's score becomes a training reward, a risk the authors name.
- Low human agreement limits what any judge can be checked against. An α of 0.07 makes "the judge disagrees with humans" hard to interpret.

## Limits

There are no agents, trajectories, or tool calls. The tasks are short single outputs. The paper reports no repeated runs, variance, confidence intervals, or cost. Dataset sizes are not printed. The bias study is a preliminary check with a GPT-4 judge on GPT-3.5 outputs, not a test of a model judging its own text. The QAGS prompt in the appendix is a yes/no question with no evaluation steps, so those results do not use the full method. Figure 1 has a typo in its scale ("1 to 10" where the text says 1 to 5). Most criterion prompts are not printed.

figures.alt: The G-Eval framework. A task introduction and evaluation criteria for coherence feed an auto chain-of-thought step that writes three evaluation steps. The steps, the article, the summary, and an evaluation form ending in Coherence go to the model. A bar chart of probabilities over scores 1 to 5 gives a weighted summed score of 2.59.

figures.alt: Summary-level Spearman and Kendall correlations with human ratings on SummEval for coherence, consistency, fluency, relevance, and their average. Average Spearman: ROUGE-1 0.192, BERTScore 0.225, BARTScore 0.385, UniEval 0.474, GPTScore 0.417, G-Eval with GPT-3.5 0.401, G-Eval with GPT-4 0.514, without probabilities 0.502, without chain-of-thought 0.500.
figures.caption: Table 1 from Liu et al. (2023). The 0.514 headline is the four-dimension average. Removing the steps or the weighting costs a little; the GPT-3.5 version is below UniEval.

figures.alt: Bars of average G-Eval scores for human-written and GPT-3.5 summaries in three groups: human summary judged better, LLM summary judged better, and equally good. The y-axis runs only from 3.75 to 4. In every group the GPT-3.5 bar is taller.

sources.title: Prometheus: Inducing Fine-grained Evaluation Capability in Language Models
sources.abstract: Recently, using a powerful proprietary Large Language Model (LLM) (e.g., GPT-4) as an evaluator for long-form responses has become the de facto standard. However, for practitioners with large-scale evaluation tasks and custom criteria in consideration (e.g., child-readability), using proprietary LLMs as an evaluator is unreliable due to the closed-source nature, uncontrolled versioning, and prohibitive costs. In this work, we propose Prometheus, a fully open-source LLM that is on par with GPT-4's evaluation capabilities when the appropriate reference materials (reference answer, score rubric) are accompanied. We first construct the Feedback Collection, a new dataset that consists of 1K fine-grained score rubrics, 20K instructions, and 100K responses and language feedback generated by GPT-4. Using the Feedback Collection, we train Prometheus, a 13B evaluator LLM that can assess any given long-form text based on customized score rubric provided by the user. Experimental results show that Prometheus scores a Pearson correlation of 0.897 with human evaluators when evaluating with 45 customized score rubrics, which is on par with GPT-4 (0.882), and greatly outperforms ChatGPT (0.392). Furthermore, measuring correlation with GPT-4 with 1222 customized score rubrics across four benchmarks (MT Bench, Vicuna Bench, Feedback Bench, Flask Eval) shows similar trends, bolstering Prometheus's capability as an evaluator LLM. Lastly, Prometheus achieves the highest accuracy on two human preference benchmarks (HHH Alignment & MT Bench Human Judgment) compared to open-sourced reward models explicitly trained on human preference datasets, highlighting its potential as an universal reward model. We open-source our code, dataset, and model at this https URL .
sources.summary: Trains an open evaluator against a fine-grained rubric. Relevant in Part 2 when discussing whether the judge is a prompted general model or a model built to score.
sources.note: arXiv submission 2023 (2310.08491). The reading checklist dates Prometheus 2024.

sources.title: Prometheus 2: An Open Source Language Model Specialized in Evaluating Other Language Models
sources.abstract: Proprietary LMs such as GPT-4 are often employed to assess the quality of responses from various LMs. However, concerns including transparency, controllability, and affordability strongly motivate the development of open-source LMs specialized in evaluations. On the other hand, existing open evaluator LMs exhibit critical shortcomings: 1) they issue scores that significantly diverge from those assigned by humans, and 2) they lack the flexibility to perform both direct assessment and pairwise ranking, the two most prevalent forms of assessment. Additionally, they do not possess the ability to evaluate based on custom evaluation criteria, focusing instead on general attributes like helpfulness and harmlessness. To address these issues, we introduce Prometheus 2, a more powerful evaluator LM than its predecessor that closely mirrors human and GPT-4 judgements. Moreover, it is capable of processing both direct assessment and pair-wise ranking formats grouped with a user-defined evaluation criteria. On four direct assessment benchmarks and four pairwise ranking benchmarks, Prometheus 2 scores the highest correlation and agreement with humans and proprietary LM judges among all tested open evaluator LMs. Our models, code, and data are all publicly available at this https URL .
sources.summary: A follow-on open evaluator aimed at finer, more transferable scores. Same Part 2 use as Prometheus: rubrics can be compiled into a model, not only pasted into a prompt.

sources.title: HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health
sources.abstract: We present HealthBench, an open-source benchmark measuring the performance and safety of large language models in healthcare. HealthBench consists of 5,000 multi-turn conversations between a model and an individual user or healthcare professional. Responses are evaluated using conversation-specific rubrics created by 262 physicians. Unlike previous multiple-choice or short-answer benchmarks, HealthBench enables realistic, open-ended evaluation through 48,562 unique rubric criteria spanning several health contexts (e.g., emergencies, transforming clinical data, global health) and behavioral dimensions (e.g., accuracy, instruction following, communication). HealthBench performance over the last two years reflects steady initial progress (compare GPT-3.5 Turbo's 16% to GPT-4o's 32%) and more rapid recent improvements (o3 scores 60%). Smaller models have especially improved: GPT-4.1 nano outperforms GPT-4o and is 25 times cheaper. We additionally release two HealthBench variations: HealthBench Consensus, which includes 34 particularly important dimensions of model behavior validated via physician consensus, and HealthBench Hard, where the current top score is 32%. We hope that HealthBench grounds progress towards model development and applications that benefit human health.
sources.summary: HealthBench scores 5,000 health conversations with physician-written criteria, positive and negative points, and a GPT-4.1 judge that marks each criterion met or not. Overall scores run from about 0.16 to about 0.60, and the hard subset's top score is 0.32.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Arora, Wei, Hicks, and colleagues built HealthBench to score model replies in health conversations with a rubric a physician wrote for that conversation. It is not an agent benchmark and it has no tools. It is still the clearest public example of the Part 2 pattern: conversation-specific criteria, a point scale that can penalize, and a model judge that returns met or not met. Part 4's question, whether that judge agrees with physicians, is a section of the paper rather than an afterthought.

## What they did

The set is 5,000 conversations, single-turn or multi-turn, each ending on a user message. Most were synthesized from situation types physicians listed, some were red-team conversations, and some were rewritten from an existing health-search set. Each example has its own criteria. A criterion carries a nonzero point value from −10 to 10. Positive points reward something the reply should do. Negative points penalize a behavior when it is present. The grader is GPT-4.1. It scores each criterion independently as met or not met. Met awards the full point value, including a penalty. Not met awards zero.

The example score is the sum of awarded points divided by the sum of the positive point values only. A met penalty can pull an example below zero. The reported model score is the mean of example scores, clipped to the range 0 to 1. Table 3 counts 57,237 criterion instances: 49,184 written for that example and 8,053 occurrences of consensus criteria. The consensus criteria are a smaller shared set, attached when a majority of reviewers agreed the category applied. The paper says there are 34 unique consensus criteria. HealthBench Consensus scores 3,671 examples on the consensus criteria only. HealthBench Hard is 1,000 examples kept because several frontier models scored them poorly.

The physician cohort is 262 people, practicing in 60 countries, across 26 specialties. The model grader was chosen because, on the consensus criteria, it matched physician agreement without the cost of a reasoning model.

{{figure:fig1-infographic.png}}

## What they found

Section 6.1 and the abstract put the overall score at 16% for GPT-3.5 Turbo, 32% for GPT-4o, and 60% for o3. Table 7, sixteen runs, prints the means as 0.1554, 0.3233, and 0.5990. Run-to-run standard deviations are about 0.002. On the Consensus subset the order changes: GPT-4.1 at 0.9398 is above o3 at 0.9282 (Table 8). On the Hard subset, o3 scores 0.32 against its 0.60 overall. Figure 10 breaks Hard out by axis. Communication quality is the tall bar. Completeness is low, and for several weaker models the dashed overall score sits at or near zero.

Figure 1 is one worked example of the arithmetic. Criteria of +7, +5, and +10 are the positive pool, 22 points. The +5 criterion is missed. A −6 penalty is met. The displayed score is 11 out of 22, 50%. The denominator never includes the penalty, so a met penalty lowers the numerator only.

The grader study covers only consensus criteria: 60,896 physician grades of met or not met. Macro F1 treats "met" and "not met" equally. GPT-4.1's macro F1 is above the average physician in five of seven themes and below in health data tasks, 0.683 against 0.730, at the 37.5th percentile of physicians on that theme (Table 5). Across grader models, GPT-4.1 is the highest at 0.709 (Table 6). The authors note it was the model used while the prompt was tuned.

{{figure:fig4-frontier.png}}

{{figure:fig10-hard.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A rubric can be specific to the conversation, with points that reward and points that penalize. A met penalty lowers the score and is not added to the denominator.
- The judge is binary per criterion, and the example score is a sum. That is a different design from asking the model for one holistic number.
- Overall, Consensus, and Hard do not rank models the same way. o3 leads the full set and the hard slice. GPT-4.1 leads the consensus slice. Part 4 should not treat one headline number as the measurement.
- Judge–physician agreement is itself a result, and it is uneven. The grader beats the average physician on five themes and loses on health data tasks. A judge chosen because it was cheap can still be the one that was tuned against.

## Limits

These are single replies, not multi-step clinical work, and not tool use. The paper does not claim health outcomes. Meta-evaluation covers consensus criteria only. Example-specific criteria were written by individual physicians and not rechecked by others. The abstract's count of 48,562 unique criteria is not the same number as Table 3's 57,237 instances, and the paper does not show the arithmetic that connects them. The grading prompt is not printed. Physicians editing September 2024 references improved them more often than not, 56.2% against 39.8%. April 2025 references were a near tie, 46.8% improved against 47.7% worsened.

sources.title: Learning to Judge: LLMs Designing and Applying Evaluation Rubrics
sources.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2026. arXiv preprint arXiv:2602.08672.
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as evaluators for natural language generation, applying human-defined rubrics to assess system outputs. However, human rubrics are often static and misaligned with how models internally represent language quality. We introduce GER-Eval (Generating Evaluation Rubrics for Evaluation) to investigate whether LLMs can design and apply their own evaluation rubrics. We evaluate the semantic coherence and scoring reliability of LLM-defined criteria and their alignment with human criteria. LLMs reliably generate interpretable and task-aware evaluation dimensions and apply them consistently within models, but their scoring reliability degrades in factual and knowledge-intensive settings. Closed-source models such as GPT-4o achieve higher agreement and cross-model generalization than open-weight models such as Llama. Our findings position evaluation as a learned linguistic capability of LLMs, consistent within models but fragmented across them, and call for new methods that jointly model human and LLM evaluative language to improve reliability and interpretability.
sources.summary: Siro, Aliannejadi, and Aliannejadi test the assumption that a model-written rubric is a more reliable way to score text than a human rubric. Within one model the scores are often stable. Agreement with humans, and agreement across models, collapses on the factual biomedical summaries.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Siro, Aliannejadi, and Aliannejadi separate two jobs that Part 2 often runs together: who writes the rubric, and who applies it. GER-Eval is a diagnostic, not a new rubric generator. It asks whether a model-written rubric is more reliable than a human one, and whether a model applies either rubric the same way a person would. The datasets are summaries, dialogues, and instruction-following replies, not agent trajectories. The lesson still sits in Part 2 and Part 4. A rubric that sounds specific can score fluency and miss the facts.

## What they did

A criterion is a name, a description, and a scale, plus a short instruction for how to score it. Generation has three conditions: the task alone, the task plus example inputs, and the task plus a high-scoring and a low-scoring output. Application has two conditions, and the words mean something else there: rubric only, which they call zero-shot, and rubric plus demonstrations, which they call few-shot. Tables 3 and 4 compare those two application setups with each other. They are not agreement with humans. Table 5 is the table that correlates model scores with human scores, and it uses the human rubrics.

They take 50 items from each of four datasets: SummEval, HelpSteer2, USR, and SumPubMed. The judges are GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Mixtral-8x22B, and Qwen2.5-72B. Scoring is greedy. Rubric generation uses temperature 0.7. They also hand a rubric written by GPT-4o or by Llama to the other models, which is the transfer test.

{{figure:fig2-task-specific.png}}

## What they found

Models produce about five to eight criteria per dataset. Figure 2 shows the share the authors counted as task-specific under three generation prompts. The paper does not print those bar heights. What it does print is alignment with the human criteria, which is high on some datasets and often below 60% on SumPubMed.

The number that matters for the tutorial is Table 5, Spearman correlation with human scores when the model applies the human rubric. On the dialogue set, USR, every model lands between 0.77 and 0.82. On HelpSteer2 the range is 0.31 to 0.65. On SummEval it is 0.24 to 0.58. On the biomedical summaries, SumPubMed, it is −0.09 to 0.30. Few-shot demonstrations raise HelpSteer2 for four of the five models and do not rescue SumPubMed.

A high correlation between a model's own zero-shot and few-shot scores is a different fact. That within-model agreement can sit near 0.9 on USR in Table 4 while the correlation with humans in Table 5 is lower. On SumPubMed, GPT-4o's zero-shot and few-shot scores agree 92% of the time on its own rubrics (Table 3) with a correlation of only 0.53. Stable is not the same as valid.

{{figure:table5-human-spearman.png}}

Figure 4 is what happens when another model applies the rubric. On USR the Spearman values stay mostly positive and often high. On SumPubMed they sit near zero, with a few cells above 0.3 and some negative. Inter-rater reliability across models on the SumPubMed rubrics has every ICC below 0.2 (Tables 8 and 9).

{{figure:fig4-transfer.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Who writes the rubric is part of the measurement. Part 2 should not treat "let the model draft the criteria" as a free improvement over a human rubric. This paper does not show that self-written rubrics agree better with humans. Table 5 is the human-rubric result.
- A model can be consistent with itself and still disagree with people. Part 4's consistency check is not a validity check. The SumPubMed row is the example: high within-model agreement, correlation with humans at or below 0.30.
- The failure is sharper where the rubric needs facts. Dialogue quality transfers. Biomedical summary quality does not. A rubric for a tool-using agent that checks "did the tool argument match the request" is closer to the factual case than to the dialogue case.
- Few-shot scoring examples help on some datasets and not on others. They are not a general fix.
- Rubrics do not travel cleanly across models. A criterion written by one model and scored by another can lose the correlation even when each model is internally coherent.

## Limits

English text only, five models, 50 items per dataset, and no check of factual accuracy beyond the existing human scores. The study does not claim GER-Eval is a better rubric generator. One sentence in the results section describes human correlations of about 0.8 to 0.9 on HelpSteer2 and USR. Table 5, the human-score table, has USR at 0.77 to 0.82 and HelpSteer2 at 0.31 to 0.65. The higher band matches zero-shot versus few-shot agreement, not agreement with humans.

sources.title: From Rubrics to Reliable Scores: Evidence-Grounded Text Evaluation with LLM Judges
sources.abstract: Rubric-based text evaluation increasingly relies on large language models (LLMs) as scalable judges, yet frozen black-box models can interpret the same criteria inconsistently, produce score attributions that are difficult to audit, and map judgments poorly onto human scoring scales. We define this challenge as criteria transfer: translating human rubric intent into a stable, auditable inference-time scoring protocol. We introduce Rulers, which locks a task-level rubric specification, executes it through structured, evidence-grounded judgments, and calibrates the resulting signals to human score boundaries. Across four rubric-governed benchmarks and multiple frozen backbone models, Rulers achieves stronger agreement with human scores in most evaluated settings, while better matching empirical score distributions and remaining more stable under semantically equivalent rubric perturbations. Calibration controls and component ablations show that these gains cannot be attributed to post-hoc alignment alone, but depend on the combination of fixed criteria, traceable evidence, and calibrated score interpretation. These findings suggest that reliable LLM judging requires faithfully operationalizing human evaluation standards rather than relying on prompt-level scoring alone. Our code is available at this https URL .
sources.summary: RULERS keeps the judge frozen, locks one rubric bundle for the whole task, and forces each checklist decision to cite evidence before a small calibration set maps the scores onto the human scale. The gain in quadratic weighted kappa is large on two essay sets and is not the best score on every row.
sources.note: The reading checklist titles this RULERS: Locked Rubrics and Evidence-Anchored Scoring for Robust LLM Evaluation. The current arXiv page uses the title stored here. Same authors (Hong et al.).
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Hong, Yao, Shen, and colleagues name the problem as criteria transfer: a human rubric has to become a scoring procedure that lands on the human scale and can be audited. RULERS does that at inference time. It does not train the judge. The tasks are essays, summaries, and data-to-text, not agent trajectories. It belongs in Part 2, where a rubric and a scale are chosen, and in Part 4, where a score that moves because the prompt was reworded is a reliability failure.

## What they did

Three stages, drawn in Figure 1. Phase I compiles the human rubric once into a locked bundle: traits, a checklist, score anchors, evidence rules, and a hash. The same bundle is reused for every instance in the task. Phase II splits the input into sentences or paragraphs. The frozen judge marks each checklist item as absent, partial, or clearly present, coded 0, 1, or 2, and cites evidence. A trait score is the average of those decisions, scaled and clipped onto the trait's range. Phase III fits a ridge regression on structured signals, using N = 200 labeled calibration examples, then a monotone map onto the human score distribution. Both the regression and the map are frozen before the test split.

The metric is quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), mean plus or minus a bootstrap standard error. Baselines are direct holistic scoring, multi-trait scoring, AutoScore, and CheckEval, all at temperature 0, without the RULERS calibration layer in the main table. Backbones are GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.1-70B. Datasets are ASAP 2.0 (argument essays, scores 1–6, 7,421 test essays), SummHF (summaries, 1–7), DREsS (learner essays, 3–15), and WebNLG (data-to-text). WebNLG has no single human overall score, so the target is the sum of semantics, grammar, and fluency, which gives the range 3–9.

{{figure:fig1-pipeline.png}}

## What they found

Table 2 is the comparison. RULERS is the highest QWK in every row except the two SummHF rows that use Llama. The highest cell is Llama-3.1-70B on ASAP 2.0, 0.7179 ± 0.0055, against 0.4804 ± 0.0079 for direct holistic scoring with the same backbone. On DREsS the RULERS scores sit near 0.53 to 0.56 while the baselines are mostly under 0.37. On SummHF with Llama-3.1-8B, CheckEval is 0.2594 ± 0.0276 and RULERS is 0.2060 ± 0.0318. With Llama-3.1-70B, CheckEval is 0.4606 ± 0.0256 and RULERS is 0.4454 ± 0.0315. A larger backbone is not always a higher QWK.

Figure 2 compares score shapes with the human histogram. The paper does not print a distance between the curves. The claim in the text is that RULERS more often keeps the center and the spread of the human scores. Table 5 separates two gains on GPT-4o-mini at N = 200. Calibrating the direct holistic score helps on all four datasets. A further gap from that calibrated baseline to RULERS remains: +0.1664 on ASAP 2.0, +0.0329 on SummHF, +0.1844 on DREsS, and +0.0527 on WebNLG. At N = 100 on SummHF, the calibrated direct score beats RULERS. The "calibration is not the whole story" claim is the N = 200 table, not every cell.

{{figure:table2-qwk.png}}

{{figure:fig2-distributions.png}}

Dropping any phase lowers QWK on all four datasets for GPT-4o-mini (Table 4). Token counts, reported only for GPT-4o-mini, put RULERS above a single-pass judge and below the multi-trait baseline.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Lock the rubric before scoring. Part 2's criteria become a different measurement if the judge reinterprets them on every call. The hash in the bundle is the version.
- Evidence is a checklist decision plus a citation, on a three-point scale, not a holistic impression. That is a concrete alternative to "score this from 1 to 6."
- A couple of hundred labeled examples can map judge signals onto a human scale. Part 4's calibration step is doing real work here, and it is not free of labels.
- The same calibration applied to a holistic score does not reproduce the full method. The checklist still matters, and on one dataset at the smaller calibration size it does not win.
- Cost is visible. The evidence-grounded judge spends more tokens than a single pass. Part 2's quality, latency, and cost comparison applies to the judge, not only to the system being judged.

## Limits

This is not an agent-trajectory paper. There is no tool use. Instability and audit coverage are defined and never given a number. Figure 3's robustness bars have no printed QWK. WebNLG is scored against a sum of trait ratings the authors built. A bad source rubric is preserved, not repaired. Each new task needs its own bundle and its own calibration map. The authors say the method is not a replacement for expert judgment in high-stakes use, and the calibration does not come with a fairness result across groups.

figures.alt: Three columns. Phase I locks a human rubric into traits, a checklist, evidence rules, and a hash. Phase II marks each checklist item 0, 1, or 2 and cites a sentence or span. Phase III fits a ridge model on a calibration set and maps the result onto the human score scale. The example ends at a final score of 4 out of 6.

Columns are direct holistic scoring, multi-trait scoring, AutoScore, CheckEval, and RULERS, across four backbones. RULERS is highest in every row except the two SummHF rows that use Llama, where CheckEval is higher.
figures.caption: Table 2 from Hong et al. (2026). The highest cell is Llama-3.1-70B on ASAP 2.0, 0.7179 ± 0.0055. The two SummHF Llama rows are the exceptions.
