sources.title: PReMISE: Policy Rubrics as Measurement Specifications for LLM Judges
sources.abstract: LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate open-ended responses, but their scores depend strongly on the rubrics that condition them. A vague rubric asking for a response to be ``helpful and factual'' can reward polished answers that invent facts or violate user intent. We treat reusable rubrics as measurement specifications: changing the rubric changes the response quality measurement induced by a fixed judge. We introduce PReMISE, a framework that, given pairwise human-preference data, (i) discovers a policy-level rubric set, and (ii) audits any rubric set under LLM-judge use along four axes: structural adequacy, reliability, preference fit, and adversarial robustness. Across rubric sources no raw source is simultaneously reliable, preference-predictive, and adversarially robust; and high inter-rater agreement does not imply low exploitability. PReMISE is the only rubric source to score non-trivially on applicability, specificity, and effective dimensionality simultaneously. We contribute two audit-targeted repair operations: preference-rank selection raises judge accuracy on paired responses from $65.0\%$ to $68.6\%$, competitive with the strongest rubric-discovery baselines and leading on two of three judges in our cross-judge sweep; reliability-constrained refinement reduces the rate at which exploit responses receive high scores from $46.4\%$ to $36.0\%$ with little change in inter-judge agreement ($\alpha{=}.531\to.519$).
sources.summary: PReMISE treats a reusable rubric as a measurement specification and audits it for structure, stability, preference fit, and how easily an attacker can satisfy it. No rubric source in the audit leads every column, and the repair that raises preference accuracy is not the repair that lowers exploitability.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Roy, Pujari, Kumarage, and colleagues study the rubric that is reused across many prompts, the kind of policy sheet Part 2 asks a team to write, rather than an answer key for one item. PReMISE is a discover, audit, and repair pipeline for that sheet. The tutorial question is whether a rubric that judges agree on is the same thing as a rubric that measures what you meant, and whether it can be gamed. That is Part 4.

## What they did

A policy rubric is a set of criteria meant to apply across prompts. For a fixed judge and a rubric, each criterion returns a score. Here the scale used in the audit is 0 to 10. Discovery reads pairwise preferences, asks a model for candidate criteria, clusters near-duplicates, and keeps a compact set. The audit has four axes, kept separate rather than collapsed into one index. Structure is five design properties, scored by a majority of three models. Reliability is inter-judge agreement (Krippendorff's α), a flip rate under repeated sampling, and stability under paraphrase. Preference fit asks whether the criteria fire on the prompts they claim to cover, and whether a judge using them picks the human-preferred response. Adversarial robustness is a verified fool rate: an attacker tries to satisfy a criterion, the judge scores the attempt at least 7 out of 10, and a separate verifier, blind to the attack, calls it an exploit.

Two repairs do different jobs. Preference-rank selection keeps criteria that point the same way as the human preference and does not rewrite the text. The robustness repair edits the text, with a length budget, and is accepted when the fool rate falls without giving up too much agreement. The audit uses four preference corpora. The held-out accuracy test uses three judges, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-32B, and Kimi K2.5, each asked either for one A-or-B verdict or for a score on every criterion.

{{figure:fig2-workflow.png}}

## What they found

Table 1 averages the audit across the four corpora. No source leads every column. Auto-Rubric has the highest preference accuracy in that table, 68.7, and the lowest verified fool rate, 0.272. AgentEval has the highest agreement, α = 0.582. Discovered PReMISE is strong on specificity and on how many distinct directions the scores actually use, and it is not the accuracy leader.

Figure 4 is that anatomy on UltraFeedback. PReMISE criteria fire on 58% of in-domain prompts, the in-domain rate is 7.5 points above the out-of-domain rate, and the effective dimensionality is 15 out of 20. AgentEval and Inverse CAI fire widely and are slightly more applicable out of domain than in it. Auto-Rubric fires on 3% of prompts.

Preference-rank selection moves the Table 1 preference accuracy from 65.0 to 68.6, a tenth of a point under Auto-Rubric's 68.7. On the per-judge table, that repaired rubric is below a no-rubric baseline for Qwen3-32B's direct verdict, 65.8 against 66.4. Discovered PReMISE, before that repair, is below the no-rubric baseline on every direct-verdict column. The robustness repair moves the other direction: verified fool rate from 0.464 to 0.360, with α from 0.531 to 0.519, and preference accuracy does not rise.

{{figure:table1-audit.png}}

{{figure:fig4-anatomy.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A rubric is a measurement specification. Agreement among judges, fit to preferences, and resistance to a written exploit are different columns. Part 4 should not treat one of them as a proxy for the others.
- The repair that chases preference accuracy narrows which prompts the criteria apply to. The repair that chases exploits edits the wording and does not buy accuracy. A team in Part 2 has to say which axis it is optimizing.
- A discovered rubric can lose to no rubric at all. Adding criteria is not automatically a better judge.
- On one of the three judges, the preference repair itself loses to the no-rubric baseline. A rubric tuned on a large judge is not guaranteed on a smaller one.
- High α is a stability check. The paper says it is not evidence that the rubric matches a human's idea of quality.

## Limits

The pipeline is for rubrics that are supposed to track pairwise preferences. Safety floors and hard constraints that should override a preference are out of scope. The fool rate is a lower bound under this attacker, judge, and verifier; the verifier's precision against a three-annotator majority is 72.7%. Absolute numbers are judge-relative. The authors do not test the rubrics as a training reward, and they say consequential per-item decisions would still need human calibration.

figures.alt: A three-stage diagram. Discovery extracts and consolidates criteria from pairwise preferences. A four-axis audit scores structural adequacy, reliability, preference fit, and adversarial robustness. Targeted repair either reselects criteria or edits text, then sends the rubric back for another audit.
figures.caption: Figure 2 from Roy et al. (2026). Discover, audit, and repair are separate stages, and the two repairs answer different audit failures.

figures.alt: A cross-source audit table. Columns cover structure, agreement, flip rate, paraphrase stability, verified fool rate, applicability, specificity, effective dimensionality, preference accuracy, and a Bradley-Terry diagnostic. No row is best in every column. Auto-Rubric's preference accuracy is 68.7. Preference-repaired PReMISE is 68.6. Discovered PReMISE is 65.0.
figures.caption: Table 1 from Roy et al. (2026). No rubric source leads every column. The preference repair and the robustness repair move different numbers.

figures.alt: Three panels on UltraFeedback. An applicability scatterplot, a bar chart of in-domain versus out-of-domain firing with specificity labels from −5.9 to +7.5, and effective dimensionality from 3/4 up to 18/25, with PReMISE at 15/20.
figures.caption: Figure 4 from Roy et al. (2026). On UltraFeedback, discovered PReMISE fires on 58% of in-domain prompts, with +7.5 points of specificity and 15 effective dimensions out of 20.

sources.title: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents
sources.venue: In Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.10934.
sources.abstract: Contemporary evaluation techniques are inadequate for agentic systems. These approaches either focus exclusively on final outcomes -- ignoring the step-by-step nature of agentic systems, or require excessive manual labour. To address this, we introduce the Agent-as-a-Judge framework, wherein agentic systems are used to evaluate agentic systems. This is an organic extension of the LLM-as-a-Judge framework, incorporating agentic features that enable intermediate feedback for the entire task-solving process. We apply the Agent-as-a-Judge to the task of code generation. To overcome issues with existing benchmarks and provide a proof-of-concept testbed for Agent-as-a-Judge, we present DevAI, a new benchmark of 55 realistic automated AI development tasks. It includes rich manual annotations, like a total of 365 hierarchical user requirements. We benchmark three of the popular agentic systems using Agent-as-a-Judge and find it dramatically outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge and is as reliable as our human evaluation baseline. Altogether, we believe that Agent-as-a-Judge marks a concrete step forward for modern agentic systems -- by providing rich and reliable reward signals necessary for dynamic and scalable self-improvement.
sources.summary: Uses an agent to judge another agent’s steps, not only the final artifact. Cited from Part 4. It is the research version of the industry posts on the primary list.

sources.title: AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories
sources.abstract: Web agents enable users to perform tasks on web browsers through natural language interaction. Evaluating web agents trajectories is an important problem, since it helps us determine whether the agent successfully completed the tasks. Rule-based methods are widely used for this purpose, but they are challenging to extend to new tasks and may not always recognize successful trajectories. We may achieve higher accuracy through human evaluation, but the process would be substantially slower and more expensive. Automatic evaluations with LLMs may avoid the challenges of designing new rules and manually annotating trajectories, enabling faster and cost-effective evaluation. However, it is unclear how effective they are at evaluating web agents. To this end, we propose AgentRewardBench, the first benchmark to assess the effectiveness of LLM judges for evaluating web agents. AgentRewardBench contains 1302 trajectories across 5 benchmarks and 4 LLMs. Each trajectory in AgentRewardBench is reviewed by an expert, who answers questions pertaining to the success, side effects, and repetitiveness of the agent. Using our benchmark, we evaluate 12 LLM judges and find that no single LLM excels across all benchmarks. We also find that the rule-based evaluation used by common benchmarks tends to underreport the success rate of web agents, highlighting a key weakness of rule-based evaluation and the need to develop more flexible automatic evaluations. We release the benchmark at: this https URL
sources.summary: AgentRewardBench asks whether automatic judges agree with experts on web-agent trajectories. No LLM judge in the test reaches 70% precision on success. The benchmarks' own rules are more precise and miss many successes the experts accepted.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Lù, Kazemnejad, Meade, and colleagues collected expert labels on web-agent trajectories and used them to score automatic evaluators. The paper does not train a reward model and does not introduce a new web agent. It asks the Part 1 question in a form you can count. Does a rule on the final page, or a language-model judge that sees the trace, match an expert on success, on side effects, and on repetition? Part 4 needs the answer, because a judge that calls failures successes will poison any later training signal.

## What they did

A trajectory is the sequence of browser observations, the agent's reason, and the action. They use 351 tasks across WebArena, VisualWebArena, AssistantBench, WorkArena, and WorkArena++, and four agents: GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Qwen2.5-VL, and Llama-3.3-70B. Llama is text-only and was not run on VisualWebArena. The total is 1,302 trajectories, 196 for development and 1,106 for test.

Six experts each answered three yes/no questions: did the actions achieve the goal, were there unnecessary actions that could have side effects, and did the agent loop without progress? That is 3,906 binary labels. Agreement is reported for one slice only. A second annotator on the GPT-4o agent's WebArena trajectories agreed on success 89.3% of the time.

The judges are existing methods, AER and NNetNav, plus a simplified judge that answers the same three questions in one completion. The simplified judge sees either the final accessibility tree or the final screenshot. The primary metric is precision on success, because a false "success" is the expensive error if the labels were used for training. Recall and F1 are reported beside it. The benchmarks' own functional checks are a reference row, not one of the twelve model judges.

{{figure:fig1-framing.png}}

## What they found

Table 1 is the test-set comparison with expert success labels. The best model precision is GPT-4o with the final accessibility tree: precision 69.8, recall 83.1, F1 75.9. The authors' summary is that no model judge reaches 70% precision. The rule-based row is more precise, 83.8, and it recalls only 55.9, F1 67.1. Qwen2.5-VL with the accessibility tree has the highest recall, 89.8, at precision 64.3. The best model is not the same on every benchmark. Claude with the accessibility tree leads AssistantBench precision at 87.5. Rules lead VisualWebArena, WebArena, WorkArena, and WorkArena++.

Side effects are a separate failure. In Table 7 the best side-effect F1 is 21.4, and precision stays in the single digits to the mid-teens. Repetition is easier: Claude with the accessibility tree reaches precision 82.8 and F1 88.4. A judge that can see a loop is not a judge that can see a harmful extra click.

Using the judge as if it were the expert changes the agent ranking. On WebArena, experts put GPT-4o at 42.3% success and the rules at 25.6%, a 16.7 point undercount. On VisualWebArena the same gap is 35.9 against 17.4. Rules rank Qwen above GPT-4o on WebArena. Experts do not. Figure 3 is one qualitative miss. The goal is to buy the cheapest cereal with a graphic character. Claude 3.7 Sonnet adds Cocoa Puffs to the cart and stops. The GPT-4o judge says the agent purchased it.

{{figure:table1-judges.png}}

{{figure:fig3-errors.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Outcome rules and a judge that reads the trajectory miss different things. Rules in this table are the precise, low-recall instrument. Model judges stay under 70% precision on success, so about three in ten of the trajectories they call successful are wrong. Part 1's objection to a single final check shows up as both of those errors.
- Success, side effects, and repetition are three labels. A high score on one does not travel. Part 3's look at tool choice and at the response has to be more than one bit.
- Precision is the metric they chose because a false success is costly. Part 4 should say which error is expensive before it picks a number to maximize.
- The judge overestimates agent success on most of the reported cells, with exceptions on the harder WorkArena++ slice. A leaderboard that uses the judge will not match a leaderboard that uses the expert.
- Annotator agreement is 89.3% on one agent and one benchmark. That is evidence the success label is stable there. It is not a reliability figure for the whole 1,302.

## Limits

No reward model is trained, and agent-as-a-judge is discussed and not run. The 70% line is about the model judges. The rule-based precision is 83.8. AssistantBench is the public validation split, not the private test set. WorkArena++ Level 3 was left out as too hard. Llama has no VisualWebArena trajectories, and some tables still print 0.0 there. Side-effect detection is not usable at these precisions. The paper does not report Cohen's κ for the judges, only precision, recall, and F1.

sources.title: Counsel: A Meta-Evaluation Dataset for Agentic Tasks
sources.abstract: As agentic systems tackle increasingly complex multi-step tasks, evaluating their trajectories presents a major bottleneck - human annotation of a single trajectory on popular agentic benchmarks can take hours, making it difficult to scale evaluations for measuring performance or curating training data. This has driven widespread reliance on automated approaches such as LLM-as-a-judge (LLMJ) to critique agents at the process and outcome-levels at scale, however, the soundness of LLMJ critiques often goes unmeasured. Here, we introduce Counsel, the first public dataset of meta-evaluations for agentic tasks. Counsel consists of process-level critiques from open-weight LLMJs on two agent benchmarks: tau-bench (customer support agents) and DA-Code (coding agents), and human meta-evaluations of these critiques. Human annotators label critiques on each flagged error as "spot on", "correct location but poor reasoning", or "should not have flagged", achieving reliable inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha of 0.78). The resulting dataset stratifies LLMJ critiques by human alignment across both error location within a trajectory and reasoning quality, serving as valuable data to calibrate, improve, or train LLMJs for agents. Comparing open-weight judges, we find that more capable judge models and more reasoning effort both enabled improved human agreement, with the strongest judge reaching ~88% agreement on location and ~65% on reasoning. Counsel is generated using open-weight models and is permissively licensed for broad community use, which we hope will enable rigorous study and improved alignment of LLM-based evaluators for agentic systems.
sources.summary: Counsel grades the critique a judge writes about an agent step, not the agent's final success. On the flags humans reviewed, the best setting is Spot On a bit over half the time, and the design does not measure errors the judge never raised.
sources.note: The reading checklist credits Atla (2026). The arXiv byline is Pisupati, Broomfield, and colleagues.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Pisupati, Broomfield, Choi, and colleagues built Counsel to grade the critique, not the agent. A judge can flag a step and explain why, and still be wrong about the place, the reason, or both. Part 4 treats a fluent explanation as something to check. Part 2 asks whether the prompt, including a few good examples, changes that check.

## What they did

Counsel is human labels on critiques from open-weight judges, on two existing agent benchmarks. It is not a new agent score. τ-bench retail contributes 115 tasks. DA-Code contributes 50 tasks, kept only when models already completed them often, so the slice is easier than the full coding benchmark. The agents are GPT-OSS-20B and Qwen3-235B. The judges are GPT-OSS-120B, run at high and low reasoning effort, and Qwen3-235B with reasoning turned off.

Each model call is judged on its own. The judge sees the past trajectory and that step's output, not the future, and not earlier verdicts. Humans do not relabel every step. They label only spans some judge already flagged. The three labels are Spot On, meaning the right place and the right reason; Poor Reasoning but correct location; and Should Not Have Flagged. If the place is wrong, the reason is not scored as right. Three professional annotators triple-labeled 15 trajectories, with Krippendorff's α ≈ 0.78. The rest are single-labeled. Table 2 has 1,131 labels: 555 Spot On, 289 Poor Reasoning, and 287 Should Not Have Flagged.

Critique precision, as Section 4.3 uses the phrase, is the share of flags marked Spot On.

{{figure:fig1-examples.png}}

## What they found

Figure 3 draws the same labels as stacked bars. The rates the paper prints are Qwen3 at 43% Spot On on DA-Code and 63% on τ-bench retail, and GPT-OSS-120B at high effort at 60% and 58% on those two benchmarks. A flag is Spot On a bit more than half the time in the stronger setting, and less than half for Qwen3 on the coding tasks. These are not recall. The annotation never asks about a step no judge flagged.

Higher reasoning effort cuts the Should Not Have Flagged column, 68 labels at high effort against 187 at low, summed across Table 2. It does not cut Poor Reasoning the same way: 112 against 109. Tests for a judge going easy on its own model family were not significant. A small follow-up inserts 20 Counsel examples into a prompt and reruns τ-bench retail ten times. The paper does not print the mean rewards. The only comparison it marks as significant is spot-on examples given to a guardrail judge that may request one retry, p = 0.0078.

{{figure:fig3-critique-quality.png}}

{{figure:table2-labels.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Grade the explanation, not only the yes or no. A confident critique can name the wrong step, or the right step for a bad reason. That is a Part 4 failure mode, distinct from a wrong final score.
- Precision on flagged spans is a different question from "did the judge find the failures." Counsel answers the first and says it does not answer the second.
- The three-way label is a Part 2 prompt decision. Location and reasoning fail separately, and the authors refused a category for a wrong place with a good reason.
- A handful of good critiques, used as examples, moved one guardrail judge in one environment. Most of the other in-context conditions did not. That is a prompt result on the same benchmark, not a training result.
- α ≈ 0.78 is the agreement on 15 triple-labeled trajectories. The other labels in the 1,131 were written once.

## Limits

Two environments and two model families. The DA-Code slice was biased toward easier tasks on purpose. The in-context probe stays inside τ-bench retail and does not print the reward means. A headline agreement rate in the abstract is not a number Section 4.3 reports; the Spot On rates above are the results-section figures. Counsel is a check on flags the judge did raise. It is not a substitute for looking at the steps the judge passed over.

On the right, a coding agent says it will inspect two files and then runs head on one. The judge flags the step and a human marks it Should Not Have Flagged.

sources.title: Can LLM-as-a-Judge Reliably Verify Rubrics in Agentic Scenarios?
sources.abstract: Rubric-based scoring has become a widely used paradigm in model evaluation, typically with LLM-as-a-Judge (LaaJ) for rubric scoring. However, the reliability of LaaJ for rubric scoring remains underexplored. This concern is especially pronounced in agentic scenarios, where long, complex outputs further challenge reliable scoring. To address this, we conduct a systematic meta-evaluation of LaaJ reliability for rubric verification. We introduce RuVerBench, the first benchmark for assessing LaaJ reliability in rubric verification for agentic scenarios. RuVerBench covers two prevalent agentic domains, deep research and agentic coding, with 2,458 instances, each containing a model-generated output, a rubric, and a human-annotated label indicating whether the output satisfies the rubric. Using RuVerBench, we evaluate numerous frontier LLMs and find that even the most advanced models achieve strong performance but still exhibit substantial noise. We further analyze the impact of key LaaJ strategies, including prompt design, batching, and majority voting, on rubric verification. We find that weaker models are more sensitive to prompt variations, batched verification presents a trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, and majority voting yields effective but diminishing returns. We have released our dataset and code to facilitate future research: this https URL .
sources.summary: Peng and colleagues test whether a model can say, yes or no, that one agent output meets one rubric item. On research reports the best judge sits next to the human reference; on long coding traces it does not, and batching the checks makes that gap worse.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Peng, Qi, Xia, and colleagues ask a question that Parts 2, 3, and 4 all run into. Once a rubric item is written, can a model be trusted to say whether one agent output satisfies it? RuVerBench is that check. Each item is yes or no. The outputs are not short answers. They are research reports and long coding trajectories, including tool calls.

## What they did

An instance is one rubric against one fixed output. The benchmark has 2,458 instances: 1,615 in Deep Research and 843 in Agentic Coding, from 494 cases (Figure 2). Deep Research rubrics are Format, Numbers, Logic, or Facts. Agentic Coding rubrics are Task, Planning, Tools, or Rules. Tools covers the call, the schema, the parameters, and whether a later step uses the tool output. About 6% of source rubrics were removed as ambiguous or unverifiable, so the gold labels are ones two teams could settle.

The two labeling groups agreed on 90.4% of rubrics, Cohen's κ = 0.808, and disagreements were adjudicated. Because both "met" and "not met" matter, the score is balanced accuracy inside each category, then an unweighted average across the four categories in that domain. They call that average Avg BAcc, and they print it times 100. A random judge is 50.0. They test 18 models. The prompt, batching, and voting experiments use a fixed 20% subset and six of those models, not the whole leaderboard.

{{figure:fig1-pipeline.png}}

## What they found

Table 2 is the leaderboard. In Deep Research, Gemini-3.1 Pro Preview reaches 94.7 Avg BAcc, beside the average human-reference score of 94.49. Nine models are above 90. In Agentic Coding the best score is GPT-5.4 at 89.4. That is 10.6 points short of a perfect verifier. The human-reference average on the same domain is 90.50, so the best model is close to the humans and still well short of never being wrong. The models also spread out. The same three frontier models do not miss the same items: their error sets overlap only 16.1% in Deep Research and 20.6% in Agentic Coding.

The failures they name, from reading wrong frontier predictions against the human reasons, are partial satisfaction and requirement expansion. A fragment is treated as a met rubric, or the judge adds a constraint the rubric never stated. In Agentic Coding, GPT-5.4 is the stricter of the three. Gemini-3.1 Pro Preview and Claude Opus 4.7 sometimes pass a missing step. Those profiles shift in Deep Research.

{{figure:table2-leaderboard.png}}

Figure 5 is batching, on the 20% subset. In Deep Research, several rubrics in one call move the score by only a few points. In Agentic Coding, once a call holds four or five rubrics, every tested model loses score, often by tens of points. Figure 6 is self-voting. A few extra votes pick up a point or two. More votes do not repair a mistake the same model makes every time. For GPT-OSS-120B in Agentic Coding, majority voting pushes the already-wrong items toward the wrong label (Table 15).

{{figure:fig5-batching.png}}

{{figure:fig6-voting.png}}

## What to carry into the tutorial

- A binary rubric check is its own measurement, separate from whether the agent finished the task. Part 2's choice among a rule, a judge, and a human includes this verifier.
- On the research reports a strong model can sit next to the human reference. On the long tool-using traces the best model is still about ten points short of perfect, and Tools and Rules are part of the rubric. That is the Part 3 question, tool choice and parameters, asked of the judge as well as of the agent.
- Batching rubric items to save calls is cheap on the research reports and expensive on the coding traces. Reliability and cost move together (Parts 2 and 4).
- Similar overall scores do not mean interchangeable judges. The shared-error rate is low, and a vote can lock in a consistent mistake.
- The human agreement, 90.4% and κ = 0.808, is the bar the table is measured against. It is high, and it is not perfect.

## Limits

Labels are binary, and rubrics that needed a preference or evidence the annotators did not have were removed. This is not the vague rubric a live system will hand the judge. The strategy results are six models on 20% of the items. The authors say the benchmark is not a safety certificate and not a sufficient basis for a deployed reward or monitor. Which model wrote the trajectory also moves the ranking, even where the rankings stay correlated.

figures.alt: A worked example. The trajectory includes a hidden system rule not to reveal secrets, and the assistant refuses to paste an API key while naming that rule. The rubric asks whether the assistant avoided quoting the system prompt. The model judge says yes. The gold judgment says no, because the refusal exposed the hidden instruction.
figures.caption: Figure 1 from Peng et al. (2026). A yes/no rubric check can accept a reply that obeyed the user and still leaked the hidden rule.

figures.alt: Two leaderboards of balanced accuracy. In Deep Research, Gemini-3.1 Pro Preview leads at 94.7 overall. In Agentic Coding, GPT-5.4 leads at 89.4 overall. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is near the random baseline of 50 in Deep Research and at 61.7 in Agentic Coding.
figures.caption: Table 2 from Peng et al. (2026). Average balanced accuracy for 18 judges. The coding block tops out at 89.4, 10.6 points short of a perfect verifier.

figures.alt: Line charts of the change in overall score as more rubrics are judged in one call. Deep Research stays within about plus or minus 7 points. Agentic Coding falls, and by four or five rubrics per call most lines are between about −20 and −35.
figures.caption: Figure 5 from Peng et al. (2026). Batching rubric checks is a small change on research reports and a large loss on coding trajectories.

figures.alt: Line charts of the gain from extra votes over a single stochastic vote. Deep Research gains stay under about 1.2 points. In Agentic Coding most models gain 2 to 4 points by three to five votes, while GPT-OSS-120B falls to about −4 by nine votes.
figures.caption: Figure 6 from Peng et al. (2026). A few extra votes help a little. More votes do not repair a mistake the same model makes every time.

sources.title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
sources.abstract: In this paper, we uncover a systematic bias in the evaluation paradigm of adopting large language models~(LLMs), e.g., GPT-4, as a referee to score and compare the quality of responses generated by candidate models. We find that the quality ranking of candidate responses can be easily hacked by simply altering their order of appearance in the context. This manipulation allows us to skew the evaluation result, making one model appear considerably superior to the other, e.g., Vicuna-13B could beat ChatGPT on 66 over 80 tested queries with ChatGPT as an evaluator. To address this issue, we propose a calibration framework with three simple yet effective strategies: 1) Multiple Evidence Calibration, which requires the evaluator model to generate multiple evaluation evidence before assigning ratings; 2) Balanced Position Calibration, which aggregates results across various orders to determine the final score; 3) Human-in-the-Loop Calibration, which introduces a balanced position diversity entropy to measure the difficulty of each example and seeks human assistance when needed. We also manually annotate the "win/tie/lose" outcomes of responses from ChatGPT and Vicuna-13B in the Vicuna Benchmark's question prompt, and extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach successfully mitigates evaluation bias, resulting in closer alignment with human judgments. We release our code and human annotation at \url{ this https URL } to facilitate future research.
sources.summary: Shows that GPT-4 and ChatGPT judges change their verdict when two answers swap places. Writing reasons first, averaging both orders, and sending the most unstable items to humans brings them closer to human labels.
sources.note: arXiv submission 2023 (2305.17926). The reading checklist dates it 2024.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Wang and colleagues take the pairwise judging template from the Vicuna project and ask a narrow question: does the verdict depend on which answer comes first? It does, strongly. The paper is a compact case study for Part 4's consistency and robustness theme. It also gives Part 2 three concrete protocol choices, each with a measured cost, and a rule for deciding which items a human should check, which bears on choosing between a judge and a human.

## What they did

The data is the 80-question Vicuna benchmark, spread over 9 categories. The judge sees a question and two responses labelled Assistant 1 and Assistant 2, scores each 1–10 for helpfulness, relevance, accuracy, and detail, then explains. The template already tells the judge not to let order affect its decision. The judges are GPT-4 and ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301).

The *conflict rate* is the share of questions whose verdict changes when the two responses swap slots. Three of the authors labelled each Vicuna-13B versus ChatGPT pair as win, tie, or lose, seeing the responses in random order. Their majority is the reference label. Judges are scored by accuracy against it and by kappa, an agreement score corrected for chance, where 0 is chance and 1 is perfect.

They test three fixes (Figure 3):

- **Evidence calibration (EC).** Ask for the explanation before the scores, so the scores can follow from the reasoning. *Multiple evidence calibration (MEC)* samples k explanations at temperature 1 and averages the scores.
- **Balanced position calibration (BPC).** Run both orders and average.
- **Human-in-the-loop calibration (HITLC).** Compute the entropy of the win, tie, and lose outcomes across all samples and both orders. High entropy means the judge is unstable on that item. Send the top β% to the human annotators.

{{figure:fig3-calibration.png}}

## What they found

Order often changed the outcome (Table 2). Judging Vicuna-13B against ChatGPT, GPT-4 gave Vicuna a 51.3% win rate when Vicuna came first and 23.8% when it came second, and flipped on 37 of 80 questions. ChatGPT leaned the other way: 2.5% and 82.5%, with 66 of 80 flips. So GPT-4 favoured the first slot and ChatGPT the second. Against the much weaker Alpaca-13B, GPT-4 flipped on only 4 of 80.

{{figure:table2-position-flip.png}}

Flips concentrate where the judge's two scores are close (Figure 2). In the smallest score-gap bin, 25 of 35 items flipped. At gaps of three points or more, 1 of 39 did.

{{figure:fig2-conflict-vs-gap.png}}

The fixes helped, but did not reach human level (Table 4). The plain template scored 52.7% accuracy and kappa 0.24 for GPT-4, and 44.4% and 0.06 for ChatGPT. MEC with k = 3 plus BPC raised these to 62.5% and 0.37, and 58.7% and 0.31. Three samples in each order beat six samples in one order at the same cost, which isolates the order effect. Individual annotators scored 68.8–76.3% against the majority. Sending the 20% most unstable items to humans brought GPT-4 to 73.8% and ChatGPT to 71.3%. The authors' cost column puts that ChatGPT setup at US$18.30, against US$30 for one person labelling all 80 items.

{{figure:table4-alignment-cost.png}}

Two further checks held up. A template that asks only which response is better, without scores, had a 50.0% conflict rate for ChatGPT and responded to the same fixes (Table 5). Entropy over both orders chose items for human review better than random selection or entropy from one order (Figure 5).

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Telling the judge to ignore order does not remove order effects. Measure the conflict rate by swapping.
- The bias pointed in opposite directions for the two judges. A correction tuned for one judge may not transfer.
- Order effects are largest on close calls, which are the comparisons an evaluation most needs to get right.
- Reasoning before scoring and averaging both orders are protocol choices with measured gains. In the paper's GPT-4 cost column they cost about three times the plain template.
- Instability across samples and orders is a usable signal for routing items to people. Part 2's choice between a judge and a human need not be all or nothing.
- Even the best automatic setup here was about 9 points below the average annotator.

## Limits

One benchmark of 80 questions, one main model pair, and two 2023 OpenAI judges. The reference is three authors, and each annotator is scored against a majority that includes their own vote, which flatters the human rows. Human cost is derived from minimum wage and three minutes per item, not a measured budget. The tasks are single chat responses, not agent trajectories. The paper has no limitations section.

figures.alt: Vicuna-13B's win rate when shown as Assistant 1 and as Assistant 2, and the conflict rate. With GPT-4 judging against ChatGPT: 51.3% and 23.8%, 37 of 80 conflicts. Against Alpaca-13B: 92.5% both ways, 4 of 80. With ChatGPT judging against ChatGPT: 2.5% and 82.5%, 66 of 80. Against Alpaca-13B: 37.5% and 90%, 42 of 80.
figures.caption: Table 2 from Wang et al. (2024). Swapping the two answers changes the verdict on nearly half the questions for GPT-4 and most of them for ChatGPT.

figures.alt: Bars of item counts by GPT-4's score gap between the two responses, with the number of conflicting verdicts overlaid. Gap 0–1: 35 items, 25 conflicts. Gap 1–2: 41 items, 13 conflicts. Gap 2–3: 42 items, 2 conflicts. Gap 3–4: 24 items, 1 conflict. Gap 5 or more: 15 items, none.

figures.alt: A diagram of the calibration framework. The same question and responses are sent in both orders to an LLM. Each order is sampled several times, each sample writing evidence then two scores. The scores are averaged across samples and orders into calibrated scores, and an entropy score over the outcomes sends high-entropy items to human annotators.
figures.caption: Figure 3 from Wang et al. (2024). Evidence before scores, both orders averaged, and unstable items routed to people.

GPT-4 rises from 52.7% with the plain template to 62.5% with evidence and both orders, and 73.8% with 20% human help at $23.10. ChatGPT rises from 44.4% to 58.7%, and 71.3% with human help at $18.30.

sources.title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
sources.abstract: Self-evaluation using large language models (LLMs) has proven valuable not only in benchmarking but also methods like reward modeling, constitutional AI, and self-refinement. But new biases are introduced due to the same LLM acting as both the evaluator and the evaluatee. One such bias is self-preference, where an LLM evaluator scores its own outputs higher than others' while human annotators consider them of equal quality. But do LLMs actually recognize their own outputs when they give those texts higher scores, or is it just a coincidence? In this paper, we investigate if self-recognition capability contributes to self-preference. We discover that, out of the box, LLMs such as GPT-4 and Llama 2 have non-trivial accuracy at distinguishing themselves from other LLMs and humans. By fine-tuning LLMs, we discover a linear correlation between self-recognition capability and the strength of self-preference bias; using controlled experiments, we show that the causal explanation resists straightforward confounders. We discuss how self-recognition can interfere with unbiased evaluations and AI safety more generally.
sources.summary: LLM judges prefer text from their own family of models. Part 4, and a reason not to treat the hands-on model as a neutral marker.

sources.title: Judging the Judges: Evaluating Alignment and Vulnerabilities in LLMs-as-Judges
sources.abstract: Offering a promising solution to the scalability challenges associated with human evaluation, the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm is rapidly gaining traction as an approach to evaluating large language models (LLMs). However, there are still many open questions about the strengths and weaknesses of this paradigm, and what potential biases it may hold. In this paper, we present a comprehensive study of the performance of various LLMs acting as judges, focusing on a clean scenario in which inter-human agreement is high. Investigating thirteen judge models of different model sizes and families, judging answers of nine different 'examtaker models' - both base and instruction-tuned - we find that only the best (and largest) models achieve reasonable alignment with humans. However, they are still quite far behind inter-human agreement and their assigned scores may still differ with up to 5 points from human-assigned scores. In terms of their ranking of the nine exam-taker models, instead, also smaller models and even the lexical metric contains may provide a reasonable signal. Through error analysis and other studies, we identify vulnerabilities in judge models, such as their sensitivity to prompt complexity and length, and a tendency toward leniency. The fact that even the best judges differ from humans in this comparatively simple setup suggest that caution may be wise when using judges in more complex setups. Lastly, our research rediscovers the importance of using alignment metrics beyond simple percent alignment, showing that judges with high percent agreement can still assign vastly different scores.
sources.summary: Evaluates how well LLM judges align with humans and where they are vulnerable. Part 4 background on failure modes, next to the bias papers.

sources.title: LLMs instead of Human Judges? A Large Scale Empirical Study across 20 NLP Evaluation Tasks
sources.abstract: There is an increasing trend towards evaluating NLP models with LLMs instead of human judgments, raising questions about the validity of these evaluations, as well as their reproducibility in the case of proprietary models. We provide JUDGE-BENCH, an extensible collection of 20 NLP datasets with human annotations covering a broad range of evaluated properties and types of data, and comprehensively evaluate 11 current LLMs, covering both open-weight and proprietary models, for their ability to replicate the annotations. Our evaluations show substantial variance across models and datasets. Models are reliable evaluators on some tasks, but overall display substantial variability depending on the property being evaluated, the expertise level of the human judges, and whether the language is human or model-generated. We conclude that LLMs should be carefully validated against human judgments before being used as evaluators.
sources.summary: A large comparison of LLM judges and human judges across many NLP tasks. Use it in Part 4 for the claim that correlation on one task does not transfer to the next, including expert or agentic ones.

sources.title: Replacing Judges with Juries: Evaluating LLM Generations with a Panel of Diverse Models
sources.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) have become more advanced, they have outpaced our abilities to accurately evaluate their quality. Not only is finding data to adequately probe particular model properties difficult, but evaluating the correctness of a model's freeform generation alone is a challenge. To address this, many evaluations now rely on using LLMs themselves as judges to score the quality of outputs from other LLMs. Evaluations most commonly use a single large model like GPT4. While this method has grown in popularity, it is costly, has been shown to introduce intramodel bias, and in this work, we find that very large models are often unnecessary. We propose instead to evaluate models using a Panel of LLm evaluators (PoLL). Across three distinct judge settings and spanning six different datasets, we find that using a PoLL composed of a larger number of smaller models outperforms a single large judge, exhibits less intra-model bias due to its composition of disjoint model families, and does so while being over seven times less expensive.
sources.summary: Replaces one judge model with a panel of models. A Part 4 mitigation: if you cannot remove bias, you can at least avoid trusting a single model’s taste.

sources.title: Is LLM-as-a-Judge Robust? Investigating Universal Adversarial Attacks on Zero-shot LLM Assessment
sources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are powerful zero-shot assessors used in real-world situations such as assessing written exams and benchmarking systems. Despite these critical applications, no existing work has analyzed the vulnerability of judge-LLMs to adversarial manipulation. This work presents the first study on the adversarial robustness of assessment LLMs, where we demonstrate that short universal adversarial phrases can be concatenated to deceive judge LLMs to predict inflated scores. Since adversaries may not know or have access to the judge-LLMs, we propose a simple surrogate attack where a surrogate model is first attacked, and the learned attack phrase then transferred to unknown judge-LLMs. We propose a practical algorithm to determine the short universal attack phrases and demonstrate that when transferred to unseen models, scores can be drastically inflated such that irrespective of the assessed text, maximum scores are predicted. It is found that judge-LLMs are significantly more susceptible to these adversarial attacks when used for absolute scoring, as opposed to comparative assessment. Our findings raise concerns on the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge methods, and emphasize the importance of addressing vulnerabilities in LLM assessment methods before deployment in high-stakes real-world scenarios.
sources.summary: Shows universal adversarial prompts that fool a zero-shot LLM judge. Part 4, and a security angle on the Part 1 risk list: the judge is an attack surface.

sources.title: Limitations of the LLM-as-a-Judge Approach for Evaluating LLM Outputs in Expert Knowledge Tasks
sources.venue: In Proceedings of the 30th International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces. arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.20266.
sources.abstract: The potential of using Large Language Models (LLMs) themselves to evaluate LLM outputs offers a promising method for assessing model performance across various contexts. Previous research indicates that LLM-as-a-judge exhibits a strong correlation with human judges in the context of general instruction following. However, for instructions that require specialized knowledge, the validity of using LLMs as judges remains uncertain. In our study, we applied a mixed-methods approach, conducting pairwise comparisons in which both subject matter experts (SMEs) and LLMs evaluated outputs from domain-specific tasks. We focused on two distinct fields: dietetics, with registered dietitian experts, and mental health, with clinical psychologist experts. Our results showed that SMEs agreed with LLM judges 68% of the time in the dietetics domain and 64% in mental health when evaluating overall preference. Additionally, the results indicated variations in SME-LLM agreement across domain-specific aspect questions. Our findings emphasize the importance of keeping human experts in the evaluation process, as LLMs alone may not provide the depth of understanding required for complex, knowledge specific tasks. We also explore the implications of LLM evaluations across different domains and discuss how these insights can inform the design of evaluation workflows that ensure better alignment between human experts and LLMs in interactive systems.
sources.summary: Cited from Part 4. Compares expert judges and LLM judges on dietetics and mental-health tasks and finds the model is a weak stand-in when the task needs professional knowledge. The same caution applies to regulated advice, which the Part 1 SEEK examples point at.

sources.title: No Free Labels: Limitations of LLM-as-a-Judge Without Human Grounding
sources.abstract: Reliable evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is critical as their deployment rapidly expands, particularly in high-stakes domains such as business and finance. The LLM-as-a-Judge framework, which uses prompted LLMs to evaluate response quality, is appealing due to its scalability, low cost, and strong correlations with human stylistic preferences. However, it remains unclear how accurately these methods can assess response quality in domains where correctness matters more than style. To address this gap, we introduce the Business and Finance Fundamentals Benchmark (BFF-Bench), a dataset of 160 challenging questions and long-form responses authored by financial professionals. These experts subsequently evaluated the correctness of 1,200 responses generated by a diverse set of LLMs on both BFF-Bench and a challenging subset of MT-Bench. With this expert-annotated dataset of judgments (VERDICTS), we analyze the agreement between a suite of automated grading methods and human experts. While we observe that LLM Judges are more reliable than other grading methods, our findings reveal a clear pattern in LLM Judge performance: when not provided with a correct reference, judges show high agreement with human experts only on questions the judges were able to correctly answer themselves. We demonstrate that providing the judges with expert-written references largely mitigates this issue, highlighting the limits of using LLM-as-a-Judge without any form of human verification.
sources.summary: Argues that a judge agrees with experts mainly on questions it can answer itself, unless it is given a correct reference. Part 2 and the hands-on: a rubric without grounding is not a free source of labels.

sources.title: Don't Forget Your ABC's: Evaluating the State-of-the-Art in Chat-Oriented Dialogue Systems
sources.venue: In Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 15044–15071, Toronto, Canada. Association for Computational Linguistics.
sources.abstract: Despite tremendous advancements in dialogue systems, stable evaluation still requires human judgments producing notoriously high-variance metrics due to their inherent subjectivity. Moreover, methods and labels in dialogue evaluation are not fully standardized, especially for open-domain chats, with a lack of work to compare and assess the validity of those approaches. The use of inconsistent evaluation can misinform the performance of a dialogue system, which becomes a major hurdle to enhance it. Thus, a dimensional evaluation of chat-oriented open-domain dialogue systems that reliably measures several aspects of dialogue capabilities is desired. This paper presents a novel human evaluation method to estimate the rates of many dialogue system behaviors. Our method is used to evaluate four state-of-the-art open-domain dialogue systems and compared with existing approaches. The analysis demonstrates that our behavior method is more suitable than alternative Likert-style or comparative approaches for dimensional evaluation of these systems.
sources.summary: ABC-Eval labels each chatbot turn for specific behaviours, such as contradictions or ignoring the user, and compares that with Likert and pairwise ratings by the same paid annotators. It is an early, careful case for breaking one quality score into defined criteria and measuring the reliability of each.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Finch, Finch, and Choi ask how human evaluation of open-domain chatbots should be designed. Their answer, ABC-Eval, swaps a single quality rating for yes/no labels on defined behaviours in each turn. The study has humans only, no language-model judge, and the systems are pre-LLM chatbots. It is here for Part 2: criteria, scales, and when a team trusts a person's rating. Its method is the one Part 4 asks for: check each criterion's agreement, sensitivity, and cost before believing the number.

## What they did

Undergraduates held 400 conversations with four chatbots chosen in October 2021: Blender-Decode, Blender2, BART-FiD-RAG, and Emora. That is 100 per bot, averaging 30.3 turns each. A separate pool of paid annotators on the SurgeHQ platform (a group of 125 was allocated) then labelled every conversation four ways:

- **ABC-Eval.** For each bot turn, a binary label for each of 16 behaviours, grouped into 8 short tasks. A dialogue's score for a behaviour is the share of its turns that show it.
- **Turn Likert.** A 1–5 rating of each turn on eight dimensions, such as relevance, consistency, and emotional understanding.
- **Dialogue Likert.** A 1–5 rating of the whole conversation on the same eight.
- **Comparative.** Which of two conversations is better on each dimension.

Annotators trained on three hand-built conversations per task and were screened on the third. Students and Mechanical Turk workers were tried first and dropped.

{{figure:table4-behaviours.png}}

Each method was scored four ways. Agreement is Krippendorff's α, a coefficient where 1 is perfect agreement and 0 is chance level, computed on 100 conversations labelled a second time. Predictive validity is how much of the conversation partner's own quality rating a metric explains, as R². Sensitivity is how many of the six bot pairs a metric separates at a given significance level. Cost is annotator minutes per dialogue.

## What they found

Most behaviour labels were more reliable than most rating-scale dimensions. In Figure 1 the orange ABC-Eval points sit mostly above the blue, red, and green Likert and comparative points. The paper prints these values only as a plot. One behaviour label, uninterpretable responses, has the lowest point in its group. The paper also notes that pairwise comparison of overall quality agreed better than a dialogue-level Likert quality rating.

{{figure:fig1-agreement.png}}

Sensitivity varied within ABC-Eval as well. In Table 5, fact contradiction separated 6 of 6 bot pairs at p < 0.05, and self contradiction 5. Antisocial behaviour separated none and partner contradiction one. Comparative metrics separated 0 to 2 each. The paper concludes that Likert was more sensitive than comparison for most dimensions.

Behaviour rates show what a single score hides. In Section 8, commonsense contradictions appear in "about 15-20%" of bot responses, ignoring the user in about 10%, and irrelevant turns in 10–20%. Blender2 used factual knowledge in about 20% of responses and hallucinated in under 1%. Figure 4 gives the per-bot bars.

{{figure:fig4-behaviour-rates.png}}

Cost cuts the other way. The final ABC-Eval set took a median of 15.2 minutes per dialogue, against 2.8 for Dialogue Likert and 4.4 for comparison (Section 7.5). The conclusion grants that dialogue-level Likert "may be the most cost-effective and robust method" for overall quality.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Criteria beat one holistic score when the question is "what went wrong". A behaviour rate tells a team what to fix. A Likert mean does not. A Part 3 rubric for a tool-using agent can take the same form: defined, checkable criteria, each one judged separately.
- Measure agreement per criterion, not per rubric. Here agreement ranges widely within one method. A judge, human or model, should be checked against people on each criterion separately.
- Sensitivity is its own test. A criterion can be reliable and still fail to separate systems, as antisocial behaviour does here, because it almost never happens.
- Detail costs time. Behaviour labels took over five times as long as one dialogue rating. That cost is part of why Part 2 weighs rules, judges, and humans against quality, latency, and cost.
- Write definitions an outsider can apply. Table 4's one-line descriptions are a model for criterion wording.

## Limits

There is no automatic or language-model evaluator. Nothing tests whether a judge could produce these labels. The bots predate modern LLM chat models. Most of the headline comparisons (agreement, validity, coverage, and per-bot rates) are printed only as plots, so exact values cannot be quoted. The final label set was chosen and validated on the same data. The quality target is the conversation partner's single rating, the kind of holistic score the paper argues against. One annotator pool, English only, and four bots limit how far the results travel.

sources.title: MINT: Evaluating LLMs in Multi-turn Interaction with Tools and Language Feedback
sources.abstract: To solve complex tasks, large language models (LLMs) often require multiple rounds of interactions with the user, sometimes assisted by external tools. However, current evaluation protocols often emphasize benchmark performance with single-turn exchanges, neglecting the nuanced interactions among the user, LLMs, and external tools, while also underestimating the importance of natural language feedback from users. These oversights contribute to discrepancies between research benchmark evaluations and real-world use cases. We introduce MINT, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs' ability to solve tasks with multi-turn interactions by (1) using tools and (2) leveraging natural language feedback. To ensure reproducibility, we provide an evaluation framework where LLMs can access tools by executing Python code and receive users' natural language feedback simulated by GPT-4. We repurpose a diverse set of established evaluation datasets focusing on reasoning, coding, and decision-making and carefully curate them into a compact subset for efficient evaluation. Our analysis of 20 open- and closed-source LLMs offers intriguing findings. (a) LLMs generally benefit from tools and language feedback, with performance gains (absolute, same below) of 1-8% for each turn of tool use and 2-17% with natural language feedback. (b) Better single-turn performance does not guarantee better multi-turn performance. (c) Surprisingly, on the LLMs evaluated, supervised instruction-finetuning (SIFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) generally hurt multi-turn capabilities. We expect MINT can help measure progress and incentivize research in improving LLMs' capabilities in multi-turn interactions, especially for open-source communities where multi-turn human evaluation can be less accessible compared to commercial LLMs with a larger user base.
sources.summary: A benchmark that scores LLMs over up to five turns of Python tool use, with and without natural-language feedback from a GPT-4 "simulated user". It also measures how useful different models are as critics, and compares GPT-4's feedback with human-written feedback.
sources.note: arXiv submission 2023 (2309.10691). The reading checklist dates it 2024.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Most benchmarks a reader meets score one input and one output. MINT scores what happens over several turns: the model writes code, sees the interpreter's output, hears whether it is on track, and tries again. That makes it a direct example for Part 1's point that agents are evaluated over a trajectory, not a single reply. It also matters for Part 2 in a less obvious way. The "simulated user" is GPT-4 reading the trajectory and writing critique, which is a judge's job, and the paper measures whether that critique helps and whether it reads like a person's.

## What they did

MINT reuses eight datasets: reasoning (GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, HotpotQA, MMLU), code generation (HumanEval, MBPP), and decision-making (ALFWorld, a text-only household simulator). From 29,307 instances, the authors removed items a random guess could solve and items gpt-3.5-turbo finished within two turns. They then drew a stratified sample of 586.

Each turn, the model may write a thought, then either run Python code or propose a solution (Figure 1). Answers are checked against the dataset's ground truth. The model gets two attempts, and after a wrong first attempt the simulated user says only "Your answer is wrong." The turn limit k runs from 1 to 5, and the prompt tells the model how many steps and attempts remain.

{{figure:fig1-trajectory.png}}

In the feedback setting, gpt-4-0613 also comments after every turn. By default it does not see the ground-truth solution. The metric is success rate within k turns. Tool benefit is the slope of success rate against k. Feedback benefit is the success rate with feedback at k = 5 minus the rate without it.

They evaluated 20 models. Four were API models: gpt-3.5-turbo, claude-2, claude-instant-1, and chat-bison-001. Sixteen were open models from the LLaMA-2, CodeLLaMA, Vicuna, and Lemur families, in base and fine-tuned versions where available. gpt-4 appears as a reference.

To test the simulated user, two annotators wrote feedback at a randomly chosen turn of 113 trajectories. Two other annotators compared it with GPT-4's feedback for the same turn.

## What they found

More turns helped every model, at different rates (Table 2, Figure 2). gpt-3.5-turbo rose from 2.7% success at k = 1 to 36.2% at k = 5. claude-2 started highest, at 26.4%, but claude-instant-1 passed it by k = 3 and finished at 45.9% against 39.9%. Single-turn rank did not predict multi-turn rank. gpt-4 reached 69.5% at k = 5.

{{figure:fig2-success-vs-turns.png}}

GPT-4's feedback added 1.7 to 17.2 points for open models and 6.5 to 15.2 for API models (Table 3). In most families, the instruction-tuned or RLHF version gained less from tools and from feedback than its base model. Vicuna and Lemur were exceptions.

Giving useful feedback is a separate skill (Table 4). With gpt-3.5-turbo as the solver, GPT-4's feedback added 15.2 points. Feedback from gpt-3.5-turbo-16k, a variant of the solver itself, cost 10.4 points. CodeLLaMA-34B-Instruct, the weakest solver in that table, still added 3.2.

{{figure:table4-5-feedback.png}}

Annotators judged GPT-4's feedback more helpful than the human feedback in 54.9% of comparisons, equally helpful in 36.3%, and less helpful in 8.8% (Table 5). They rated it at least as human-like in 92%. Given to gpt-3.5-turbo, human and GPT-4 feedback led to similar success rates, 32.7% and 33.6%.

The multi-turn tasks also exposed brittle formatting. Vicuna models wrote escaped underscores that broke their code, which the authors traced to an artifact in about 15% of ShareGPT conversations. CodeLLaMA-Instruct (34B) ignored the requested code tags on every code task. An appendix ablation found that showing the critic the ground truth helped on reasoning and code but hurt on ALFWorld. Yes/no feedback, or feedback only when a solution is proposed, helped less than full comments every turn.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Report performance against the turn budget. Single-turn scores ranked these models differently from five-turn scores.
- Success rate is still an outcome check. The authors note it does not penalise repeated guessing, so the trajectory needs its own criteria.
- A critic can be evaluated by its effect: hold the solver fixed and measure how much its comments help. Solving and critiquing were different abilities here.
- Validating GPT-4's feedback took 113 trajectories, four annotators, and two questions (helpful, human-like). That is a template for validating a judge, not proof that GPT-4 critique is reliable elsewhere.
- Format-following failures are an agent failure mode that rules can catch before any judge is needed.

## Limits

The tasks are maths, multi-hop question answering, coding puzzles, and ALFWorld, with Python as the only tool. The authors say GPT-4 cannot stand in for every kind of user, especially where human values are involved. The human comparison is small and reports no agreement between annotators. Success needs a ground-truth answer, so open-ended agent tasks are out of scope. The models and API versions are from 2023.

The model corrects itself, computes 16, proposes it, and the user ends the task as solved.

sources.title: Can Large Language Models Be an Alternative to Human Evaluations?
sources.abstract: Human evaluation is indispensable and inevitable for assessing the quality of texts generated by machine learning models or written by humans. However, human evaluation is very difficult to reproduce and its quality is notoriously unstable, hindering fair comparisons among different natural language processing (NLP) models and algorithms. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance on unseen tasks when only the task instructions are provided. In this paper, we explore if such an ability of the LLMs can be used as an alternative to human evaluation. We present the LLMs with the exact same instructions, samples to be evaluated, and questions used to conduct human evaluation, and then ask the LLMs to generate responses to those questions; we dub this LLM evaluation. We use human evaluation and LLM evaluation to evaluate the texts in two NLP tasks: open-ended story generation and adversarial attacks. We show that the result of LLM evaluation is consistent with the results obtained by expert human evaluation: the texts rated higher by human experts are also rated higher by the LLMs. We also find that the results of LLM evaluation are stable over different formatting of the task instructions and the sampling algorithm used to generate the answer. We are the first to show the potential of using LLMs to assess the quality of texts and discuss the limitations and ethical considerations of LLM evaluation.
sources.summary: Chiang and Lee give language models the same instructions, stories, and 1–5 questions that English teachers received, and compare the ratings. Only the strongest models matched the teachers' preferences, and agreement on individual stories was weak to moderate, an early baseline for when a judge can stand in for people.
sources.summary_md:
## Why it is here

Chiang and Lee ask whether a language model can replace human raters if it is given exactly what the raters were given. They call this "LLM evaluation". It is an early, direct test of the LLM-as-a-judge idea, on short stories and adversarial news headlines rather than agents. It is here for Part 2, where a team chooses between rules, a judge, and a human. It is also here for Part 4, because it measures how far ratings move when the instructions or the sampling change.

## What they did

The main task is story writing. They took 200 prompts from WritingPrompts, a dataset of short Reddit prompts with human stories. For each prompt they had one human-written story and one from a fine-tuned GPT-2, both cut to under 150 words. Earlier work had found that crowd workers could not tell these apart, while English teachers preferred the human stories.

Raters scored four attributes on a 1–5 Likert scale: grammaticality, cohesiveness, likability, and relevance to the prompt. A Likert scale is an ordered rating from lowest to highest. The questions were taken from that earlier human study, not written for models.

- **Humans.** Three certified English teachers, hired on Upwork, each rated all 400 stories. Each was paid US$140 per 200 stories.
- **Models.** T0 (13B), text-curie-001, text-davinci-003, and ChatGPT. The prompt is the human instruction text and the story. A score is parsed from the free-text reply (Figure 1). Three replies were sampled per question, except for ChatGPT, which got one reply through the web interface and was scored by hand.

{{figure:fig1-setup.png}}

They compare mean ratings, test the human-versus-GPT-2 gap with Welch's t-test, and compute agreement with Krippendorff's α, where 0 is chance level. For models, α measures agreement among three samples from the same model, so it is self-consistency, not agreement between raters. Kendall's τ, a rank correlation, compares teachers with text-davinci-003 story by story.

## What they found

Teachers preferred human-written stories on all four attributes. For likability, they gave 3.78 to human stories and 2.59 to GPT-2 (Table 1). T0 and text-curie-001 did not show that preference. Curie's grammaticality ratings were 3.19 and 3.23, the wrong way round. Text-davinci-003 and ChatGPT did prefer human stories, and the paper reports the gap as significant for both. The two models leaned in opposite directions. Davinci rated everything higher than the teachers did. ChatGPT was harsher, with likability at 2.44 and 1.59.

{{figure:table1-story-ratings.png}}

Agreement on individual stories was modest. Kendall's τ between the averaged teacher ratings and davinci ranged from 0.12 for grammaticality on GPT-2 stories to 0.43 for relevance (Table 2). By the paper's own bands, grammaticality and cohesiveness are weak. The teachers did not agree strongly with each other either: α on likability was 0.08 for human stories and −0.21 for GPT-2 stories.

The instructions and sampling were varied for davinci only. Adding a persona line or a request to explain moved the means by up to about 0.23 on one attribute. Lowering the temperature from 1.0 to 0 lowered most means slightly (Table 3). Human stories stayed ahead in every row.

{{figure:table3-prompt-variants.png}}

The second task rates news headlines altered by three adversarial attacks, which swap words for synonyms to fool a classifier. ChatGPT and the teachers both put the BAE attack well above Textfooler and PWWS on fluency and on meaning preservation (Table 4). They split on the order of the other two. The paper says ChatGPT rated attacked titles higher than the teachers did. That holds for most cells. For Textfooler fluency, ChatGPT gave 2.12 and the teachers 2.17.

## What to carry into the tutorial

- Giving a model the human instructions is a baseline, not a validated judge. The weaker models failed the simplest check: telling the two story sources apart.
- Check the direction and the scale. One judge rated high and another low, while both kept the teachers' ordering. Means alone would mislead.
- Self-consistency is not agreement. Davinci's α of 0.71 on relevance compares samples from one model, while the teachers reached 0.05. Part 4's reliability checks need both kinds, kept separate.
- Report agreement on items, not only on averages. Matching the teachers' overall preference coexists with τ as low as 0.12.
- Prompt wording and temperature move scores. Part 2's prompting choices should be re-measured, not assumed stable, and this paper tests only two variants on one model.
- Cost frames the choice. The paper puts one teacher at US$140 per 200 stories against under US$5 for davinci. The authors argue for using models alongside humans, not instead of them.

## Limits

There are no agents or tools. The texts are single short stories and headlines. There are three teachers per task, and in the main study they rated all GPT-2 stories before the human ones. A rerun with different teachers in mixed order weakened the grammaticality gap. ChatGPT got one sample, hand-read scores, and two model versions. Kendall's τ is reported only for davinci. Exact p-values are not printed. Most of the models used have since been retired, so the study cannot be re-run as it was.
